# RF Sentinel: full site text

> RF Sentinel (also written RFSentinel) is a free, open-source (GPL-3.0) Android app that passively detects police and surveillance equipment from Bluetooth LE, WiFi, cell data and optional USB radios (RTL-SDR, HackRF, USB WiFi adapters, ESP32 boards). No root, no account, no analytics. Download: https://github.com/CIS-C0/RFSentinel/releases/latest


---

# RF Sentinel: Free Police Detector App for Android, No Root
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/

RF Sentinel is a free police detector for Android: body cams, patrol cars, Flock cameras, trackers, drones, fake cell towers, speed cameras, RTL-SDR and Android Auto. No root.

marcus@ctOS-2.0:~$ ./rf_sentinel --passive

## RF_SENTINELRF Sentinel - police detector for Android

RF Sentinel is a free, open-source police detector for Android. It listens to the Bluetooth LE advertisements and WiFi beacons around you and flags police and surveillance equipment: body cameras, Flock and other plate-reader cameras, patrol-vehicle gear, trackers following you, Remote ID drones and camera glasses. It also watches the cell network for fake-tower (IMSI catcher) signs.

RX ONLYNo root · no Termux · no account · no analytics · GPL-3.0 · Android 8.0+ (ARM, 64 and 32-bit)

Signed APK from GitHub Releases. Not on Google Play. Install guide · Q&A

### Police equipment it detects

| Category | Examples | How |

| Body cameras | Axon (TASER), Motorola / WatchGuard, Digital Ally, Zepcam, Vievu, Utility, Getac, in-car video | BWCDEVICE payload tag, company ID 0x034D, service UUIDs 0xFC81 / 0xFE6B / 0xFE6C, IEEE vendor prefixes |

| License-plate readers (ALPR) | Flock Safety, Genetec, Perceptics, Quercus, Tattile | Flock- SSIDs, Penguin- / FS- / FS Ext Battery BLE names, company ID 0x09C8, plus OpenStreetMap / DeFlock camera locations |

| Speed & red-light cameras | Fixed cameras mapped in OpenStreetMap | Offline map layer, warned about ~30 s ahead with the mapped limit |

| Audio sensors | Flock Raven gunshot detectors | 128-bit service UUIDs with short IDs 0x3100-0x3500 |

| Patrol vehicles | Two or more kinds of police-type gear moving together | RSSI correlation (Pearson r ≥ 0.6 over ≥ 8 s) across body cam, radio, in-car router, printer, rugged laptop roles |

| Public-safety gear | P25 / TETRA radio makers, in-car cellular routers (Sierra Wireless, Cradlepoint, Peplink, Inseego), in-car printers (Zebra, Brother), police radar makers, vehicle upfit, breath / drug screening devices | Company IDs, UUIDs, IEEE prefixes, Zebra factory-serial names |

| Trackers | AirTag & Find My, Google Find Hub, Samsung SmartTag, Tile, Chipolo | Separated-from-owner frames, then follow detection (default 10 min and 800 m with you) |

| Drones | Any ASTM F3411 / FAA Remote ID broadcaster (DJI, Skydio, Autel, Parrot...) | Decoded Remote ID over BLE and WiFi: serial, position, altitude, speed, heading, operator location |

| Camera glasses | Ray-Ban / Oakley Meta, Snap Spectacles, Vuzix, HeyCyan-based glasses such as Nilox Smart AI Glasses | Luxottica 0x0D53, Snap 0x03C2, Vuzix 0x060C, Meta UUIDs |

| Fake cell towers | IMSI catchers / cell-site simulators | Test MCCs, sudden 4G→2G, cloned or reserved cell IDs, unexpected networks (no root) |

| Card skimmers | Bluetooth modules inside gas-pump and ATM skimmers | HC-05 / HC-06 / HC-03 / RN42 / BT04-A names, serial-port service |

| Hacking tools (optional) | Flipper Zero, Pwnagotchi, WiFi Pineapple, deauthers, evil twin WiFi, Bluetooth spam floods, WiFi deauth attacks | Flipper IDs, Pwnagotchi beacon JSON, default network names, same network name from two makers with mismatched security, bursts of pairing pop-ups; with a USB WiFi adapter, floods of deauthentication frames knocking devices off a network |

| Emergency vehicles (V2X, Europe) | Police, fire, ambulance and safety cars broadcasting European car-to-car radio (ITS-G5) | An ESP32-C5 with the V2X2MAP firmware: the vehicle's role, light bar and siren state and its own position, and "emergency vehicle approaching" warnings. Not in North America (C-V2X) |

| Action & hidden cameras (optional) | GoPro, Insta360, DJI Osmo, YI, SJCAM, AKASO and other action cams; WiFi spy cameras in setup mode (V380, LookCam Pro...) | Bluetooth company IDs and services, maker prefixes, default camera and setup-hotspot network names |

| Two-way radios (RTL-SDR or HackRF) | Police, fire and EMS radios transmitting nearby: the North American public-safety bands, and TETRA handsets on 380-385 MHz (Europe and beyond) | Energy per 12.5 kHz channel on channels that are normally quiet, and TETRA's ~14 ms time-slot bursts; nothing is decoded |

| Police aircraft (optional) | Police, sheriff, state patrol, federal and RCMP / provincial police aircraft; unlisted aircraft circling low overhead | Community ADS-B feeds (adsb.fi / adsb.lol), and / or ADS-B heard directly by an RTL-SDR with no internet, matched against ~1,400 law-enforcement airframes from the FAA and Transport Canada registries |

| Waze reports (online, optional) | Police reported by Waze users, and any other kind you tick (accidents, hazards, road closures, traffic jams), inside an alert range you choose | Your own OpenWeb Ninja API key, or Waze direct (opt-in: sends Waze your IP address and a position rounded to a 1 km grid); scored by distance and age and re-scored every second as you move; third-party service, at your own risk |

Every match shows its evidence, its source and a confidence tier: weak (< 50), probable (50-79) or strong (80+). Full rules: how detection works and the signature reference.

### What happens to every packet

[ble] adv 00:25:DF:xx:xx:xx rssi -71 mfr 0x034D svc 0xFC81
[sig] TASER company ID .............. 60 (SIG)
[sig] Axon service UUID ............. 60 (SIG)
[oui] 00:25:DF Axon Enterprise ...... 75 (IEEE MA-L)
[fuse] noisy-OR, support x0.5 ........ 88 STRONG body camera
[grp] + Motorola radio + Cradlepoint router, r=0.74 over 12 s
[alrt] Possible police vehicle (3 kinds of gear) ... 70

Illustrative trace: actual scores depend on what each device advertises. The app logs the evidence the same way on each device's detail screen.

### Features

#### Live list, radar & map

Every device in range (each leaves 30 s after it was last heard on Bluetooth, 60 s on WiFi, adjustable) with vendor, type, radio, RSSI, rough distance and NEW / ★ / FOLLOWING badges. Flagged devices sort first. Filter chips with live counts, by kind too (vehicles, phones, computers, audio, cameras, routers, hotspots, TVs, smart home, Apple, other), and the list grouped by category. Show the list, the radar and the map one at a time or together, resizable.

#### Alerts

Sound, vibration pattern per tier (1 / 2 / 3 pulses), spoken announcements through the phone's TTS, optional radar-detector beeps that speed up as a flagged device gets closer, discreet mode, floating threat bubble over Waze or Google Maps with a pop-up saying what was detected. Radar-detector sound style with selectable alert effects and an optional intro.

#### Navigation

Turn-by-turn directions on the map: search a place (Home, Work, starred and recent places are kept on the phone, and starred ones can be renamed; or long-press the map), pick one of up to three routes, avoid tolls, highways or ferries, and go. A banner shows the next turn, lane arrows and the turn after it; spoken directions play as navigation audio so your music dips under them; it re-routes by itself, takes stops, and finds petrol, charging or food along your route. Your arrival time follows how you really drive. Open the destination in Google Maps or Waze if you prefer. No live traffic. The map goes to its night look after sunset.

#### Map & traces

A vector map (OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap data, or Mapbox if you prefer) with your GPS trace, devices placed where their signal peaked and flagged ones pinpointed from every spot you passed (with the circle they're very likely in), history heatmap and timeline, offline known-camera layer. Save a snapshot of the device list to look at again later. North up, heading up, or a 3D driving view like a navigation app that zooms with your speed, with the default zoom and angle in Settings; a light map and a readable night map with shops, landmarks and one-way arrows. Optional CCTV layer: street, shop and building cameras mapped in OpenStreetMap, with their view cones.

#### Android Auto

Police alerts on the car screen as messages read aloud (reply "mute"), and an RF Sentinel screen with threats, cameras ahead, recent alerts and Scan / Mute buttons. The full car app with live map and navigation runs on Google's Desktop Head Unit. Details

#### Auto start in the car

Starts when the phone connects to your car's Bluetooth or Android Auto, stops when you leave. It can also record a trace of every drive by itself.

#### Sentinel Link

Link RF Sentinel phones near each other over Bluetooth with a 6-digit code: each one shows what the others detect, external hardware included, on its list, radar and map, marked VIA with the phone's name, with full alerts. Encrypted, no internet. Phones far apart can share through Meshtastic LoRa nodes, watchlist matches first (not yet tested on real hardware). Details

#### Tools

Cell towers (serving and neighbour cells, IDs, channel, signal, history, optional map layer and change alert) and WiFi channel / spectrum analyzers for 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.

#### USB WiFi adapters

ALFA AWUS036ACS, AWUS1900, AWUS036ACM, AWUS036H, AWUS036NH / NEH, AWUS036NHA, AWUS036AXML / AXM, TP-Link Archer T3U and other RTL8812BU dongles - 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz on the AC adapters and 6 GHz on the WiFi 6E AWUS036AXML - in receive-only monitor mode over OTG, no root: no scan limit, longer range, devices connected to networks, and the network names devices ask for. The Bluetooth part of a combo adapter, or a USB Bluetooth dongle, adds a second Bluetooth LE scanner. Details

#### RTL-SDR and HackRF

An RTL-SDR dongle or a HackRF One on OTG notices two-way radios transmitting nearby, TETRA handsets by their time-slot bursts, and optionally cellular modems, from signal strength. It can also follow a P25 control channel (experimental: which talkgroups get a channel), play clear voice (analog FM, P25, DMR and NXDN; experimental, off by default; encrypted calls are never decoded), spot a vehicle following you by its tire-pressure sensors, receive ADS-B aircraft directly, with no internet, and shows a live radio waterfall of the watched bands (tap a signal to zoom in). The HackRF is used to receive only.

#### ESP32 boards

OUI-Spy over USB OTG or Bluetooth, GhostESP and Marauder over USB (dual-band on ESP32-C5, or through a Flipper Zero with a BFFB). The board's detections merge into the app. Details

#### Device details

Evidence, identity, decoded protocol data, signal graph, Locate mode (beeps faster as you get closer, keeps following a tag when it changes its address, and keeps going on the map, where a live read card shows the signal, rough distance and trend), history and the raw advertisement. Give a device your own name or write a note on it: the name shows in the list and on the map, and named or noted devices stay in the history. I saw it adds a device to your watchlist with what you say it is, including its Bluetooth advert pattern or WiFi probe fingerprint, so it's recognised next time even under a new random address. Search every device the app remembers, in range or not, by address, name, vendor, type, your name for it or your note.

#### Export

CSV, JSON, KML, GPX, GeoJSON. Match history and the watchlist are searchable. Everything stays on the phone until you export or share it.

#### 13 themes and a theme maker

Including DedSec (Watch Dogs 2) and fsociety (Mr. Robot) fan themes with animated terminal headers, Night Drive red HUD, Night Vision, Amber CRT. Make your own: colours, font, banner, header and map marker, and share it as a file.

### Compared with other options

| | RF Sentinel | Crowd-reported apps (Waze) | Phone's built-in tracker alerts |

| Price | Free | Free | Free |

| Open source | GPL-3.0 | No | No |

| Works where nobody reported | Yes, reads the equipment's own signals | No, needs other drivers | Trackers only |

| Account / tracking | None | Location shared with the service | Phone account |

| Install | Regular APK | App store | Built in |

| Bluetooth LE / WiFi signatures | Yes | No | Trackers only |

| Police / ALPR / body cam rules | Yes, sourced | User reports | No |

| Remote ID drone decode | Yes | No | No |

| Fake cell tower signs | Yes | No | Android 15+ only (network notifications) |

| Android Auto | Yes, alerts and a status screen | Yes | No |

Crowd-reported apps and RF Sentinel work well together: one knows what other drivers saw, the other hears the equipment itself.

### Privacy

- Receive-only. The app never transmits, jams, spoofs or connects to the devices it detects.

- No accounts, no cloud, no analytics. Detections live in a local database excluded from cloud backup.

- Network use: the map (vector tiles from OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap data, or from Mapbox if you pick it in Settings with Mapbox's own usage statistics switched off), camera data (Overpass API, DeFlock CDN), the roads of your area while the Waze option to alert only for reports on your road is on, and, when you search for a destination or start a route, Photon and Nominatim (place search) and Valhalla (routes), only when used. Those servers see your IP and the area or route, never your scans. Two optional sources are off by default: police aircraft (a position rounded to ~1 km goes to the ADS-B feeds adsb.fi / adsb.lol, unless you turn the online feeds off and use only an RTL-SDR's own ADS-B receiver) and Waze reports, either through your own OpenWeb Ninja key or straight from Waze (Waze direct: your IP address and a position rounded to a 1 km grid), at your own risk.

- Data leaves the phone only when you export or share it.

# What is RF Sentinel (RFSentinel)? Free Police Detector App
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/what-is-rf-sentinel.html

RF Sentinel (also written RFSentinel) is a free, open-source Android app that detects police body cams, plate-reader cameras, trackers and drones from Bluetooth and WiFi.

rf_sentinel / guides / what-is-rf-sentinel

## What is RF Sentinel?

RF Sentinel (written RFSentinel in its code and on GitHub, sometimes RF-Sentinel) is a free, open-source Android app that passively listens to the Bluetooth LE and WiFi signals around you and tells you when police or surveillance equipment is nearby. It needs no root, no account and sends none of your scans anywhere.

### What RF Sentinel does

Many devices announce themselves over the air all the time: body cameras, license-plate cameras, patrol-vehicle equipment, Bluetooth trackers, Remote ID drones and smart glasses. RF Sentinel recognises those signatures and shows them in a live list, a radar and a map, with the evidence for each, so you know what is around you and why it was flagged.

- Police and surveillance gear: body cams, Flock and other plate-reader cameras, patrol-vehicle equipment, trackers following you (AirTag, SmartTag, Find Hub), drones, camera glasses, and signs of fake cell towers.

- Known cameras on the map: speed, red-light and plate-reader cameras from OpenStreetMap, with warnings before you reach them, and routes that can go around them.

- Navigation and the map: turn-by-turn directions, a 3D driving view, a speedometer with the posted limit, and Waze police reports on your road.

- In the car: Android Auto support and optional ESP32 boards and USB WiFi adapters for more range.

It is receive-only: RF Sentinel never transmits to, connects to, jams or spoofs any device. See how it works for the detection logic and how to detect police with Android for a practical guide.

### Where to get it

RF Sentinel is downloaded as an APK from GitHub Releases (the RFSentinel repository), not from Google Play. The install guide covers allowing the install, updating in the app and what to expect. Its source code is public under the GPL-3.0 licence.

### Questions people ask

Q: Is "RF Sentinel" the same as "RFSentinel"?
A:

Yes. The app is called RF Sentinel; "RFSentinel" is the same name written without a space, as used in the GitHub repository (CIS-C0/RFSentinel), the package name and the code. Searching for either finds the same project.

Q: Is RF Sentinel free?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel is free and open source under the GPL-3.0 licence, with no accounts, no ads and no analytics.

Q: Is RF Sentinel on Google Play?
A:

No. RF Sentinel is distributed as a signed APK on GitHub Releases. The in-app "Check for updates" can download and install new versions for you once you have allowed it.

Q: Does RF Sentinel need root or a special device?
A:

No. RF Sentinel runs on an ordinary Android 8.0+ phone (64-bit or 32-bit ARM) using the phone's own Bluetooth and WiFi. External hardware such as ESP32 boards or USB WiFi adapters is optional and adds range.

Q: Is RF Sentinel safe and legal to use?
A:

RF Sentinel only listens to signals that devices broadcast openly and never transmits to them (the one exception is Sentinel Link, which you can turn on to share detections with your own phones). The rules for scanning and for using any alerts differ between countries and states, so check your local laws; the Q&A page has the details. This is not legal advice.

Q: Who makes RF Sentinel?
A:

RF Sentinel is an independent open-source project by CIS-C0 and contributors, developed in the open on GitHub. It is not affiliated with Flock Safety, Axon, Waze or any detection product it is compared with. Questions and bug reports are welcome in the repository's issues or on Discord.

# Flock You, OUI-Spy & Wardrive Go Alternative | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/alternatives.html

How RF Sentinel compares with Flock You, OUI-Spy, Wardrive Go, Fieldwatch, SØPHIA and AirGuard: a free Android police and Flock camera detector. Compare now.

rf_sentinel / guides / alternatives

## RF Sentinel compared with other surveillance-detection tools

There's a small, good community of tools for spotting Flock cameras, police gear and trackers. Here's what each one does, where RF Sentinel fits, and which ones work together. Short version: if you want one free Android app that covers Bluetooth LE, WiFi and cell signals, warns you while you drive, and can also read an OUI-Spy / Flock You ESP32 board, that's RF Sentinel.

### At a glance

| Tool | Type | Radios | Focus | With RF Sentinel |

| RF Sentinel | Android app, GPL-3.0, free | BLE, WiFi, cell (+ ESP32) | Police, ALPR, trackers, drones, glasses, fake cells, camera map, Android Auto | - |

| Flock You | ESP32 firmware, MIT | WiFi (promiscuous), BLE | Flock Safety cameras | Reads its detections through OUI-Spy's Flock-You mode |

| OUI-Spy / OUI-APEX | ESP32 firmware (+ OUI-APEX app) | BLE, WiFi | Watchlists, Flock, drones, foxhunting | Connects over USB or Bluetooth |

| Wardrive Go | Android app, GPL-3.0 | WiFi, BLE, cell | Wardriving maps, WiGLE / WDGWars upload | Complementary |

| Fieldwatch | Android app, MIT | WiFi, BLE | General receive-only field survey | Complementary |

| SØPHIA (s0phia ops) | Android app, closed source, sold | WiFi, BLE | Passive recon radar | Free open-source alternative |

| Flock-You for Android | Android app | Several, + Flipper Zero | Broad counter-surveillance | Different approach |

| AirGuard | Android app, Apache-2.0 | BLE | AirTag / Find My trackers | Overlaps on trackers |

| BLE Radar (MetaRadar) | Android app, GPL-3.0 | BLE | BLE monitoring, custom filters | Overlaps on BLE |

| Rayhunter | Firmware for a hotspot, EFF | Cell (modem diagnostics) | IMSI catchers | Use alongside |

| WiGLE WiFi Wardriving | Android app | WiFi, BLE, cell | Mapping and upload | Complementary |

### Flock You alternative for Android (and how to use both)

Flock You is open-source ESP32 firmware (MIT) dedicated to Flock Safety cameras. Its radio runs in 2.4 GHz promiscuous mode, so it catches Flock cameras' WiFi probe requests and SoftAPs that a phone's WiFi scan can't see, plus Flock battery-pack BLE adverts, and it beeps or feeds a GPS-tagged dashboard.

RF Sentinel brings Flock detection to a phone with no extra hardware: Flock- SSIDs, FS Ext Battery / Penguin- / FS- BLE names, company ID 0x09C8, Raven audio sensors, and the offline OpenStreetMap / DeFlock map with warnings before cellular-only cameras a radio can't hear. It also covers body cams, patrol gear, trackers and drones. Want both? Plug an ESP32 running OUI-Spy's Flock-You mode into the phone: RF Sentinel shows its Flock hits next to its own. Flock detection guide · ESP32 setup

### OUI-Spy app for Android

OUI-Spy is ESP32 firmware for the XIAO ESP32-S3 with Detector, Flock-You, Foxhunter and Sky Spy modes, a buzzer and LED, and a web flasher. OUI-APEX (lukeswitz's fork) runs those engines in one firmware and pairs with its own app.

RF Sentinel is an Android app that works with OUI-Spy boards: over a USB OTG cable, or wirelessly with OUI-SPY App-Controlled firmware (Settings → Pair OUI-SPY board). It switches the board's Flock, Sky Spy and Detector engines on while scanning and merges their detections with the phone's own (blue ESP32 badge), then adds its rules, patrol-vehicle grouping, alerts, camera map and Android Auto. How to connect an OUI-Spy board

### Wardrive Go alternative: detection instead of mapping

Wardrive Go (GPL-3.0) is an Android wardriving app: live maps of WiFi, Bluetooth and cell networks, WiGLE and WDGWars upload, USB monitor-mode WiFi adapters, channel and spectrum analyzers, Android Auto and Wear OS. It also flags Flock cameras and Axon body cams.

RF Sentinel is built for being warned rather than for mapping: sourced signatures with confidence tiers, evidence fusion, patrol-vehicle grouping, follower alerts, Remote ID decoding, fake-cell signs and warnings before mapped plate, speed and red-light cameras, with spoken alerts in Android Auto. Map for WiGLE with Wardrive Go; drive with RF Sentinel.

### Fieldwatch alternative for police and surveillance gear

Fieldwatch (MIT) is a receive-only WiFi and BLE observer for Android with customizable views, a filtering engine, an extensible signature library and reports, fully offline. A great general field-survey tool.

RF Sentinel shares the receive-only, offline approach and is tuned for surveillance and police equipment: alert tiers, patrol-vehicle grouping, tracker follow detection, drone and cell analysis, the camera map and Android Auto.

### SØPHIA (s0phia ops) alternative

SØPHIA is a closed-source passive BLE and WiFi recon app for Android sold by DetecX. RF Sentinel does the same kind of recon for free and open source, with police, ALPR, tracker, drone and fake-cell detection on top. Full comparison

### Tetra Hunter alternative

Tetra Hunter is a paid Android app that detects TETRA emergency-service radios with two RTL-SDR dongles. RF Sentinel does it for free and open source, with one dongle or more, a signal bar and beeps that speed up as you get closer. Full comparison

### Flock-You for Android alternative

Flock-You (Android) is a counter-surveillance app with broad multi-protocol goals (BLE, WiFi, cellular, GNSS, ultrasonic) and Flipper Zero integration. RF Sentinel sticks to what a phone's radios can verify, cites a source for every rule, and connects to ESP32 boards instead of a Flipper.

### Bluetooth-only and WiFi-only tools

- AirGuard (Bluetooth): AirTag / Find My tracker protection. RF Sentinel covers Find My, Google Find Hub, Samsung SmartTag and Tile, with adjustable follow alerts. Tracker guide

- BLE Radar (MetaRadar) (Bluetooth): BLE environment monitoring with custom filters. RF Sentinel adds WiFi, cell and a sourced police / surveillance rule set.

- nRF Connect / RF Party (Bluetooth): developer and research BLE scanners.

- WiFi analyzers (WiFi): access points and channels, no surveillance identification.

- Rayhunter (cell): IMSI catcher detection on dedicated hardware. RF Sentinel checks the signs Android shows without root. IMSI guide

- WiGLE WiFi Wardriving: mapping and upload.

Because RF Sentinel listens to Bluetooth LE, WiFi and cell at once, evidence from different radios adds up: a router, a radio and a printer moving together is flagged as a possible police vehicle, something a single-radio tool can't see. How grouping works

Descriptions of other projects come from their own public pages at the time of writing. RF Sentinel is independent and not affiliated with any of them; some of its prefix data was cross-checked with lists from Flock You, OUI-Spy, Wardrive Go, Fieldwatch and Flock-You for Android (thank you).

# Police & Camera Alerts on Android Auto | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/android-auto.html

RF Sentinel brings police and camera alerts to Android Auto: alerts read aloud, threats, cameras ahead and scan control on the car screen. Setup for the GitHub APK.

rf_sentinel / android-auto

## Android Auto

RF Sentinel is a driver-safe, template-based Android Auto app: what's around you, on the car screen, with alerts through the car speakers.

home
recent alerts
nearby devices
flagged devices
more
live map
known cameras

Demo data. These screens are the full car app, shown on Google's Desktop Head Unit; from the GitHub APK a real car shows the screen and alert messages described below.

### Screens

- Home, most important first (a car shows about six rows while driving): the threat headline (tap for the flagged devices), the next known camera on your way with its distance, recent alerts, the map, nearby devices and More. Start/Stop and a speaker button that mutes or unmutes all alert sound sit in the header.

- Nearby devices: the phone's filters with live counts (flagged, trackers, drones, favorites, new, Bluetooth, WiFi, ESP32 / USB). Each row says which radio heard it.

- Device details: Whitelist, Watch and Favorite; trackers get the phone's three ignore choices (it's mine, today only, pause follow warnings). Navigate hands drones with a known position to your navigation app. A device that has left still shows its last alert.

- Recent alerts: the last 40 alerts (devices, cameras, cell warnings), kept after the device is gone.

- Cameras: tap one to see it alone on the map, navigate to it, or tap its row to turn its alerts off or back on (faded on the maps).

- More: snooze alerts (5 to 60 minutes, set under Alerts on the phone), spoken alerts in the car, short spoken alerts, whether AirTags count as trackers, cell towers (fake-cell check status, serving cell and neighbours) and hardware status (phone radios and the scan watchdog, ESP32 / Marauder / Flipper on USB, OUI-SPY over Bluetooth, USB WiFi adapter).

- Live map: RF Sentinel's own OpenStreetMap map on the car screen with devices in list / radar colours, plate-reader, speed and red-light cameras, and your position. Drag, pinch or + / −; ◎ follows the car again. Needs car API level 7; older Android Auto gets car-drawn maps with device and camera lists.

- Navigation: Navigate to... starts from Home, Work, starred and recent places kept on the phone or a search with Photon and Nominatim (on submit only), routes with Valhalla, draws the route with next turn, ETA and distance, speaks turns and re-routes. The same navigation is on the phone.

- Alerts: heads-up cards on the car screen with Mute (the snooze length) and Ignore buttons, spoken through the car speakers as navigation guidance audio, briefly lowering music.

- Phone screen off: Android limits Bluetooth scanning then. The car warns you when a scan starts that way and shows "Bluetooth limited" on its home screen; WiFi, cell checks and known cameras keep working.

### The GitHub APK in a real car

Google lets apps built with its Car App Library, as RF Sentinel is, run in a real car only when they're installed from a trusted store (Google Play or ONE store). Android Auto's Unknown sources developer setting covers media and messaging apps, not these (Google's testing guide). So the GitHub APK doesn't appear in a real car's launcher, whatever its settings; its car screens run on Google's Desktop Head Unit emulator.

The GitHub APK still works in a real car, through the two app types that setting does cover:

- Open Android Auto settings on the phone and tap Version ten times to unlock developer mode.

- ⋮ → Developer settings → enable Unknown sources, then reconnect to the car.

- RF Sentinel screen (media-style): tabs for Threats, Cameras (nearest known cameras, the one ahead first), Alerts and Status (start / stop scanning, mute, cell towers, hardware), plus a card with the current threat and Scan / Mute buttons. It never plays anything, so your music keeps playing and keeps the steering-wheel buttons.

- Alerts as messages: every alert arrives as a message from RF Sentinel, which the car shows and can read aloud. Reply "mute" to snooze alerts (30 minutes unless you change it), or "ignore" to stop alerting about the latest device.

- If RF Sentinel is missing from the car's launcher, tick it under Customize launcher. The live map needs the full car app, so it stays on the Desktop Head Unit.

### Auto start

Settings → Start scanning automatically in the car: scanning starts when the phone connects to your car's Bluetooth or to Android Auto, and stops when you leave if the car started it.

### Navigation privacy

Photon, Nominatim and Valhalla see the search, your start and destination, and your IP address, only when you search or start a route. They never see your scans.

# Bluetooth Card Skimmer Detector for Android: Gas Pumps & ATMs
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/card-skimmer-detector.html

Check gas pumps and ATMs for Bluetooth card skimmers with an Android phone: HC-05 / HC-06 / RN42 / BT04-A modules and the serial-port service. Free, open source, on by default.

rf_sentinel / guides / card-skimmer-detector

## Bluetooth card skimmer detector

Many gas-pump and ATM skimmers carry a cheap Bluetooth serial module so the thief can download stolen card data from the car park. Those modules announce themselves with factory names. RF Sentinel flags them while it scans.

### What it looks for

| Sign | Score |

| A Bluetooth name starting with HC-03, HC-05, HC-06, RN42 or BT04-A | 70 (probable) |

| The Serial Port Profile service (0x1101) with no telling name | 50 (probable, low end) |

The Card skimmers category is on by default. Signatures follow SquachWatch's detection list, re-checked against the Bluetooth SIG and IEEE registries.

### At the pump

- Open the app while you pull up; it scans in the background.

- A Possible card skimmer alert near the pump means a serial module is broadcasting close by. Tap it → Locate: the beeps speed up as you get closer.

- If it peaks at a pump, pay inside or use another one, and tell the station.

### Questions

Q: Can my phone detect a credit card skimmer?
A:

A Bluetooth one, often: RF Sentinel flags its serial module. Skimmers that store data on a chip without a radio, or send it over a cellular modem, broadcast nothing a phone can identify: also check the card slot and keypad by hand.

Q: Can an HC-05 alert be something harmless?
A:

Yes. The same modules are used in hobby electronics, some car gadgets and industrial gear. That's why RF Sentinel rates it a probable match, not a strong one: what matters is where the signal peaks.

Q: How can I tell if a gas pump has a Bluetooth skimmer?
A:

Open RF Sentinel at the pump: Bluetooth skimmers often use cheap serial modules (HC-05 / HC-06 style) whose names RF Sentinel flags. Also check the panel seal and the card reader. No alert doesn't prove a pump is clean, because many skimmers have no radio.

Q: Is there an app like Bluetana?
A:

Bluetana was a university research app for finding Bluetooth skimmers at gas pumps. RF Sentinel does a similar check for anyone, free and open source: it flags the Bluetooth module names skimmers commonly use, along with its other detections.

# Remote ID Drone Detector for Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/drone-detector.html

RF Sentinel decodes FAA / EU Remote ID drones on Android: serial, position, altitude, speed and the pilot's location on a live map, with an overhead alert. Free, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / drone-detector

## Remote ID drone detector

Drones flying under FAA and EU Remote ID rules broadcast their identity and position in the clear. RF Sentinel decodes the broadcast and puts every drone and its operator on a map.

### Transports decoded

| Transport | Identifier | Score |

| Bluetooth LE (legacy and BT5 extended advertising, LE Coded where supported) | Service data 0xFFFA, app code 0x0D | 95 |

| WiFi beacon | Vendor IE, OUI FA:0B:BC, type 0x0D | 95 |

| Wi-Fi Aware (NAN), on phones that have it | Service org.opendroneid.remoteid, passive subscribe | 95 |

| Maker MAC blocks | DJI, Parrot, Skydio, Autel /28, Yuneec /28 and others | 60 |

### ASTM F3411 messages

- Basic ID (0): serial number or registration, UA type.

- Location / Vector (1): latitude, longitude, altitude, height, speed, vertical speed, heading.

- Self ID (3): free-text description.

- System (4): operator / take-off position, area count.

- Operator ID (5): registered operator ID.

- Message Pack (0xF): several of the above in one extended advert.

Message layout follows opendroneid-core-c (Apache-2.0).

### In the app

- Live map of each drone with heading, altitude and speed, plus its operator.

- Drone overhead alert (95) when one is within 200 m horizontally of you, once per drone per 5 minutes.

- Drone and operator positions open in your maps app; in Android Auto, Navigate hands them to your navigation app.

- Drones filter chip with a live count.

### Questions

Q: Can it detect DJI drones without Remote ID?
A:

Not their video / control link: DJI OcuSync is a proprietary wideband link a phone can't decode. DJI aircraft sold under Remote ID rules broadcast standard Remote ID, which is what RF Sentinel reads.

Q: How far away can it see a drone?
A:

RF Sentinel hears what the phone's radios hear: Remote ID over Bluetooth is designed for a few hundred metres in the open; phones with LE Coded PHY hear the long-range variant further. WiFi Beacon Remote ID usually carries further than legacy Bluetooth.

Q: Is that a drone over my house? Which app can tell me?
A:

If the drone broadcasts Remote ID, RF Sentinel shows it with its serial number, height, speed and the pilot's position on the map, and alerts when one is overhead. Drones without Remote ID (older, home-built or exempt) can't be identified this way.

Q: Is there a free drone detection app for Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel decodes FAA and EU Remote ID over Bluetooth, WiFi beacons and Wi-Fi Aware on Android for free, with no root and no account, alongside its police, camera and tracker detection.

# Flipper Zero, Pwnagotchi & WiFi Deauth Attack Detector for Android
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/flipper-zero-detector.html

Detect a Flipper Zero, Pwnagotchi, WiFi Pineapple, ESP deauthers, evil twin WiFi, Bluetooth spam floods and WiFi deauthentication attacks from an Android phone. Free, open source, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / flipper-zero-detector

## Flipper Zero & WiFi attack detector

Pocket hacking tools have identifiers of their own, and the attacks they run (Bluetooth pop-up spam, evil twin networks, deauthentication floods) leave patterns a receiver can spot. RF Sentinel's optional Hacking tools category watches for both.

### Devices

| Device | Identified by | Score |

| Flipper Zero | Service UUIDs 0x3081-0x3083 (one per case colour), company ID 0x0E29, IEEE block 0C:FA:22; name "Flipper ..." (60); STM32WB address only (30, a hint) | 85-90 |

| Pwnagotchi | The JSON in its WiFi beacon, with its name | 90 |

| WiFi Pineapple | Default Pineapple_ network name; Hak5 addresses (30) | 60 |

| ESP deauther | Default pwned network name | 55 |

### Attacks

- Evil twin WiFi: the same network name from two different makers with mismatched security (60).

- Bluetooth spam floods: bursts of new pairing pop-up adverts and fake-tracker floods.

- WiFi deauthentication attacks (needs a USB WiFi adapter in monitor mode): floods of unprotected deauthentication frames knocking devices off a network, with the tool's pattern where it has one (ESP32 Marauder, also on Flipper WiFi boards, sends only reason code 2).

Off by default: turn on Hacking tools under Settings → detection.

### Questions

Q: Can I tell if someone has a Flipper Zero near me?
A:

Yes, while its Bluetooth is on: it advertises a Flipper service UUID, company ID or address block that RF Sentinel matches at 85-90. With Bluetooth off it sends nothing a phone can see.

Q: Can an Android phone detect a WiFi deauth attack?
A:

Not with its own WiFi: Android doesn't hand apps management frames. Plug a supported USB WiFi adapter into the phone and RF Sentinel reads them in monitor mode, no root.

Q: Is there a Bluetooth spam detector for Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel flags Bluetooth pop-up spam floods (bursts of new pairing adverts and fake-tracker floods) and names the Flipper Zero devices it hears, on a non-rooted phone.

# Flock Camera Detector for Android: ALPR Alerts | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/flock-camera-detector.html

RF Sentinel detects Flock Safety plate-reader cameras and Raven sensors from their WiFi and Bluetooth, and warns offline before every mapped ALPR camera. Free Android app.

rf_sentinel / guides / flock-camera-detector

## Flock & plate-reader cameras

RF Sentinel finds Flock and other plate-reader cameras in two layers: radio signatures for cameras that broadcast, and an offline map of every plate reader, speed and red-light camera volunteers have mapped in OpenStreetMap, for the ones that don't.

### Layer 1: radio signatures

| Signal | Rule | Score |

| WiFi SSID | starts with Flock- | 88 |

| BLE name | FS Ext Battery | 80 |

| BLE name | Penguin-<digits> or FS-<hex> | 70, 80 with 0x09C8 |

| BLE name | starts with Flock (loose) | 55 |

| BLE company ID | 0x09C8 XUNTONG, alone (shared silicon) | 45 |

| BLE 128-bit UUIDs | short IDs 0x3100-0x3500: Flock Raven audio sensor | 80 |

| WiFi probe requests (USB adapter) | wildcard probes from a Flock radio-module block; with the Wi-Fi Alliance element 50:6F:9A:16 03 01 03 | 60, 75 |

| WiFi probe shape (USB adapter) | FlipDeFlock's candidate Flock shapes 42d75cd1, d0bbec4c; shapes common to phones never count | 35, 50 on a Flock module |

Sources: all-cameras-are-beacons field captures (ryanohoro, GainSec) and Bluetooth SIG assigned numbers. The SSID -FALCON suffix is deliberately not matched: the evidence behind it turned out to be circular.

### Layer 2: the known-camera map

- Automatic: for the area on screen, cameras tagged surveillance:type=ALPR plus fixed speed and red-light cameras are fetched once from the Overpass API and kept offline, refreshed weekly.

- Download nearby cameras: every plate reader within the radius set in Settings or the setup wizard (10-200 km, 100 by default).

- Download Flock: every plate reader mapped in the US and Canada, ~18 MB, about 143,000 cameras, refreshed weekly on WiFi. Uses DeFlock's hourly snapshot, then adds cameras it leaves out (other tagging, Flock cameras mapped as ordinary cameras) straight from OpenStreetMap.

While scanning, you're warned once per camera per 30 minutes when one is within about 20 s of travel (150 m minimum, 600 m maximum) and two GPS fixes show you getting closer. Speed cameras warn about 30 s ahead with the mapped limit. Where OpenStreetMap has the camera's direction, a cone in its colour shows which way it faces when you zoom in; while you're moving, a camera facing across your road (watching a cross street) doesn't warn, while one facing you or away (front or rear plates) does. Tap a camera → Ignore alerts to silence it for good, or Set direction when its direction isn't mapped (kept on your phone only).

### Why the map matters

Most plate readers that aren't Flock (Genetec AutoVu, Motorola Vigilant, Perceptics, Quercus, Tattile) send their data over cellular modems or wired links and broadcast nothing a phone can match. The map layer is the only way a phone can warn about those. If a camera near you is missing, add it to OpenStreetMap, for example through DeFlock.

### Questions

Q: How close do I need to be to detect a Flock camera by radio?
A:

Close: Flock units' WiFi and BLE are low-power and often only heard within tens of metres, depending on the install. RF Sentinel's camera map layer warns from further away.

Q: Does the camera download reveal my location?
A:

When RF Sentinel downloads cameras, the Overpass API and DeFlock's CDN see your IP and the area requested (DeFlock: which 20° region), like map tiles. Turn off Show known cameras automatically to fetch only when you tap a download.

Q: Can I export where I've seen Flock cameras?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's recorded traces export as GPX, KML, GeoJSON or CSV with the devices heard along them, including flagged-only.

Q: Is there an app that detects Flock cameras?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel is a free, open-source Android app that detects Flock Safety cameras and Raven sensors from their WiFi and Bluetooth, and warns offline before every plate reader mapped on OpenStreetMap through DeFlock. No root, no account.

Q: Can RF Sentinel tell me if my plate was read or searched?
A:

No. Plate reads and searches stay in the camera company's and police systems, and no app can see them from the road. RF Sentinel tells you where the cameras are and alerts as you approach one, so you know when you pass one. Public-records requests for audit logs are the way to learn about searches.

Q: How do I avoid Flock cameras while driving?
A:

Turn on Avoid plate readers in RF Sentinel's built-in navigation: it plans the route around the known cameras and says how many are left on it. A camera on the only way in or out can't be avoided, and RF Sentinel still warns about 20 seconds before it. See routes that avoid cameras.

Q: Can I get Flock camera alerts on Android Auto?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel reads plate-reader and camera alerts aloud through the car. See Android Auto for what shows on the car screen and how to set it up.

Q: Can I use an ESP32 Flock detector like Flock You or OUI-Spy with my phone?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel reads Flock You and OUI-Spy ESP32 boards connected to the phone and merges what they hear with its own detections and alerts. See ESP32 boards.

# GPS Jammer & Spoofing Detector for Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/gps-jammer-detector.html

Spot GPS jamming and spoofing with an Android phone: receiver noise (AGC), satellite strength across GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, QZSS and NavIC, clock and position jumps. Passive, free, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / gps-jammer-detector

## GPS jammer & spoofing detector

A phone's satellite receiver already reports the strength and position of every satellite it tracks, and on many phones its input noise. RF Sentinel reads that and warns when it looks like a jammer or a spoofer nearby. Nothing is transmitted.

### Jamming signs

- GNSS jamming signs: the receiver's noise (AGC) rises by 10 dB or more while every satellite weakens by 8 dB or more, held for 4 s (60, or 75 from a 15 dB rise). A tunnel or a garage weakens the satellites too but doesn't raise the noise, so it isn't mistaken for jamming. A cheap "GPS blocker" in a vehicle is the usual cause.

- On phones that don't report AGC, a sudden total loss of every system after a clear sky is only a weak sign.

### Spoofing signs

- Every satellite equally strong whatever its height in the sky (one transmitter), held 15 s, only when the satellites are spread over the sky.

- Only GPS left while GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou vanish right after being heard: cheap spoofers fake GPS only.

- The GPS clock drifting 60 s or more from the network-set clock over 3 fixes.

- A position jump faster than 340 m/s that the next fixes confirm. Rough fixes are skipped.

Covers every system the phone hears: GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, QZSS, NavIC and SBAS. Tools → Satellites shows each satellite's signal and the receiver noise. On by default; it listens whenever something already uses GPS (the map, a trace, camera warnings or the Satellites screen) and never turns GPS on by itself. These are signs, not proof.

### Questions

Q: Can an Android phone detect a GPS jammer?
A:

Often, yes. Phones that report the receiver's AGC let RF Sentinel tell a jammer (noise up, satellites down) from a roof or tunnel (satellites down, noise unchanged). Phones without AGC only get a weak sign on a total loss.

Q: Can it tell if a GPS tracker on my car is being jammed?
A:

RF Sentinel notices jamming around your phone, wherever it comes from: a jammer in your own or a nearby vehicle shows up the same way. To find a tracker itself, see the tracker detector.

Q: Can my phone detect GPS spoofing?
A:

RF Sentinel watches for the signs: only GPS left while GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou vanish right after being heard (cheap spoofers fake GPS only), a position jumping faster than an aircraft could fly, and the GPS clock drifting 60 s or more from the network clock. Each is a sign, not proof.

---

# RF Sentinel Hardware Internals: RTL-SDR, P25, USB WiFi Drivers
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/hardware-technical.html

How RF Sentinel drives RTL-SDR, HackRF and rtl_tcp, the radio sweep, P25 decoding, ADS-B, USB WiFi monitor mode, USB Bluetooth HCI, ESP32 protocols, V2X and Sentinel Link.

rf_sentinel / hardware / internals

## How the external hardware works

What RF Sentinel does with each radio you plug in, down to sample rates, frame formats and thresholds. Every number here is a constant in the public source; file names point at the Kotlin classes under app/src/main/java/com/rfsentinel/app/. Which hardware to buy is on External hardware.

- Ground rules

- SDR basics

- RTL-SDR driver

- HackRF One

- Network SDR (rtl_tcp)

- Modes, turns and the waterfall

- Radio activity sweep

- Cellular uplink

- TETRA bursts

- P25 control channel

- P25 voice (experimental)

- ADS-B aircraft

- USB WiFi monitor mode

- USB Bluetooth

- ESP32 boards over USB

- OUI-Spy over Bluetooth

- V2X emergency vehicles

- Sentinel Link and Meshtastic

- Limits

- Questions

### Ground rules

- Receive only. Only the features whose job is to send (Sentinel Link, Meshtastic, and an OUI-SPY board relaying every network, which sends probe requests) transmit. No driver here does: the HackRF's transmitter, amplifier and antenna bias stay off, the rtl_tcp bias-T is set off, the WiFi drivers have every transmit path removed (no injection, no deauth, no handshake or PMKID capture), and USB Bluetooth never advertises or connects.

- No root, no kernel driver. Every USB device is driven from the app through Android's USB host API (UsbManager, control and bulk transfers). Android asks you once per device for permission.

- No decryption. Encrypted P25 calls, WPA traffic and TETRA are never decoded. Radio scanning measures energy, timing and clear signalling only.

- Nothing leaves the phone unless you turn on something that says so (RadioReference lookups, Sentinel Link, Meshtastic).

### SDR basics

An SDR (software-defined radio) is a tuner plus an analogue-to-digital converter: it hands the app a stream of I/Q samples, pairs of numbers that describe the amplitude and phase of everything within a slice of spectrum around the tuned frequency. The app does all filtering and decoding in software (sdr/SdrRadio.kt).

| Setting | Value |

| Sample rate | 2.048 MS/s (2 MS/s for ADS-B), so each tune sees about 2 MHz of spectrum |

| Gain | Fixed 29.7 dB for sweeps and P25; 49.6 dB (the tuner's maximum) for ADS-B. No AGC, so levels are comparable over time |

| USB read | 16 KB (8192 complex samples), about 4 ms of signal each; 8 reads per tuned chunk (16 for TETRA, to see whole frames) |

| Stalled stream | After 8 empty chunks the stream is reset, as librtlsdr's reset_buffer does |

| Unplug detection | The device is checked every couple of seconds; a USB SDR plugged in takes over from a network SDR |

Driver messages go into each piece of hardware's own log (Settings › External hardware › Export a hardware log, or Export all hardware logs for one file), without positions.

### RTL-SDR driver

sdr/RtlSdr.kt is a Kotlin port of osmocom's librtlsdr (GPL-2.0-or-later) for the RTL2832U demodulator chip with an R820T, R820T2, R860 or R828D tuner.

- Tuner access: the tuner sits behind the RTL2832U on I²C; every register write goes through the RTL2832U's I²C repeater with 3 retries, and the driver keeps shadow copies of the tuner registers so partial writes don't need a read-back.

- Low IF, not zero IF: the R82xx tuners mix the signal to a 3.57 MHz intermediate frequency, which the RTL2832U shifts back to baseband with spectrum inversion. That avoids the DC spike zero-IF tuners put in the middle of the spectrum.

- IF filter chosen to match the sample rate (0.9 to 3.2 MS/s supported).

- RTL-SDR Blog V4: an R828D with a 28.8 MHz crystal and an input band switch; its notch filters are turned off inside the FM and DAB bands as the RTL-SDR Blog code does.

- Gone: after 25 control transfers in a row fail, the dongle is treated as unplugged and released.

### HackRF One

sdr/HackRf.kt speaks libhackrf's USB vendor requests, receive only: amplifier off, antenna port power off, sample rate 2 to 20 MS/s. The HackRF sends signed 8-bit I/Q; it is converted to the RTL-SDR's unsigned format so the rest of the code is shared. About 48 KB of samples still in flight after a retune are dropped, so they don't land in the wrong channel.

### Network SDR (rtl_tcp)

Settings › RTL-SDR radio › Network SDR reads an RTL-SDR plugged into another device on your WiFi, such as a computer running rtl_tcp (default port 1234 if left out) (sdr/RtlTcp.kt).

- The server first sends a 12-byte header starting with RTL0 (tuner type and gain count).

- Each command is 1 byte plus a 32-bit big-endian value: 0x01 frequency, 0x02 sample rate, 0x03 gain mode, 0x04 gain, 0x08 AGC, 0x0E bias-T (always sent as off).

- Samples are the same unsigned 8-bit I/Q as over USB, about 5 MB/s of WiFi, so use a fast local network.

- A lost connection is retried every 10 s, and a USB SDR plugged into the phone is used first. rtl_tcp has no password: only run it on a network you trust.

### Modes, turns and the waterfall

Settings › RTL-SDR radio has four uses: radio sweep, ADS-B, P25 and pagers. One dongle can only listen to one frequency range at a time, so with more than one ticked the SDR takes turns: 60 s each by default, 30 to 300 s per scan.

The live waterfall (Tools › Radio waterfall, sdr/SdrWaterfall.kt) shows each sweep as one row. Zoom in on a few channels and it switches to a tuned view (4 reads per row, up to about 25 rows per second); the sweep and ADS-B pause while you look. Tune › Listen demodulates the zoomed frequency (AM for aircraft, wide FM for broadcast, narrow FM otherwise) to the media speaker.

Find a remote's frequency hops ten centres where remotes send (300, 303.875, 310, 315, 318, 390, 418, 433.92, 868.35 and 915 MHz), about 60 ms each. A peak counts when it stands 15 dB above the median noise in at least 2 of the look's 15 spectra; peaks within 30 kHz are one signal. The first two rounds, before you press, learn the signals already on the air (sensors, data) and those are never shown. The strongest signal stays on screen for 3 s.

### Radio activity sweep

sdr/RadioWatch.kt answers one question: is someone transmitting on a public-safety channel near me? It measures energy only. Nothing is demodulated, unless Play voice transmissions is on: then the first new transmission of a chunk is tuned to (its spectrum peak, not the 12.5 kHz grid) and played, as narrow FM with a squelch, or as P25 voice when the identification listen heard P25. Back to the sweep after 1.5 s of closed squelch (P25: the call's end) or 60 s.

- The tuner steps across each band. Every chunk is cut into 1024-point FFTs with a Hann window, averaged and shifted so 0 Hz is in the middle.

- Only the middle ±800 kHz of each 2 MHz chunk is used (the edges are filtered off), and ±15 kHz around the centre is ignored for DC leakage.

- The spectrum is grouped into 12.5 kHz channels. The noise floor is the median of the chunk; a channel's SNR is its peak above that median.

- A channel at or above the sensitivity (default 30 dB, settable 6 to 50 dB) is a candidate; 12 dB counts as "active" for learning.

- Splatter: a strong transmitter spills into its neighbours, so candidates within 37.5 kHz of each other are merged and only the strongest is kept.

- Busy-channel learning: the last 32 visits of every channel are kept. A channel active on 40 % or more of them (after at least 6 visits) is a busy local channel (a repeater, a paging tower, data) and is never reported. No alerts during the first 6 sweeps, while it learns.

- The same channel alerts again only after 120 s.

| Band | Range | Note |

| 700 MHz public safety | 799-805 MHz | Narrowband public-safety channels |

| 800 MHz | 806-813.9 MHz | Mobile and portable transmit side |

| VHF high | 150.8-174 MHz | Shared with business and other users |

| UHF | 450-470 MHz | Shared with business and other users |

Always skipped: MURS, marine VHF, railroad, NOAA weather, FRS / GMRS and paging frequencies, and any range you exclude. Frequencies you add as targets skip the learning and alert straight away. A hit is "a radio transmitted nearby", not "police": VHF and UHF are shared, which is why the default sensitivity is high.

### Cellular uplink

Detect cellular transmitters (experimental, off by default). Phones transmit on the uplink half of each LTE band; a sudden crowd of uplink energy around you (many phones, or a vehicle's modem) can be measured without decoding anything. The same sweep looks at about 1.6 MHz slices of the uplink bands 71, 12/17, 13, 14 (FirstNet), 5/26 and part of 4/66, learns each slice's quiet level (a slow average, alpha 0.1) and flags a rise of 8 dB or more. Downlinks (towers) are left out on purpose: they are always on.

### TETRA bursts

TETRA (used by police in Europe and elsewhere) is TDMA: a handset transmits in one 14.17 ms slot of a 56.67 ms frame. On the 380-385 MHz handset band (the 390-395 MHz base stations are left out), the app reads 16 USB blocks per tune, measures energy in 2 ms steps and calls a channel TDMA when it is on for runs of 0.5 to 2 slots, quiet at least a third of the time and on no more than 60 %. That rhythm is TETRA's fingerprint; the content is never decoded.

### P25 control channel

A P25 trunked system has one control channel that tells radios which voice channel to use for each call. RF Sentinel decodes that signalling (experimental), which shows which talkgroups are active, without listening to calls. The chain follows TIA-102.BAAA and the open-source OP25 project.

- Hunt (sdr/P25Hunt.kt): sweeps the 769-775 and 851-869 MHz downlinks, tries the strongest channels first and keeps the first one whose messages pass their CRC. No ppm calibration is needed: the demodulator's frequency loop follows the dongle's drift. If nothing is found it tries again after 30 s.

- Demodulate (sdr/P25Demod.kt): mixes the 12.5 kHz channel to 0 Hz, decimates by integrate-and-dump to 48 kS/s, low-pass filters, then an FM discriminator gives the C4FM signal (4 levels, 4800 symbols/s, 2 bits each). The 48-bit frame sync 0x5575F5FF77FF (24 symbols) sets symbol timing, the ±3 level and the DC offset.

- Frame (sdr/P25Frame.kt): removes the status symbol after every 35 data symbols, corrects the Network ID with BCH(63,16,23) (up to 11 bit errors), then takes each TSBK block (98 symbols), de-interleaves it, decodes the rate-1/2 trellis code with a Viterbi decoder and checks its CRC.

- Messages (sdr/P25Tsbk.kt): standard (MFID 0) messages only.

| Opcode | Message | Used for |

| 0x00 | Group voice channel grant | A talkgroup got a voice channel: the log entry |

| 0x02 | Grant update | Calls still running |

| 0x28 | Group affiliation response | A radio joined a talkgroup |

| 0x3D, 0x34 | Identifier update | Turns channel numbers into frequencies |

| 0x3A, 0x3B | RFSS / network status | Site and system identity |

| 0x3C | Adjacent site | Neighbour sites |

Input check: 400 ms after a grant, at most every 5 s, the app tunes for about 70 ms to the voice channel's input (the frequency the radios transmit on). Energy there means a radio transmitting close to you, not just somewhere on the system.

Talkgroup names (optional, off by default, US only, sdr/RadioReference.kt): with your own RadioReference Premium login and developer key (stored encrypted on the phone), the app looks up the FCC-licensed system around you. It sends a position rounded to about 1 km, at most once a day per area.

### P25 voice (experimental)

With Listen to P25 voice (Off, Watched talkgroups or All clear calls), the app follows a clear (unencrypted) call's grant to the voice channel (sdr/P25Follow.kt), one call at a time, and misses control-channel messages meanwhile. It gives up if no voice frame arrives in 1.5 s, ends after 1 s of quiet and stops at 120 s.

- Frames (sdr/P25Voice.kt): LDU1 / LDU2 frames (840 symbols after the sync) carry nine IMBE codewords each. Each codeword is de-interleaved, error-corrected (Golay(23,12), PN descrambling, Hamming(15,11)) into 88 bits. The algorithm ID must be 0x80 (clear); any encrypted call is skipped.

- Vocoder (sdr/ImbeDecoder.kt): a Kotlin port of mbelib's IMBE 4400 decoder; each 20 ms frame becomes 160 samples at 8 kHz. A damaged frame repeats the last good one, at most 3 times.

- Record P25 voice calls (sdr/P25Record.kt, for testing): the raw radio signal of a clear call as a 6 s two-channel 16-bit I/Q WAV at 48 kS/s (about 1 MB), at most one every 20 s, the last 20 kept on the phone. Nothing in the file is decoded.

- Save played calls (on by default): the decoded speech of each call played, and of each transmission the sweep plays, as a mono 16-bit WAV (8 kHz for P25, the analog audio rate for the rest), named by time and talkgroup or frequency. The last 200 are kept on the phone; P25 talkgroups › Played calls plays and shares them.

Frame layout and tables from DSD and mbelib (ISC). IMBE is a voice coding method of Digital Voice Systems, Inc. Listening to radio voice traffic is illegal in some places: check the law where you are.

### ADS-B aircraft

Aircraft broadcast their position on 1090 MHz. sdr/ModeS.kt decodes it at 2 MS/s:

- Finds the 8 µs preamble, then reads 56 or 112 bits of pulse-position modulation (1 µs per bit).

- Checks the 24-bit CRC (polynomial 0xFFF409) and corrects a single bit error in DF17 messages.

- Decodes DF11, DF17 and DF18: ICAO address, call sign, altitude, CPR-encoded position and ground speed.

sdr/AdsbTracker.kt turns an even and an odd CPR message into a position, then decodes later ones locally against the aircraft's last position and drops anything beyond 450 km. The aircraft list goes to the police-aircraft check every 2 s, with no internet needed.

### USB WiFi monitor mode

In monitor mode an adapter hands over every 802.11 frame it hears, not just its own network's. The app's userspace drivers (usb/, ported from the Linux drivers, Wardrive Go, devourer and mt76; see NOTICE.md) bring the chip up, tune it and read the frames. They follow the Linux drivers' initialisation order.

| Chip | Channels hopped | Dwell per channel |

| AR9271 | 2.4 GHz, 1, 6, 11 first | 500 ms |

| RT3070, RTL8187 | 2.4 GHz 1-13 | 350 ms |

| RTL8811AU / 8821AU, RTL8812AU | 1-13, 36-48, 149-165 | 350 ms |

| RTL8814AU | 1-13, 36-48, 149-165 | 125 ms |

| RTL8812BU / 8822BU | 1-13, 36-48, 149-165, DFS 52-144 | 200 ms |

| MT7612U | 1-13, 36-165 including DFS | 125 ms |

| MT7921AU | 2.4 + 5 GHz and the 6 GHz preferred scanning channels (5, 21, 37 ... 229), visited less often unless active | 150 ms |

- Receive loop (usb/BulkRx.kt): 16 KB asynchronous USB requests (24 queued for RTL88xxAU, 16 for RTL8822BU), with a synchronous fallback, strict frame boundaries and a guard that resets a stream that keeps returning nothing.

- Frames read (usb/MonitorFrames.kt): beacons, probe responses, probe requests and data frames. A beacon's own channel field wins over the tuned channel (adjacent-channel leakage). The beacon timestamp gives "WiFi on since", data bytes are counted, and hidden network names are revealed by probe responses and associations. Results are grouped every 2 s.

- Device intel (usb/ProbeIntel.kt): the WPS block (maker, model, device name, and the UUID-E that links a phone's random addresses), a probe-request fingerprint (order of information elements plus capability fields, 8 hex digits), the FlipDeFlock probe shape and Flock's Wi-Fi Alliance element.

- Deauth floods (usb/DeauthWatch.kt): 25 deauthentication / disassociation frames in 30 s, or a burst in 5 s, spread over at least 3 time slices; protected (802.11w) frames are ignored; one alert per 5 min.

- Karma / evil-twin APs (usb/KarmaWatch.kt): one transmitter answering for 4 or more network names within 60 s; idea from SignalSweep.

- Antenna check (usb/AntennaCheck.kt, after Wardrive Go): holds one reference AP's channel and compares the signal on each antenna chain, with an A / B swap test. It compares received signal, it is not an SWR meter.

- Capture (usb/PcapRecorder.kt): saves frames as a pcap with radiotap headers (link type 127, opens in Wireshark), up to 200 MB.

- Firmware: the full build includes the chips' firmware. The F-Droid / FOSS build asks before downloading the non-free files once from linux-firmware (commit e981caea6ed3) and checks each SHA-256. The free ath9k_htc firmware (AR9271) is in both. An MT7612U that says "not calibrated" needs to be unplugged and plugged back in.

### USB Bluetooth

A USB Bluetooth dongle, or the Bluetooth side of a MT7921AU / Realtek combo adapter, becomes a second Bluetooth LE scanner (usb/HciUsb.kt), as Linux's btusb drives it: HCI commands as class requests on endpoint 0, events read from the interrupt endpoint. No data (ACL / SCO) channels are opened.

- Realtek (usb/BtRealtek.kt, after Linux btrtl): reads the chip's LMP subversion and ROM version, then sends the v1 epatch and its config file in 252-byte pieces. The newer RTBTCore chips (RTL8822CU, RTL8852) aren't supported yet.

- MediaTek MT7961 (usb/BtMediatek.kt, after btmtk): WMT patch download and function-on, with a subsystem reset and retry.

- Plain CSR or Broadcom dongles need no firmware.

- Scan: passive, duplicates kept, interval 0x60 / window 0x30. Extended scanning on LE 1M and LE Coded (long range) when the controller has it, otherwise the legacy scan. It never connects, pairs or advertises.

### ESP32 boards over USB

esp/SerialPort.kt opens the board's USB serial port at 115200 baud, 8N1:

- Native USB (ESP32-S2 / S3 / C3 / C6, FREE-WiLi 2): CDC-ACM, DTR raised.

- CP210x (10C4:EA60): DTR and RTS kept low so the board doesn't reset into its bootloader.

- CH340 / CH341 / CH9102 (1A86:7523, 5523, 55D4).

esp/EspReader.kt then works out which firmware is talking, in this order, and only sends read-only commands:

| Firmware | How it is recognised and read |

| OUI-Spy / Flock You | Streams JSON lines by itself ({"event":"detection",...}, Sky Spy drone lines); the app may ask CMD:VERSION and CMD:DUMP_LIVE |

| V2X2MAP | Its binary ITS5 stream (see V2X) |

| GhostESP | help, then its scan and list commands |

| ESP32 Marauder | help, then sniffbeacon / sniffprobe; also through a Flipper Zero's USB-UART bridge |

| FREE-WiLi 2 | The console's WiFi menu keys and its AP scan only |

### OUI-Spy over Bluetooth

The OUI-SPY App-Controlled firmware is driven over Bluetooth GATT (esp/OuiSpyBle.kt): a 128-bit service ending -0a15-4b70-ba00-c010ae1ba01c, MTU 247, reconnect every 8 s if lost. The app turns on the engines it needs (Detector, Flock BLE, Flock WiFi, Sky Spy, survey) and sends DISABLE_ALL (0x0F) when you stop. With relaying on, its survey engine sends standard WiFi probe requests. Detections the board saved while offline arrive as spooled frames (0xFF ... 0xFE). Its attack-style engines (UniPwn, PCAP, Foxhunter) are never used.

### V2X emergency vehicles

An ESP32-C5 running V2X2MAP (MIT) listens to 5.9 GHz vehicle-to-everything messages (ETSI ITS-G5). Its USB stream is "ITS5", seconds (u32), microseconds (u32), length (u16), then the raw 802.11 frame, little-endian. esp/V2x.kt finds the GeoNetworking ethertype 0x8947, decodes CAM and DENM messages (ETSI EN 302 637-2 / -3) and lists only emergency vehicles: light bar or siren on, or a DENM warning. The stream has no signal strength, so a nominal −70 dBm is shown.

### Sentinel Link and Meshtastic

- Phone to phone (link/PhoneLink.kt): Bluetooth LE GATT, no system pairing. Phones in a group find each other by a group tag in their advert that changes every 15 min.

- Pairing and encryption (link/LinkCrypto.kt): P-256 ECDH key exchange confirmed by a 6-digit code both screens show (numeric comparison, so a man in the middle shows a different code). Keys come from HKDF-SHA256; each connection uses AES-256-GCM with one key per direction and counter nonces, and replayed messages are refused.

- Meshtastic (link/MeshNode.kt): talks to your Meshtastic node over its phone Bluetooth API and adds a private "RFSentinel" channel keyed from the group key, so only your group can read it. Watchlist matches go first; up to 12 messages wait in the queue, retried every 10 to 120 s. A node serves one app at a time, so close the Meshtastic app. Not yet tested on real hardware.

### Limits

- An SDR alert means energy on a channel, not a confirmed police radio. VHF / UHF are shared with businesses, and an encrypted P25 system still shows grants but no voice.

- P25 Phase 2 (TDMA) voice and non-standard (vendor MFID) messages aren't decoded. P25 voice is experimental and untested on many systems.

- One dongle covers about 2 MHz at a time: a band is swept, so a short transmission can be missed while the tuner is elsewhere.

- USB power: an SDR or AC WiFi adapter can draw more than some phones give; use a powered hub or Y-cable if it keeps dropping.

- Monitor-mode WiFi drivers marked experimental (RTL8812AU, AR9271, MT7921AU) may not start on every board revision.

### Questions

Q: Does the radio sweep listen to police radio?
A:

Not by default in RF Sentinel. The sweep measures how much energy each 12.5 kHz channel carries. Only the experimental options decode audio: Play voice transmissions (the sweep's new transmissions, analog or unencrypted P25) and Listen to P25 voice (unencrypted trunked calls).

Q: Which SDR should I buy?
A:

For RF Sentinel, an RTL-SDR with an R820T2 or R828D tuner, such as the RTL-SDR Blog V3 or V4. A HackRF One works too but costs more and gives nothing extra here. For ADS-B, a 1090 MHz antenna helps a lot.

Q: Do I need to calibrate the dongle's ppm error?
A:

No. RF Sentinel's sweep works on 12.5 kHz channels wide enough for a dongle's drift, and the P25 demodulator's frequency loop follows the drift itself.

Q: Can I use an SDR that is plugged into my computer?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel can use one over WiFi: run rtl_tcp -a 0.0.0.0 on the computer and enter its address under Settings › RTL-SDR radio › Network SDR. It needs a fast, trusted local network.

Q: Can the USB WiFi drivers deauth or capture handshakes?
A:

No. In RF Sentinel's USB WiFi drivers every transmit path, and the handshake / PMKID capture of the original drivers, was removed. They only listen.

### Sources

- librtlsdr (osmocom, GPL-2.0-or-later): RTL2832U and R82xx tuner driver

- OP25 and TIA-102.BAAA: P25 framing, BCH, trellis and TSBK layout

- DSD and mbelib (ISC): P25 voice frames and the IMBE vocoder

- Linux kernel drivers (rtl8187, rt2x00, ath9k, mt76, btusb, btmtk, btrtl), aircrack-ng rtl8812au, OpenIPC devourer, Network Weather mt76-usb-macos

- Wardrive Go by RocketGod: USB WiFi drivers, FREE-WiLi 2 reader, antenna check idea

- V2X2MAP (MIT), SignalSweep (karma idea), OUI-Spy / Flock You, GhostESP, ESP32 Marauder

Full credits and licences: usb/NOTICE.md and sdr/NOTICE.md.
