# RTL-SDR, USB WiFi Monitor Mode & ESP32 on Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/hardware.html

Use an RTL-SDR, HackRF, USB WiFi adapter in monitor mode, USB Bluetooth dongle, ESP32 (OUI-Spy, Marauder, Flipper BFFB) or Meshtastic radio with Android in RF Sentinel. No root.

rf_sentinel / hardware

## External hardware

Optional add-ons that hear further than a phone and see things Android hides: ESP32 boards, USB WiFi and Bluetooth adapters, and RTL-SDR / HackRF radios. Plug them in with a USB OTG cable while scanning, no root. What they hear merges into RF Sentinel's own list with a badge (ESP32, USB WIFI, USB BT). Settings → External hardware has the switches, and a log for each piece of hardware to export. How each one works inside, with the numbers: Hardware internals.

### ESP32 boards

#### Supported firmware

| Firmware | Link | What RF Sentinel gets |

| OUI-Spy (recommended) | USB OTG | Flock-You, Detector and Sky Spy detections as they happen: Flock cameras, the board's watchlist matches, Remote ID drones with position |

| OUI-SPY App-Controlled | Bluetooth | Flock-BLE, Flock-WiFi, Sky Spy, Detector and (optional) Wardrive survey engines |

| GhostESP | USB OTG | The WiFi networks it scans, about every 10 s (no Bluetooth over USB) |

| ESP32 Marauder | USB OTG, or through a Flipper Zero | WiFi networks and client devices from its passive beacon and probe sniffers, batched every 2 s; on ESP32-C5 boards (Marauder v8, BFFB v2, LilyGo T-Dongle C5, C5 DevKit) both 2.4 and 5 GHz |

| V2X2MAP (ESP32-C5, Europe) | USB OTG | European car-to-car radio (ITS-G5, 5.9 GHz): emergency vehicles with their light bar and siren state at the position they broadcast, and their "emergency vehicle approaching" warnings. RF Sentinel only listens to the board's stream; nothing is sent to it. Not in North America, which uses C-V2X |

| FREE-WiLi 2 | USB OTG | The WiFi networks its ESP32-C5 scans from its console's WiFi menu (2.4 + 5 GHz) |

#### USB

Plug the board into the phone with a USB OTG cable while scanning: Android offers to open RF Sentinel for it, and with Always ticked it never asks again. Native-USB boards (ESP32-S2 / S3 / C3 / C5 / C6) and boards with CP210x or CH340 USB bridges work. RF Sentinel only asks OUI-Spy for its version and live table, only asks GhostESP to scan and list networks, and only runs Marauder's passive sniffbeacon / sniffprobe sniffers (no attack commands, no settings changes). Settings shows the board's status.

#### ESP32 Marauder, ESP32-C5 and Flipper Zero

Dual-band: Marauder on an ESP32-C5 (Marauder v8, BFFB v2, LilyGo T-Dongle C5, C5 DevKit) hears 5 GHz networks that the phone's throttled WiFi scan misses, which helps catch vehicle routers on a pass. Keep Channel Hop on in Marauder's settings; RF Sentinel says so if the board stays on one channel.

Flipper Zero (e.g. with the BFFB board): plug the Flipper into the phone and open GPIO → USB-UART Bridge on the Flipper; RF Sentinel then talks to the board's Marauder through it. A BFFB v2 can also be plugged in by its own USB-C port. The original BFFB uses a 2.4 GHz-only ESP32.

#### Bluetooth (OUI-SPY App-Controlled)

- Power the board and start scanning in RF Sentinel.

- Settings → Pair OUI-SPY board → pick OUI-SPY-xxxx.

- Pair only there, not in Android's Bluetooth settings: the board keeps no pairing keys, so a phone-side bond breaks the link. The app tells you to tap Forget if it finds one.

While scanning, RF Sentinel switches on the board's Flock-BLE, Flock-WiFi, Sky Spy and Detector engines and switches them off when scanning stops. By default it also runs the Wardrive survey engine so the board relays every WiFi network and Bluetooth device; those go through RF Sentinel's own watchlist, presets and rules. In that mode the board sends standard WiFi probe requests, so turn off OUI-SPY: relay every network and Bluetooth device to keep it purely listening. Settings → OUI-SPY engines chooses which detection engines run (turn the two Flock engines off where there are no Flock cameras). With Phone Bluetooth scan with OUI-SPY off, the phone's own Bluetooth scan pauses while the board is live and the board does the Bluetooth scanning (it hears farther); the phone's scan comes back if the board drops out. Keep relaying on with it, or only the board's engine matches come in. The board's UniPwn, PCAP and Foxhunter engines are never used.

The status line under Scanning shows connecting… / live · N reports; the ESP32 filter chip lists only what the board reported.

### USB WiFi adapters

RF Sentinel drives the adapter itself in receive-only monitor mode and hops the channels: no Android scan limit, longer range, and client devices (laptops, phones, cameras connected to a network) that a phone's WiFi scan can't see. It also lists the WiFi names nearby devices ask for (Menu → Requested networks). Allow USB access on the prompt; single-antenna dongles are handled automatically.

| Chip | WiFi | Bluetooth | Adapters |

| RTL8811AU / RTL8821AU | 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz experimental | 8821AU | ALFA AWUS036ACS |

| RTL8812AU | 2.4 + 5 GHz, experimental | - | ALFA AWUS036ACH, TP-Link Archer T4U, Netgear A6200v2 |

| RTL8812BU / RTL8822BU | 2.4 + 5 GHz | 8822BU | TP-Link Archer T3U, ASUS USB-AC53 / AC58, Wise Tiger AC1200 |

| RTL8814AU | 2.4 + 5 GHz | - | ALFA AWUS1900, TP-Link Archer T9UH, ASUS USB-AC68 |

| MT7612U | 2.4 + 5 GHz | - | ALFA AWUS036ACM, Netgear A6210, ASUS USB-AC55 |

| MT7921AU (WiFi 6E) | 2.4 + 5 + 6 GHz | Yes, long range | ALFA AWUS036AXML / AXM, Comfast CF-952AX, Netgear A8000 |

| RTL8187 | 2.4 GHz | - | ALFA AWUS036H, Netgear WG111v2 |

| RT3070 | 2.4 GHz | - | ALFA AWUS036NH / NEH |

| AR9271 | 2.4 GHz, experimental | - | ALFA AWUS036NHA, TP-Link TL-WN722N v1 |

Recognised but not supported yet: RTL8811CU / 8821CU / 8812CU, RT5370, MT7610U, AR7010.

- Firmware: the GitHub build includes each chip's firmware. The F-Droid build asks once before downloading the non-free files from linux-firmware and checks each one's SHA-256; the AR9271's free firmware is built in.

- Antenna check (Tools): compares the signal on each of the adapter's antennas from one access point, with an A / B swap test.

- Record frames (Settings → External hardware): saves what the adapter or a V2X board hears as a .pcap for Wireshark, up to 200 MB.

- It also flags deauthentication floods and karma / evil-twin access points (details).

### USB Bluetooth

The Bluetooth part of a combo adapter (MT7921AU, RTL8821AU, RTL8822BU), or a plain USB Bluetooth dongle, works as a second Bluetooth LE scanner next to the phone's own, listening only, with LE Coded long range where the chip has it. Turn it off in Settings → External hardware → Scan Bluetooth with a USB adapter to leave a combo adapter to WiFi only.

| Bluetooth chip | Dongles |

| Any standard controller | CSR8510 (TP-Link UB400), Broadcom BCM20702 (ASUS USB-BT400) |

| RTL8761B / RTL8761C | TP-Link UB500, ASUS USB-BT500, UGREEN CM390 |

| RTL8723BU / RTL8821CU | Edimax EW-7611ULB |

### RTL-SDR and HackRF One

An RTL-SDR dongle (R820T / R820T2 / R860 tuner, e.g. RTL-SDR Blog V3 or V4) or a HackRF One (receive only: its transmitter stays off) adds:

- Two-way radio transmitting nearby: sweeps the public-safety radio bands and measures only how much energy each channel carries; nothing is demodulated or decoded.

- P25 control channel (experimental): finds a P25 trunked system's control channel (700 / 800 MHz) and lists which talkgroups get a channel and when (Tools › P25 talkgroups), with alerts for talkgroups you watch. Listen to P25 voice (experimental, off by default) plays clear calls; encrypted calls can't be played. Receiving radio signalling is legal in many places but not all: check the law where you are. With more than one SDR scan ticked, the dongle takes turns.

- Cellular transmitters (experimental, off by default): a rise on the LTE uplink bands, such as a vehicle modem travelling with you.

- TETRA handsets (Europe and elsewhere): spots their burst rhythm on 380-385 MHz. A second (and third) RTL-SDR on a powered USB hub watches that band nonstop, with a TETRA bar on the main screen (Far / Closer / Very close) and beeps that speed up as one gets closer. Antenna: a vertical whip about 19.5 cm long, on the roof if you can; two dongles can share it through a 2-way splitter.

- ADS-B aircraft (Settings → RTL-SDR radio): decodes aircraft on 1090 MHz with no internet, for the police-aircraft check.

- A live radio waterfall (Tools).

Network SDR: an RTL-SDR plugged into a computer running rtl_tcp on your WiFi works too (Settings → RTL-SDR radio → Network SDR, about 5 MB/s of WiFi). Step by step, with every setting and status line: RTL-SDR guide. How the sweep, P25 and ADS-B decoding work: Hardware internals.

### Meshtastic

A Meshtastic LoRa node paired over Bluetooth lets Sentinel Link phones far apart share detections on a private channel (setup, details, troubleshooting). Not yet tested on real hardware.

### Hardware logs

Each piece of hardware keeps its own log on the phone: what it did, step by step, so a problem can be found without the developer having the same hardware. Nothing leaves the phone unless you share it.

| Log | What it records |

| USB WiFi adapter | Driver start-up, firmware, channel hopping, frames received, recoveries. |

| USB Bluetooth adapter | Start-up, firmware, advertising reports per minute. |

| RTL-SDR / HackRF | Plug-in, which scan has its turn, P25 and pager searches, stalls and restarts, Network SDR connection. |

| ESP32 board | Serial port opened, which firmware answered, status changes, why it stopped. |

| Mesh radio (Meshtastic / MeshCore) | The node-list radio over Bluetooth: connecting, live, out of reach. |

| OUI-SPY over Bluetooth | Connection states, setup, failed commands. |

| Sentinel Link Meshtastic node | Pairing, reading its settings, the RFSentinel channel, and every 10 minutes: packets sent, received from other Sentinels, other mesh packets, dropped and unreadable. |

| Sentinel Link Bluetooth | Waiting or linked, advertising failures, bad messages. |

| Sentinel Link internet relay | Connecting, connected, refused or unreachable, without the broker's name or any IP address. |

To send one: Settings → External hardware → Export a hardware log, pick it (an empty one is marked "empty"), and share the text file by email, messages or Drive. Export all hardware logs puts every log that has something in it into one file: the easiest choice when you're not sure which part is failing. Each export starts with the app version, the phone model, the hardware's status at that moment and, for USB hardware, the USB devices plugged in.

What's never in them: nearby devices' addresses or names, network names, your position, or the relay server's name. Each log keeps about 1 MB on the phone, plus the one before it. A crash has its own log: Settings → Lists, tools & about → Export crash log.

Attach the file to a GitHub issue with the hardware's model and what you expected to happen.

### Questions

Q: Which ESP32 board should I buy?
A:

RF Sentinel works with any board the firmware supports: XIAO ESP32-S3, ESP32-S3 DevKitC, LilyGO T-Dongle-S3 and others are targets of OUI-Spy. An external antenna connector (u.FL / IPEX) is worth having for range.

Q: How do I flash OUI-Spy?
A:

Follow the firmware's own README (PlatformIO or its flash script). RF Sentinel doesn't flash boards.

# Hidden Camera & Spy Cam Detector for Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/hidden-camera-detector.html

Find WiFi spy cameras (V380, LookCam Pro, TinyCam), action cams and home security cameras with an Android phone, and check a hotel room or Airbnb with Watch this place. Free, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / hidden-camera-detector

## Hidden camera & spy cam detector

Cheap clock, charger and smoke-detector spy cameras give themselves away while they broadcast their setup hotspot, and action and security cameras carry known Bluetooth and WiFi identifiers. RF Sentinel looks for both, and Watch this place tells you what turns up in a room after you arrive.

### WiFi spy cameras in setup mode

| Camera app | Setup hotspot name | Score |

| LookCam Pro | DGK-XXXXXX-XXXXX | 80 |

| V380 | MV + 8 digits | 75 |

| TinyCam Pro | AI_ + 6-12 characters | 60 |

| HDSmartIPC | AI + 12 characters | 55 |

| Generic IP camera | IPC- / IPC_ + an ID | 50 |

Once a spy camera has joined the home network it looks like any other device to a phone's WiFi scan. A USB WiFi adapter in monitor mode also sees client devices connected to networks.

### Action cameras

GoPro (company ID 0x02F2, UUIDs 0xFEA5 / 0xFEA6), Insta360 (0x10D7 / 0xFC30), DJI Osmo, YI, SJCAM, AKASO, Garmin VIRB, Ricoh THETA, Kodak PIXPRO, Sony action cams and others, from company IDs, maker address blocks and default names.

### Home and business security cameras

Arlo, Blink, Ezviz, Wyze, Ring, Verkada, Axis, Hanwha, Bosch and more, from network names and maker address blocks. Camera glasses (Ray-Ban Meta and others) are their own category, on by default.

Action & hidden cameras and Network / home security cameras are off by default (many false alarms at home): turn them on under Settings → detection.

### Watch this place: check a hotel room

Settings → Trackers & followers → Watch this place. Leave the phone in one place (home, a hotel room, a rental). It learns every device around for 5 minutes, then, counting only devices heard at -60 dBm or stronger, reports:

- New: a device it didn't learn, heard twice within a minute.

- Gone: a device quiet for 2 minutes. Back: one that returns within 5 minutes.

- Moving: one whose signal keeps jumping by 20 dB or more.

Phones and tags that change their random address count as the same device. It pauses while you are more than 300 m away, and keeps what it learned across a restart. The rules follow AntiHunter's; the numbers can be changed.

### Questions

Q: Can I check an Airbnb or hotel room for hidden cameras with my phone?
A:

Partly. In RF Sentinel, turn on the camera categories and Watch this place: cameras broadcasting a setup hotspot, Bluetooth or a known maker's address show up, and anything that switches on after you arrive is reported. Wired, SD-card-only and cellular cameras send nothing a phone can identify: look for lenses and IR LEDs too.

Q: Does it find cameras by lens reflection or infrared?
A:

No. RF Sentinel works only from radio signals. A flashlight lens check or the phone camera (to see IR LEDs) complements it.

Q: Do hidden camera detector apps actually work?
A:

Partly. A phone's magnetometer or camera can't reliably tell a hidden camera from other electronics. RF Sentinel looks for what cameras transmit instead: spy-camera WiFi names and setup networks, and with Watch this place, devices that appear in the room. A camera that only records to a memory card sends nothing, so no radio app can see it; check with a flashlight too.

# How RF Sentinel Detects Police & Surveillance Gear
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/how-it-works.html

How RF Sentinel's police detector works: passive Bluetooth LE and WiFi scanning, vendor signatures, confidence tiers, evidence fusion and patrol-car signal correlation.

rf_sentinel / how-it-works

## How it works

How RF Sentinel goes from radio packet to alert. Every rule and threshold here is in the public source; file names point at the Kotlin classes.

### 1. Scanning (receive only)

- Bluetooth LE (service/BleScanEngine.kt): continuous BluetoothLeScanner scan, no batching, aggressive match mode, legacy + BT5 extended advertising and LE Coded PHY when the chip supports them. Scan mode: low latency (default), balanced or low power.

- Screen off: Android suspends unfiltered scans, so a second, hardware-filtered scan runs on the identifiers that matter (vendor company IDs, Remote ID, tracker and glasses service data and UUIDs, watchlisted exact addresses).

- WiFi: WifiManager scans every 30 s by default (Android allows about 4 per 2 minutes), including raw information elements on Android 11+.

- Cell: getAllCellInfo() every 15 s for fake-tower signs.

- External: OUI-Spy / GhostESP / Marauder ESP32 boards over USB or Bluetooth (also through a Flipper Zero), FREE-WiLi 2, and USB WiFi adapters: RTL8811AU / 8821AU, RTL8812AU (experimental), RTL8812BU / 8822BU, RTL8814AU, MT7612U (2.4 + 5 GHz), the WiFi 6E MT7921AU (2.4 + 5 + 6 GHz), RTL8187, RT3070 and, experimental, AR9271; and USB Bluetooth (the Bluetooth part of MT7921AU / RTL8821AU / RTL8822BU combo adapters, or a USB Bluetooth dongle) as a second Bluetooth LE scanner.

Nothing is ever transmitted to, connected to or paired with a scanned device.

### 2. Signatures

detect/SignatureEngine.kt matches payload tags (BWCDEVICE), Bluetooth SIG company IDs, 16 and 128-bit service UUIDs, service data, names and SSIDs. The watchlist matches exact addresses, IEEE MA-L / MA-M / MA-S prefixes, name, name-prefix (starts:) and vendor rules, Bluetooth advert patterns (adv:, learned with I saw it, probable at most) and WiFi probe fingerprints, seeded by regional presets (assets/oui_presets/: Global, Canada, US). Every prefix used in code is checked against its IEEE registrant by tools/gen_assets.py, which fails the build data if one changes.

| Tier | Confidence | Meaning |

| Weak | < 50 | Shared identifier; amber, silent by default |

| Probable | 50-79 | Vendor-specific identifier; alerts at the default threshold |

| Strong | 80+ | Payload tag or vendor-assigned network name |

Rejected on purpose: bare 10-digit BLE names, the -FALCON SSID suffix, Liteon module blocks, Motorola Mobility blocks (consumer phones), Sierra Wireless / Cradlepoint blocks as standalone matches, and company ID 0x058E alone.

### 3. Evidence fusion

detect/EvidenceFusion.kt, every 2 s per device. Different rules of the same category combine by noisy-OR with each supporting hit at half weight:
fused = 1 - (1 - top) × Π (1 - 0.5 × support_i) support_i ≥ 30, result ≤ 90

Example: watchlisted address 70 + Zebra serial name 50 → 78. The patrol-vehicle hit is never fused, because it is derived from the device's own matches.

### 4. Patrol-vehicle grouping

detect/PatrolCluster.kt. Each device gets a role (body camera, plate reader, two-way radio, vehicle cellular router, mobile printer, in-car computer, rugged laptop, police camera) from its matches or IEEE registrant. Two or more different roles form a vehicle when their RSSI correlates (Pearson r ≥ 0.6 over ≥ 8 aligned seconds) or both are parked (flat) and appeared within 30 s of each other. The group needs a police-specific role, or both a two-way radio and a vehicle router: printers, breath-screening devices and vehicle interface modules only add to a group. Score: 24 + 12 × roles, +10 if moving together, cap 88. A device's own match is held 2 minutes after its evidence was last seen.

### 5. Address-rotation linking

detect/AdvertFingerprint.kt. Fingerprint = names, service UUIDs, service-data and company-ID payload sizes, TX power, connectable flag. A new private address with the same fingerprint as exactly one device that went silent 1.5-30 s earlier inherits its matches (−5), follow history (time with you, GPS path) and ignore state. Apple-Continuity-only adverts are never linked.

### 6. Follow detection

A tracker or flagged device heard continuously (gaps under 3 minutes) for at least 10 minutes while you moved at least 800 m raises may be following you, once per device. Both thresholds are adjustable.

### 7. Identifying ordinary devices

- Decoded vendor protocols (Apple Continuity incl. exact AirPods / Beats model, iBeacon, Eddystone, Fast Pair named by model from Momentum-Apps' genuine-device list (GPL-3.0, @Willy-JL, @Spooks4576), Remote ID)

- GAP appearance

- Standard SIG services (heart rate, HID, LE Audio, medical...)

- Name patterns

- Member-service owner

- IEEE registrant

- Company ID

### 8. WiFi fingerprinting

detect/WifiFingerprint.kt: WPS element (manufacturer 0x1021, model name 0x1023, model number 0x1024, device name 0x1011, primary device type 0x1054), Cisco CCX AP name (IE 133, bytes 10-25), BSSID registrant (unless chipset-only), vendor IE owners split into equipment and chipset makers. BSSIDs are the same AP when octets 2-5 match, the last octet is within 16 and the first is equal or locally administered.

### 9. Known cameras

alpr/: OpenStreetMap elements tagged surveillance:type=ALPR, speed and red-light cameras, fetched via Overpass (overpass-api.de, with overpass.kumi.systems and overpass.private.coffee as fallbacks) and DeFlock's region snapshots, cached privately, refreshed weekly. Warnings when a camera is ~20 s ahead (150-600 m) and getting closer.

### Sources

- all-cameras-are-beacons signature reference (Apache-2.0): confidence ladder and field-validated values

- opendroneid-core-c (Apache-2.0): Remote ID message layout

- IEEE Registration Authority (via Wireshark's weekly copy) and Bluetooth SIG assigned numbers

- Community prefix lists cross-checked: Flock You, OUI-Spy, nite-oui-collection, Wardrive Go, Flock-You-Android, Fieldwatch

Full tables: docs/SIGNATURES.md.

# IMSI Catcher & Stingray Detector for Android, No Root | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/imsi-catcher-detector.html

RF Sentinel spots fake cell tower (Stingray, IMSI catcher) signs on a non-rooted Android phone: test networks, sudden 2G downgrades, cloned cell IDs. What it can and can't see.

rf_sentinel / guides / imsi-catcher-detector

## Stingray / IMSI catcher signs

A cell-site simulator pretends to be a tower so phones attach to it, often forcing them down to 2G where encryption is weak or absent. Without root a phone can't read the signalling, but the cell data Android does expose still shows some of the tell-tale signs, and RF Sentinel checks it every 15 seconds.

### What Android exposes without root

TelephonyManager.getAllCellInfo() returns the serving and neighbour cells: radio technology (GSM / WCDMA / LTE / NR), MCC-MNC, cell ID, area code (LAC / TAC), and signal. It does not expose ciphering, identity requests or other layer-3 messages; that needs the modem's diagnostic interface (root, or dedicated hardware like Rayhunter).

### Signs RF Sentinel checks every 15 s

| Sign | Score |

| Serving cell on a test / reserved MCC (001, 002, 999) | 85 |

| Sudden switch from 4G/5G to 2G while strong LTE (≥ −105 dBm) is still visible | 70 |

| Sudden 4G/5G → 2G without strong LTE; or downgraded to 2G with strong LTE visible | 50 |

| Network country code differs from the SIM's while not roaming | 55 |

| Reserved identity: area code 0, 0xFFFE or 0xFFFF, or cell ID 0 | 45 |

| Known cell number reappearing in a different area (cloned identity) | 50 |

| Location / tracking area changed while GPS shows you still for 2+ minutes | 40 |

| Switched to a cell with no neighbours where several were visible | 35 |

| A never-seen cell took over at −65 dBm or stronger, 20+ dB above the last, while you stood still (after AIMSICD / SnoopSnitch) | 40 |

| Serving cell's area code shared by none of 3+ neighbours of the same network, which all agree on another (after AIMSICD) | 35 |

| Several signs at once | max + 15, cap 90 |

### Cutting false alarms

- Persistence: a sign must be present on two consecutive checks.

- Calls: drops to 2G during a call (and for 2 minutes after) are ignored: many networks hand voice to 2G/3G.

- Borders: area codes ping-ponging at a coverage border don't count.

- Known areas: which area each cell lives in is remembered on the phone (cleared with "Forget device history"); a genuinely moved cell is adopted after 8 snapshots.

### Actual protection

- Settings → Network → SIM → turn off Allow 2G (Android 12+, if your carrier allows it).

- Android 15+: Cellular security → Network notifications warns when a network requests your SIM identity in clear or disables encryption. RF Sentinel's Settings links straight there.

- For signalling-level detection, run EFF's Rayhunter on a supported hotspot.

### Questions

Q: Is a rooted phone better for IMSI catcher detection?
A:

Yes, with a Qualcomm or similar modem that exposes diagnostic logs, a rooted phone (or Rayhunter) can see identity requests and cipher mode. RF Sentinel stays root-free and limits itself to what public APIs show.

Q: Does 5G protect against IMSI catchers?
A:

5G standalone encrypts the permanent identity (SUCI), but most networks still run non-standalone 5G anchored on LTE, and downgrade attacks to 2G/3G remain the main vector. Disabling 2G closes the easiest one, and RF Sentinel still watches for sudden 2G downgrades.

Q: Is there a Stingray detector app for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel checks for fake cell tower signs on a normal, non-rooted Android phone: test networks, sudden 2G downgrades, cloned cell IDs and area codes no neighbour shares. It can't prove a Stingray is there; for signalling-level detection, run EFF's Rayhunter alongside.

# Install RF Sentinel: Free Police Detector APK for Android
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/install.html

Download and install the RF Sentinel APK for Android 8.0+, update it without losing data, set it up for Android Auto or build it from source.

rf_sentinel / install

## Install

RF Sentinel runs on Android 8.0 or newer on an ARM phone, 64-bit or 32-bit (practically every Android phone). One signed APK from GitHub Releases, about 46 MB.

### Steps

- On your phone, tap Download APK above, or open the latest release and under Assets tap the file ending in -release.apk. Don't pick the "Source code" archives.

- Open the downloaded file from the notification, or from Files → Downloads.

- If Android blocks it as an unknown source, tap Settings, enable Allow from this source, go back and tap Install.

- Open RF Sentinel. The setup wizard walks through theme, region preset, alerts, camera download radius, screen behaviour and permissions.

- Tap Start scanning and grant location and Nearby devices.

Only free software? The same release also has a file ending in -foss.apk (about 23 MB): no Mapbox map (the map is OpenFreeMap), and the few USB WiFi adapters that need non-free chip firmware ask before downloading it from kernel.org. Either file replaces the other.

### With Obtainium

Obtainium installs apps straight from their GitHub releases and keeps them updated. Install Obtainium, then on the phone tap the Get it on Obtainium badge above. It adds RF Sentinel with the -release.apk already picked. For the free-software build, use this link for the FOSS APK instead.

Adding it by hand: in Obtainium tap Add app, enter https://github.com/CIS-C0/RFSentinel and set APK filter to -release\.apk$ (or -foss\.apk$). Obtainium installs the same signed APKs as GitHub, so it updates over a copy you installed by hand and the other way round.

### Updating

Settings → Lists, tools & about → Check for updates asks GitHub for the latest release and links its APK (when you tap it; on first start the app asks once whether it may also check when it opens, and keeps your answer). Install the newer APK over the existing one. History, watchlist and settings are kept. Every release is signed with the same key; Android refuses an update signed with a different one.

### Android Auto

In a real car, Android Auto only shows Car App Library apps like RF Sentinel when they're installed from a trusted store (Google Play or ONE store); its Unknown sources setting doesn't cover them. The GitHub APK's car screens run on Google's Desktop Head Unit emulator, and once that setting is on it gets a media-style RF Sentinel screen and alert messages in the car. More on Android Auto.

### Battery settings

On phones with aggressive battery management (Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus, Huawei), set RF Sentinel's battery usage to Unrestricted. Settings has a shortcut.

### Build from source

Android Studio, or JDK 17+ with the Android SDK (platform 37).
git clone https://github.com/CIS-C0/RFSentinel
cd RFSentinel
./gradlew assembleDebug # app/build/outputs/apk/debug/
./gradlew testDebugUnitTest lintDebug # tests and lint

| Component | Version |

| Gradle | 9.6.0 (wrapper) |

| Android Gradle Plugin | 9.4.0 (built-in Kotlin) |

| KSP / Room | 2.3.12 / 2.8.5 |

| compileSdk / targetSdk / minSdk | 37 / 36 / 26 |

A self-built debug APK has a different signature from the release, so uninstall the release first (that clears its data).

# rtl_433, dump1090, multimon-ng & SDRTrunk on Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/open-source-tools-android.html

Can rtl_433, dump1090, multimon-ng, SDRTrunk, DSD, OP25, AirGuard, Chasing Your Tail or AntiHunter run on an Android phone? What RF Sentinel took from each, credited.

rf_sentinel / guides / open-source-tools-android

## rtl_433, dump1090, multimon-ng, SDRTrunk and more on Android

RF Sentinel stands on the work of many open-source projects. This page lists each one, what it is, what RF Sentinel took from it (ported code, a reference, or only an idea) and what you get on an Android phone. Short version: RF Sentinel runs parts of rtl_433, dump1090, multimon-ng, DSD, OP25 and SDRTrunk's work directly on the phone with an RTL-SDR, no root and no computer, but it does only the parts it needs for detection. For everything those tools do, use them on a computer.

### At a glance

| Project | What it is | In RF Sentinel | Licence |

| rtl_433 | Decoder for hundreds of 315 / 433 / 868 MHz devices (PC, Raspberry Pi) | Tire-sensor (TPMS) decoders follow it | GPL-2.0 |

| dump1090, dump1090-fa | ADS-B / Mode S decoders | dump1090-fa's 2.4 MS/s demodulator and automatic gain ported; dump1090 a reference | BSD-3 / GPL-2.0+ |

| SkyPulse, The 1090 MHz Riddle | ADS-B decoder; Junzi Sun's book on Mode S | References for the ADS-B decoder | GPL-3.0 |

| multimon-ng | Decoder for many digital modes | POCSAG and FLEX pager decoders follow it | GPL |

| DSD, mbelib | Digital voice decoder and vocoder library | P25 voice ported; AMBE+2 for DMR and NXDN | ISC |

| dsd-neo, DSD-FME | Modern DSD forks | DMR voice (dsd-neo) and NXDN48 (DSD-FME) ported | ISC |

| SDRTrunk, OP25 | Desktop trunking decoders | P25 checks, call-follow timings, auto-PPM, MDC-1200 | GPL-3.0 |

| RFAnalyzer | Android SDR receiver | The waterfall's Listen demodulator follows it | GPL-2.0+ |

| rtl-sdr-blog librtlsdr | RTL-SDR driver | Bias-tee switch, RTL-SDR Blog V4 support | GPL-2.0+ |

| AIMSICD, SnoopSnitch | Android fake-cell detectors | Two fake-cell checks (ideas only) | GPL-3.0 |

| Rayhunter | EFF's IMSI-catcher detector for a hotspot | Compared; use alongside | GPL-3.0 |

| AirGuard | Android tracker detector (TU Darmstadt) | Tracker service IDs follow it | Apache-2.0 |

| Chasing Your Tail | Follower detection from Kismet logs | The "keeps turning up" follower check follows it | MIT |

| AntiHunter | ESP32 area-watch project | Watch this place follows its rules | - |

| OpenDroneID receiver-android | Official Remote ID receiver | Remote ID over Wi-Fi Aware follows it | Apache-2.0 |

| FlipDeFlock | Flipper Zero Flock detector | Probe-shape hash ported, values match | GPL-3.0 |

| Momentum BLE Spam | Flipper Zero app | Its genuine Fast Pair list names devices | GPL-3.0 |

| V2X2MAP | ESP32-C5 V2X receiver | ITS-G5 frames read its way | MIT |

| aircrack-ng rtl8812au, devourer, Linux drivers | WiFi drivers | Receive-only USB WiFi drivers, no root | GPL-2.0 |

| DeFlock, OpenStreetMap | Map of plate-reader cameras | Offline camera snapshot | ODbL |

| nyanBOX, RF Party, BLE Radar, ESPsoup, SØPHIA | Detectors and scanners | Ideas only, no code | - |

| Wardrive Go, Flock You, OUI-Spy, Fieldwatch | Wardriving and ESP32 detectors | See Compared with other tools | - |

### rtl_433 on Android: tire sensors

rtl_433 decodes hundreds of kinds of 315, 433 and 868 MHz devices: weather stations, doorbells, car keys and tire-pressure sensors. It runs on a computer or Raspberry Pi.

RF Sentinel ports only rtl_433's tire-pressure (TPMS) decoders, and runs them on the phone with an RTL-SDR: Ford, Toyota (PMV-C210 and PMV-107J), Citroen / Peugeot, Hyundai (VDO) and Schrader (GM / Chrysler, Saab / Opel, Subaru, Nissan / Renault, BMW). The goal isn't to read tire pressure. It's to notice the same car's wheels turning up with you at place after place, a car following you even when its driver's phone is off. Your own car is learned first and never alerts. See car-following detection.

### dump1090 on Android: ADS-B without internet

dump1090 and FlightAware's dump1090-fa decode the 1090 MHz ADS-B messages aircraft send. RF Sentinel's ADS-B decoder was written from the published format and Junzi Sun's The 1090 MHz Riddle, with SkyPulse and dump1090 as references; its 2.4 MS/s demodulator and automatic gain are ports of dump1090-fa's (Oliver Jowett and FlightAware).

With an RTL-SDR on the phone, RF Sentinel shows the aircraft around you on its map with no internet, and warns about police helicopters and planes circling low. For a 24/7 feeder station, dump1090-fa on a Raspberry Pi is still the tool.

### multimon-ng on Android: POCSAG and FLEX pagers

multimon-ng decodes many digital modes from audio. RF Sentinel's POCSAG (512, 1200, 2400 baud) and FLEX decoders follow it, and run straight from the RTL-SDR's samples on the phone: no audio piping, no computer. RF Sentinel keeps pages in memory only and alerts on the capcodes and words you watch. See the pager decoder.

### DSD, mbelib, dsd-neo and DSD-FME on Android: digital voice

RF Sentinel's P25 voice is ported from DSD and mbelib (szechyjs), with mbelib's AMBE+2 for DMR and NXDN. DMR voice is ported from dsd-neo by arancormonk and NXDN48 from DSD-FME by lwvmobile.

On the phone, RF Sentinel plays clear (unencrypted) P25 Phase 1 calls it follows from the control channel, and clear DMR and NXDN48 voice through Play voice transmissions in the radio sweep. Encrypted calls are never decoded, and P25 Phase 2 isn't supported. See the P25 scanner.

### SDRTrunk and OP25 on a phone

SDRTrunk (Dennis Sheirer) and OP25 are full trunking decoders for a computer. RF Sentinel checked its P25 fields, Reed-Solomon and NID decoding against SDRTrunk, follows SDRTrunk's auto-PPM frequency correction and its MDC-1200 decoder (unit IDs and emergencies on analog FM radios), and takes its P25 call-follow timings from dsd-neo and OP25.

RF Sentinel is narrower: one P25 Phase 1 system at a time, built around "is someone transmitting near me?" rather than monitoring a whole county. If you run a scanner station, keep SDRTrunk. If you want P25 talkgroups and clear calls in your pocket or your car, RF Sentinel does it on the phone.

### RFAnalyzer

RFAnalyzer by Dennis Mantz is an Android spectrum analyzer and receiver for HackRF and RTL-SDR. RF Sentinel's waterfall Listen follows its demodulator. RFAnalyzer is the better general-purpose receiver; RF Sentinel's waterfall is a tool around its detections.

### rtl-sdr-blog librtlsdr

The RTL-SDR Blog driver is where RF Sentinel's bias-tee switch comes from. RF Sentinel drives RTL-SDR Blog V3, V4 and V4L, Nooelec NESDR and most generic dongles with its own USB driver, so no driver app and no root are needed.

### AIMSICD, SnoopSnitch and Rayhunter

AIMSICD and SnoopSnitch are Android fake-cell (IMSI catcher) detectors. Two of RF Sentinel's fake-cell checks follow their ideas; no code was taken. SnoopSnitch's deeper checks need a rooted phone with a Qualcomm chip; RF Sentinel uses only what non-rooted Android shows.

EFF's Rayhunter runs on a cheap mobile hotspot and reads the modem's signalling directly, which a normal phone can't. RF Sentinel's 2G-downgrade check is the visible side of what Rayhunter watches; running both is reasonable. See IMSI catcher detector and RF Sentinel vs Rayhunter.

### AirGuard alternative

AirGuard by SEEMOO / TU Darmstadt is a focused, research-backed Android tracker detector. RF Sentinel's tracker service IDs follow AirGuard's. AirGuard is the simpler choice if trackers are all you want; RF Sentinel adds trackers to police, camera, drone and fake-cell detection in one app, a Locate screen to find the tag, and car-following detection from tire sensors. See tracker detection.

### Chasing Your Tail on Android

Chasing Your Tail (NG) looks for devices that keep turning up around you, from Kismet logs on a computer. RF Sentinel's "keeps turning up" follower check follows it on the phone, with no Kismet or Raspberry Pi: a tracker or flagged device that turns up at 3 or more places along your way within 2 hours raises may be following you.

### AntiHunter on Android

AntiHunter is an ESP32 project for watching an area for devices. RF Sentinel's Watch this place follows its rules: it learns the place for 5 minutes, then reports what's new, gone, back or moved, on the phone. See Watch this place.

### OpenDroneID receiver

OpenDroneID's receiver-android is the reference Remote ID app. RF Sentinel's Remote ID over Wi-Fi Aware follows it, and adds Bluetooth and WiFi beacon Remote ID, overhead alerts and the pilot's position on its map. See drone detector.

### FlipDeFlock

FlipDeFlock spots Flock cameras on a Flipper Zero from the shape of their WiFi probe requests. RF Sentinel ports its probe-shape hash so the values match, with its candidate and generic shape lists, and uses it with a USB WiFi adapter on the phone. See Flock camera detector.

### Momentum BLE Spam

RF Sentinel names Google Fast Pair devices from the genuine-device list in Momentum-Apps' BLE Spam. RF Sentinel also flags Bluetooth spam floods and Flipper Zero devices nearby: see Flipper Zero detector.

### V2X2MAP

An ESP32-C5 running V2X2MAP by Peter Holzhauser hears European 5.9 GHz vehicle-to-everything (ITS-G5) messages. RF Sentinel reads its frames the same way and decodes the CAM / DENM messages from ETSI's ASN.1, so vehicles and road warnings show on the phone's map.

### WiFi monitor mode on Android without root

On Linux, adapters like the ALFA AWUS036ACH use kernel drivers such as aircrack-ng/rtl8812au, which Android can't load without root. RF Sentinel ships its own receive-only USB drivers instead: the Realtek 88xxau chips (RTL8811AU, RTL8821AU, RTL8812AU), RTL8814AU, MT7612U, RT3070 and AR9271 ported from Wardrive Go (register tables from Realtek's Linux driver), RTL8812BU / RTL8822BU from OpenIPC's devourer, MT7610U and MT7921AU following the Linux mt76 driver, and RTL8187 with Kismet's Android PCAP Capture as reference. Every transmit path and handshake capture was removed. See hardware.

### DeFlock

DeFlock maps plate-reader cameras on OpenStreetMap with volunteers. RF Sentinel ships a snapshot of those cameras with OpenStreetMap's speed and red-light cameras, and warns before each one offline, on the phone and on Android Auto. If you add cameras, add them to OpenStreetMap through DeFlock; every RF Sentinel user benefits on the next update. See camera alerts.

### Inspiration

RF Sentinel was inspired by the nyanBOX hardware device and the RF Party app, which came from Alan Meekins' DEF CON 31 talk Snoop Unto Them As They Snoop Unto Us. Feature ideas also came from SØPHIA, BLE Radar (MetaRadar) and ESPsoup; no code from those projects is included. Thank you to every project here.

### Questions

Q: Is there an rtl_433 app for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel runs rtl_433's tire-pressure sensor decoders on an Android phone with an RTL-SDR, no root and no computer, to spot cars following you. It doesn't decode rtl_433's other devices (weather stations, doorbells); for those, run rtl_433 on a computer or Raspberry Pi.

Q: Can I run dump1090 on an Android phone?
A:

RF Sentinel includes a port of dump1090-fa's demodulator and automatic gain, so an RTL-SDR on the phone decodes ADS-B with no internet and shows aircraft on RF Sentinel's map, with alerts for police aircraft circling low. It isn't a feeder for flight-tracking sites.

Q: Is there multimon-ng for Android?
A:

For pagers, yes: RF Sentinel's POCSAG and FLEX decoders follow multimon-ng and run on the phone from an RTL-SDR or HackRF. RF Sentinel doesn't do multimon-ng's other modes (DTMF, EAS, AFSK and so on).

Q: Does SDRTrunk run on Android?
A:

SDRTrunk is a desktop Java application. On a phone, RF Sentinel decodes a P25 Phase 1 control channel, shows active talkgroups and plays clear calls with an RTL-SDR, using checks taken from SDRTrunk. It's narrower than SDRTrunk: one system at a time and no Phase 2.

Q: Can I use OP25 or DSD on a phone?
A:

RF Sentinel ports DSD and mbelib's P25 voice, dsd-neo's DMR voice and DSD-FME's NXDN48 voice to Android, so clear digital voice plays on the phone with an RTL-SDR and no computer. Encrypted calls are never decoded.

Q: Is there a police scanner app that works without internet?
A:

Streaming scanner apps need internet. RF Sentinel with an RTL-SDR receives the radio itself, offline: it shows nearby transmissions, P25 talkgroups and, if you turn it on, plays clear analog, P25, DMR and NXDN voice. Check your local law before listening.

Q: Can I use an RTL-SDR on Android without root or a driver app?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel has its own USB driver for RTL-SDR dongles (RTL-SDR Blog V3, V4 and V4L, Nooelec and most generic ones) and HackRF One, so it needs no root and no separate driver app. An OTG adapter is all you need; weak phones may need a powered hub.

Q: Does the RTL-SDR Blog V4 work on Android?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel supports the RTL-SDR Blog V4 and V4L (R828D tuner, 28.8 MHz crystal, its band inputs and notch filters), including its bias-tee. If the phone doesn't see it, try another OTG adapter, a shorter cable or a powered hub.

Q: Can an RTL8812AU or ALFA adapter do monitor mode on Android without root?
A:

Yes, with RF Sentinel. Its own receive-only USB drivers put RTL8812AU, RTL8812BU, RTL8814AU, MT7612U, MT7921AU, RT3070, AR9271 and RTL8187 adapters in monitor mode on a non-rooted phone, to hear probe requests and every network. They never transmit.

Q: What is a good AirGuard alternative?
A:

RF Sentinel uses the same tracker IDs as AirGuard (AirTag, SmartTag, Tile, Chipolo, Find Hub tags) and adds a Locate screen, car-following detection from tire sensors, and police, camera, drone and fake-cell detection in the same free, open-source app. If you only want tracker alerts, AirGuard is a fine, focused choice.

Q: Is there Chasing Your Tail for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel's follower check is modelled on Chasing Your Tail: a tracker or flagged device that turns up at 3 or more places along your way within 2 hours raises "may be following you". It runs on the phone, with no Kismet or Raspberry Pi.

Q: Can my phone do what AntiHunter does?
A:

RF Sentinel's Watch this place follows AntiHunter's rules on an Android phone: leave the phone in a room or a parked car and it reports the devices that arrive, leave, come back or move. For a fixed perimeter with many sensors, AntiHunter's ESP32 nodes do more.

Q: Is there a SnoopSnitch or AIMSICD alternative that works without root?
A:

RF Sentinel checks for fake cell tower signs on a non-rooted Android phone (test networks, sudden 2G downgrades, cloned cell IDs, area codes no neighbour shares), with two checks following AIMSICD and SnoopSnitch ideas. Without root it can't see signalling; for that, use EFF's Rayhunter.

Q: Can I detect Flock cameras like FlipDeFlock but on a phone?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel uses FlipDeFlock's probe-shape hash with a USB WiFi adapter on the phone, and also finds Flock cameras from their WiFi and Bluetooth with the phone alone, plus offline alerts before every mapped plate reader.

Q: Is there an app like DeFlock that warns me while I drive?
A:

RF Sentinel ships DeFlock's OpenStreetMap snapshot of plate-reader cameras and warns about 20 seconds before each one, offline, on the phone and on Android Auto. It also detects cameras that aren't mapped yet from their radio signals.

Q: Is RF Sentinel allowed to use this code?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel is GPL-3.0, and every ported project's licence (GPL, ISC, BSD, MIT, Apache-2.0) allows it. RF Sentinel keeps their notices in the source (sdr/NOTICE.md, usb/NOTICE.md) and credits each project in its README.

# P25 Scanner App for Android with RTL-SDR | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/p25-scanner.html

Turn an Android phone and an RTL-SDR into a P25 trunking scanner: talkgroups, emergency and encrypted flags, clear P25 voice, plus analog FM, DMR and NXDN calls. Free, no root, no internet.

rf_sentinel / guides / p25-scanner

## P25 scanner on an Android phone

With an RTL-SDR dongle on USB OTG, RF Sentinel follows a P25 trunked system's control channel, lists the talkgroups and their calls, and can play clear voice through the phone. No root, no computer, no internet stream. Experimental.

### P25 control channel

P25 trunked systems (700 / 800 MHz) announce on a control channel which talkgroup gets which voice channel. RF Sentinel finds that channel and reads the announcements. Tools → P25 talkgroups lists each talkgroup with its calls, last channel and radio, and emergency / encrypted flags. Alerts are available for talkgroups you watch, radios nearby, patches and radio GPS positions. On by default in the United States and Canada when an RTL-SDR is plugged in.

### Listening to calls

- Listen to P25 voice (off by default): follows clear calls on the talkgroups you pick and plays them. Encrypted calls are never decoded.

- Save played calls keeps them to play again; Transcribe P25 calls (Android 13+, off by default) turns each saved call into text with Android's on-device speech recognition: nothing leaves the phone.

- Play voice transmissions (radio sweep, off by default): a new transmission anywhere in the swept bands is tuned to and played until it goes quiet: analog FM, clear P25, DMR and NXDN48, and FRS / GMRS / MURS walkie-talkies on their real channel.

### What you need

- An RTL-SDR with an R820T / R820T2 / R860 tuner (RTL-SDR Blog V3, V4 or V4L), or a HackRF One (used to receive only).

- A USB OTG adapter or cable. A powered hub helps with a second dongle.

- The userspace driver is built in: no driver app, no root.

With more than one SDR scan ticked (radio sweep, ADS-B, P25, pagers) one dongle takes turns. Details on each status line: RTL-SDR guide. How it works inside: hardware internals.

### Check the law

Receiving radio signalling is legal in many places but not all, and some restrict using or passing on what you hear. Check the law where you are.

### Questions

Q: Can I listen to a P25 police scanner on my Android phone without a computer?
A:

Yes, with an RTL-SDR plugged into the phone. RF Sentinel decodes the control channel and clear P25 voice on the phone itself. Encrypted talkgroups stay silent.

Q: Does it decode DMR and NXDN too?
A:

In RF Sentinel, clear DMR and NXDN48 voice can be played through Play voice transmissions in the radio sweep. Trunking control-channel decoding is P25 only.

Q: Can it decode TETRA?
A:

No. TETRA is encrypted in most networks. RF Sentinel detects TETRA handsets transmitting nearby by their time-slot bursts, without decoding them: see the TETRA detector.

# POCSAG & FLEX Pager Decoder for Android (RTL-SDR) | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/pager-decoder.html

Decode POCSAG (512 / 1200 / 2400 baud) and FLEX pager messages on an Android phone with an RTL-SDR or HackRF: capcode and keyword alerts, named channels, kept in memory only. Free, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / pager-decoder

## POCSAG & FLEX pager decoder for Android

Plug an RTL-SDR or HackRF into the phone and RF Sentinel finds paging channels and decodes the pages, with no computer and no multimon-ng setup. Experimental, off by default.

### What it does

- Decodes POCSAG at 512, 1200 and 2400 baud (pick the speeds) and FLEX into Tools → Pager messages.

- Alerts on the capcodes (RICs) and words you watch; the page's text stays out of the alert unless you turn that on.

- Drops the capcodes you ignore.

- Named channels: switch between them in one tap on the messages screen, and import or export the list.

Turn it on in Settings → RTL-SDR radio → Pager messages. The decoders follow multimon-ng.

### Kept in memory only

Pages can hold private or medical details, so they are never saved, exported or sent, their text is never logged, and they are gone when the app closes or you untick the setting.

### Check the law

Canada, the United States and many other places restrict using or passing on messages you intercept, and some forbid listening at all. Check the law where you are.

### Questions

Q: Can I decode pagers on an Android phone?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel does it with an RTL-SDR (or HackRF One) on USB OTG. The decoding runs on the phone; no root, no PC, no extra app.

Q: Can one RTL-SDR do pagers and other scans at once?
A:

RF Sentinel takes turns: with the radio sweep, ADS-B, P25 and pagers ticked, the dongle switches between them for the length you set. A second dongle on a powered hub avoids the gaps.

# Police Helicopter & Plane Tracker (ADS-B) | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/police-aircraft-tracker.html

See police helicopters and planes overhead on Android: ~1,400 law-enforcement aircraft from the FAA and Transport Canada registries, low circling aircraft, online ADS-B or an RTL-SDR with no internet.

rf_sentinel / guides / police-aircraft-tracker

## Police helicopter & plane tracker

Police and sheriff helicopters, state patrol planes and federal aircraft broadcast ADS-B like every other aircraft. RF Sentinel matches them against the law-enforcement registry and alerts when one is overhead, from community feeds or from an RTL-SDR on your phone with no internet at all.

### What counts as a police aircraft

- Its ICAO address is in the bundled registry of about 1,400 law-enforcement airframes from the FAA and Transport Canada: police, sheriff, state patrol, federal agencies, RCMP and provincial police.

- The feed names a police owner, or a government owner (shown as a government aircraft, not always police).

- Aircraft circling overhead: an unlisted aircraft that keeps orbiting low over the same area. Police and surveillance flights do this, but so do news, training and survey flights: verify.

A strong match within the alert distance (5 km by default) alerts; the rest are listed and logged. Aircraft show on the map with altitude, speed and heading (Tools → Aircraft), and on the Android Auto Threats tab.

### Two sources

| Source | Needs | Privacy |

| Community ADS-B feeds (adsb.fi, adsb.lol) | Internet | Every minute while scanning, a position rounded to about 1 km. Unlike commercial flight trackers, these feeds don't hide law-enforcement flights. |

| RTL-SDR as an ADS-B receiver | An RTL-SDR dongle on USB OTG (a 1090 MHz antenna helps) | Nothing leaves the phone: turn the online feeds off. |

Off by default: turn on Police aircraft under Settings → detection. The RTL-SDR receiver is in Settings → RTL-SDR radio; see the RTL-SDR guide.

### Questions

Q: Can my phone tell me when a police helicopter is overhead?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel does when the helicopter broadcasts ADS-B and is in the registry or circling low. With internet, the community feeds cover it; without, an RTL-SDR on the phone receives ADS-B directly.

Q: Why don't Flightradar24 and similar apps show police aircraft?
A:

Commercial trackers honour blocking requests from aircraft owners, and many law-enforcement aircraft are blocked. The community feeds RF Sentinel uses don't filter them, and an RTL-SDR hears whatever the aircraft broadcasts.

Q: Will it see an aircraft with its transponder off?
A:

No. Without ADS-B, RF Sentinel has nothing to decode. Drones are different: Remote ID drones are covered by the drone detector.

Q: Who is flying over my house right now?
A:

RF Sentinel shows the aircraft around you from their own ADS-B broadcasts, from community feeds or from an RTL-SDR with no internet, and matches them against the law-enforcement registry, so police and government aircraft stand out.

---

# Police Detector for Android: Body Cams & Patrol Cars | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/police-detector.html

Turn an Android phone into a police detector with RF Sentinel: body cams (Axon, Motorola), radios, e-ticket printers and patrol cars from Bluetooth and WiFi. Free, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / police-detector

## Detect police with Android

Police equipment talks constantly over Bluetooth LE and WiFi: body cameras pair with phones and holster sensors, cars carry cellular routers, printers and radios pair with tablets. RF Sentinel lets an Android phone hear all of that without root and without transmitting anything.

### What gives police gear away

| Equipment | Signal | Rule | Score |

| Body camera (multiple brands) | BLE payload | BWCDEVICE ASCII in service / manufacturer data or raw advert, either byte order | 90 |

| Axon / TASER | BLE | Company ID 0x034D; UUID 0xFC81, 0xFE6B, 0xFE6C | 60 each, fused |

| Axon | MAC prefix | 00:25:DF (IEEE MA-L, Axon Enterprise) | 75 |

| Utility Inc. body cam | BLE name | contains BodyWorn Remote | 80 |

| Motorola Solutions radios / gear | BLE | Company ID 0x04EC; UUID 0xFD8E / 0xFE04 | 45 |

| Zebra e-ticket printer | BLE | UUID 0xFE79 / 0xFD66 + factory-serial name | 50 (30 otherwise) |

| In-car router | WiFi / MAC | Cradlepoint, Sierra Wireless registrant (role only, never alone) | via grouping |

| Flock plate reader | WiFi / BLE | Flock- SSID, FS Ext Battery, Penguin-, FS-, 0x09C8 | 45-88 |

Plus vendor prefixes of Digital Ally, WatchGuard, Getac, Zepcam, Vievu, P25 / TETRA radio makers, police radar makers and vehicle upfitters in the Global, Canada, US, France, UK, Portugal, Germany, Spain and Italy presets. Every prefix cites its IEEE registrant. Full list: SIGNATURES.md.

### Patrol vehicles: grouping gear that moves together

One Motorola radio is a security guard as often as a cop. A body camera, a radio and a vehicle router whose signals rise and fall together are a patrol car. RF Sentinel gives each device a role from its matches or IEEE registrant, then groups two or more different roles when:

- their RSSI series correlate (Pearson r ≥ 0.6 over at least 8 aligned seconds), or

- both are flat (parked) and appeared within 30 s of each other.

# score = 24 + 12 x roles (+10 if moving together), max 88
2 roles, parked ........... 48 weak
2 roles, moving together .. 58 probable
3 roles, moving together .. 70 probable
5 roles, moving together .. 88 strong

Gear that shops, guards and utility trucks carry too can't make a group without help: a label printer, a breath-screening device or a remote-starter module only adds to one, and a radio or a vehicle router needs the other (or a police-specific role such as a body camera, plate reader or lightbar). A stockroom with a Zebra printer and a cellular router is not a patrol car.

Consumer brands that also make car audio or office gear (Kenwood, Panasonic Connect, Havis) get no role from their vendor name alone, and whitelisted devices never count. The group is recomputed every 2 s, so it disappears when the vehicle leaves.

### Setup for driving

- Install and run the setup wizard: pick your region preset (Global, Canada, US) and alert threshold.

- Settings → Start scanning automatically in the car → pick your car's Bluetooth.

- Enable the floating bubble if you drive with Waze or Google Maps on screen, or use Android Auto.

- Leave screen-on while charging (default) on a car mount: Android limits Bluetooth scans with the screen off.

### Limits

- A match is a signature, not an officer. Every hit shows its evidence; verify weak ones.

- Gear that's off, docked, or only on cellular is invisible. Radios' voice channels (VHF/UHF/700/800 MHz P25, TETRA) are not received.

- Not a radar detector: X/K/Ka-band radar and lidar can't be received by a phone.

- Range is limited by phone antennas; an ESP32 board helps.

### Questions

Q: Do body cameras advertise all the time?
A:

Many do, on and off. Some only include their tag in some packets, so RF Sentinel holds a device's match for 2 minutes after the evidence was last seen before it fades.

Q: Does it detect an officer's phone?
A:

No. Phones use random addresses and generic Apple / Google adverts with nothing police-specific. RF Sentinel detects the equipment, not the person.

Q: Can it tell if a body camera is recording?
A:

No. Recording state isn't in the advertisement RF Sentinel matches.

Q: Is there an app that tells me if a cop is nearby?
A:

RF Sentinel is the closest thing: it alerts when it hears police gear's Bluetooth or WiFi (body cameras, in-car systems, radios, ticket printers) and raises a patrol-car alert when several of them move together. It can't see officers whose gear is off or doesn't transmit, so no alert doesn't mean no police.

Q: Is a police detector app legal?
A:

RF Sentinel only listens to signals devices broadcast openly and transmits nothing. Passive Bluetooth and WiFi scanning is legal in most places, but laws differ, so check yours. This isn't legal advice.

Q: What's the best free police detector app for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel is free and open source (GPL-3.0), with no account, no ads and no analytics. It detects body cams, patrol cars, Flock cameras, trackers, drones and fake cell towers on a non-rooted phone, and works on Android Auto. Download it from GitHub Releases; see install.

# RF Sentinel Q&A: What Can an Android Phone Detect?
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/qa.html

Can Android use an RTL-SDR, WiFi monitor mode or detect police, Flock cameras, AirTags, Stingrays, drones, skimmers and GPS jammers? RF Sentinel's straight answers.

rf_sentinel / q&a

## Q&A

Straight answers about what a phone can and can't pick up, and how RF Sentinel does it. Every link to a code file points at the public source.

- Can my Android phone do it? RTL-SDR, monitor mode, ADS-B, P25...

- Detecting police

- Flock, ALPR, speed and hidden cameras

- AirTags and trackers

- Drones and Remote ID

- Stingray / IMSI catchers

- Smart glasses

- SØPHIA and other apps

- Install, update, devices

- How detection works

- Range, accuracy, battery, screen off

- Android Auto and driving

- ESP32, OUI-Spy, GhostESP, Marauder

- Sentinel Link and Meshtastic

- Privacy, safety and legality

- Themes, data, contributing

### Can my Android phone do it?

Q: Can you use an RTL-SDR on Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel, a free Android app, drives an RTL-SDR plugged into the phone with a USB OTG adapter: its userspace driver is built in, so there is no driver app, no root and no computer. RTL-SDRs with an R820T / R820T2 / R860 tuner work (RTL-SDR Blog V3, V4 and V4L), and an RTL-SDR on a computer running rtl_tcp works over WiFi too.

What RF Sentinel does with it: a radio sweep that notices radios transmitting nearby, a live waterfall, ADS-B aircraft with no internet, a P25 scanner with clear voice, a pager decoder, TETRA detection and tire-pressure sensors. Step by step: RTL-SDR guide.

Q: Can I use a HackRF One with an Android phone?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel uses a HackRF One over USB OTG for the same scans as an RTL-SDR, and only ever receives with it: the transmitter and RF amplifier stay off, and so does antenna-port power unless you turn on Bias-tee power. Details: HackRF internals.

Q: Can an Android phone use WiFi monitor mode without root?
A:

Not with its built-in WiFi, but yes with a USB WiFi adapter and RF Sentinel: the app drives RTL8811AU / 8821AU, RTL8812AU, RTL8812BU / 8822BU, RTL8814AU, MT7612U, MT7921AU (2.4 + 5 + 6 GHz), RTL8187, RT3070 and others in receive-only monitor mode over OTG, no root. That removes Android's scan limit and shows client devices connected to networks. Adapter list: USB WiFi adapters.

Q: Can I see WiFi probe requests on Android?
A:

Yes. With a USB WiFi adapter or an ESP32 Marauder board, RF Sentinel lists the network names nearby devices ask for (Requested networks), and you can watch a name to get an alert whenever any device asks for it. Each device also gets a probe fingerprint that survives MAC randomization.

Q: Can I capture WiFi packets to a .pcap file on Android without root?
A:

Yes. With a USB WiFi adapter in monitor mode (or a V2X board), RF Sentinel's Record frames (Settings → External hardware) saves every frame heard, with its channel and signal, as a .pcap for Wireshark (up to 200 MB).

Q: Can I use a USB Bluetooth adapter on Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel uses a plain USB Bluetooth dongle (Realtek RTL8761B / 8761C and other standard controllers), or the Bluetooth part of a combo WiFi adapter, as a second Bluetooth LE scanner next to the phone's own. Listening only, with LE Coded long range where the chip has it. See USB Bluetooth.

Q: Can an Android phone receive ADS-B aircraft without internet?
A:

Yes, with an RTL-SDR on 1090 MHz: RF Sentinel decodes position, altitude, speed and call sign on the phone, and flags police and government aircraft. See the police aircraft tracker.

Q: Can I listen to police radio on my phone without an internet scanner app?
A:

With an RTL-SDR, yes, for clear (unencrypted) traffic: RF Sentinel's P25 scanner follows a trunked system and plays clear calls, and Play voice transmissions plays the analog FM, P25, DMR and NXDN calls its radio sweep finds. Encrypted calls are never decoded. Check the law where you are.

Q: Can my phone tell when a two-way radio is transmitting near me?
A:

With an RTL-SDR or HackRF, yes. RF Sentinel's radio sweep learns which channels are always busy where you are and alerts on a strong burst on a normally quiet one: a probable public-safety radio on 700 / 800 MHz, a weak sign on shared VHF / UHF. TETRA handsets are recognised by their time-slot bursts. See the radio sweep.

Q: Can I decode pager messages on Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel decodes POCSAG and FLEX pages with an RTL-SDR or HackRF and keeps them in memory only: pager decoder.

Q: Can my phone detect a GPS jammer or GPS spoofing?
A:

RF Sentinel spots the signs from what the phone's satellite receiver reports: receiver noise rising while every satellite weakens (jamming), and equal-strength satellites, GPS-only skies, clock drift or impossible jumps (spoofing). See the GPS jammer detector.

Q: Can my phone detect a card skimmer at a gas pump?
A:

Bluetooth skimmers, often: RF Sentinel flags the HC-05 / HC-06 / RN42 / BT04-A modules inside them as possible card skimmers. See the card skimmer detector.

Q: Can my phone detect a Flipper Zero or a WiFi deauth attack?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel detects a Flipper Zero with Bluetooth on, a Pwnagotchi, a WiFi Pineapple, evil twin networks and Bluetooth spam floods from the phone alone; deauthentication floods need a USB WiFi adapter. See the hacking tool detector.

Q: Can my phone tell if a car is following me?
A:

RF Sentinel has several ways: a tracker or flagged device that stays with you raises may be following you, and so does one that keeps turning up at 3 or more places along your way. With an RTL-SDR, the same car's tire-pressure sensors heard with you place after place mean a vehicle following you. See tire sensors.

Q: Can my phone check a hotel room for new devices?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's Watch this place learns every device around for 5 minutes, then reports what is new, gone, back or moving. See Watch this place.

Q: Can my phone show police helicopters overhead?
A:

Yes, when they broadcast ADS-B: RF Sentinel takes them from community feeds or an RTL-SDR and matches them against about 1,400 law-enforcement aircraft. See the police aircraft tracker.

Q: Can I get Waze police reports as sound and voice alerts?
A:

Yes, optionally: RF Sentinel turns Waze police reports into alerts, with spoken call-outs at 1 km, 500 m and 200 m and only for reports on your road ahead.

Q: Can I get directions that avoid speed cameras and plate readers?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's built-in navigation plans routes around the known cameras on the phone and says what is left on each route. See routes that avoid cameras.

Q: Can I see Meshtastic or MeshCore nodes on a map on Android?
A:

Yes. A Meshtastic or MeshCore radio on USB or Bluetooth puts the nodes it hears on RF Sentinel's map, read-only (experimental). RF Sentinel phones can also share detections through Meshtastic: Sentinel Link.

Q: Can a phone pick up emergency vehicles' car-to-car radio (V2X)?
A:

In Europe, yes: with an ESP32-C5 running the V2X2MAP firmware on USB, RF Sentinel shows police, fire and ambulance vehicles broadcasting ITS-G5 with their role, light bar and siren state and position, and alerts on "emergency vehicle approaching" warnings. North America uses C-V2X, which it can't receive. See V2X.

Q: Can I see every Bluetooth and WiFi device near me on Android?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's live list shows every Bluetooth, WiFi and cell signal it hears, with signal strength, maker where known and why anything was flagged. Tap one to see its details or Locate it.

Q: Is there a counter-surveillance app for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel is a free, open-source counter-surveillance app for Android: it detects police gear, plate-reader cameras, trackers, drones, smart glasses, skimmers, hacking tools and fake cell towers from Bluetooth, WiFi and cell data, with no root. Optional USB radios add more.

Q: Can my phone find a lost Bluetooth device?
A:

Often, if it still has battery. Open it in RF Sentinel's nearby devices list and tap Locate: the beeps speed up as you get closer. See finding a lost device.

Q: Can I run rtl_433, dump1090 or multimon-ng on Android?
A:

Parts of them, inside RF Sentinel: its tire-sensor, ADS-B and pager decoders are ported from or follow rtl_433, dump1090-fa and multimon-ng, and run on the phone with an RTL-SDR. See open-source tools on Android.

### Detecting police

Q: How do I detect police with an Android phone?
A:

Modern police gear is full of radios that broadcast on their own: body cameras advertise over Bluetooth LE so the officer's phone and holster sensors can find them, in-car routers run WiFi access points, radios and e-ticket printers pair over Bluetooth. Any phone can receive those broadcasts without connecting to anything.

RF Sentinel runs a continuous BLE scan and periodic WiFi scans, and matches every packet against vendor company IDs, service UUIDs, payload tags, network names and IEEE MAC prefixes assigned to law-enforcement equipment makers (Axon/TASER, Motorola Solutions, Digital Ally, Getac, Zebra, Flock Safety and others). When two or more kinds of police-type gear rise and fall in signal together, it flags a possible police vehicle.

Install the APK, tap Start scanning, grant location and Nearby devices. See the police detection guide.

Q: Is there an app that detects police nearby?
A:

Yes: RF Sentinel is a free, open-source Android app that does this passively from Bluetooth LE and WiFi signals, with no root and no subscription. It detects the equipment, not people: a match means a device with a police-equipment signature is in range. Crowd-sourced apps (Waze) rely on users reporting; RF Sentinel relies only on what the hardware itself broadcasts, so it also works where nobody has reported anything.

Q: Can my phone detect a police body camera?
A:

Often, yes. Body cameras use Bluetooth LE to pair with the officer's phone app, holster and light-bar triggers, and many advertise continuously. RF Sentinel matches:

- the BWCDEVICE ASCII tag in service data, manufacturer data or the raw advert, in either byte order (confidence 90, field-validated);

- TASER International company ID 0x034D and Axon / TASER service UUIDs 0xFC81, 0xFE6B, 0xFE6C (60 each);

- Utility Inc. BodyWorn Remote names (80);

- IEEE MAC prefixes registered to Axon (00:25:DF), Digital Ally, WatchGuard, Getac, Zepcam and others.

Independent matches on the same device are fused, so an Axon camera with the company ID, UUID and prefix lands in the strong tier. Cameras that are switched off, or that only use WiFi to dock, are not visible.

Q: How do I detect Axon body cameras and TASERs?
A:

Axon (formerly TASER International) gear is identifiable from the Bluetooth SIG company ID 0x034D, the 16-bit service UUIDs 0xFC81 (Axon Enterprise), 0xFE6B and 0xFE6C (TASER International), and the IEEE block 00:25:DF. Axon Signal Sidearm holster sensors and Signal units, which start body cameras when a gun is drawn or the light bar turns on, are Bluetooth LE too. RF Sentinel ships all of these rules on by default.

Q: Can it detect a police car or unmarked car?
A:

Indirectly. A single Motorola radio, Zebra printer or Cradlepoint router proves nothing, because civilians use them too. RF Sentinel assigns each device a role (body camera, plate reader, two-way radio, vehicle cellular router, mobile printer, in-car computer, rugged laptop, police camera) and groups devices with at least two different roles when their RSSI moves together (Pearson r ≥ 0.6 over at least 8 aligned seconds), or when both are flat (parked) and appeared within 30 s of each other.

The group is flagged "Possible police vehicle" at 24 + 12 × roles, +10 when the signals move together, capped at 88: two roles stay weak (48), three moving together reach 70. An unmarked car is detected the same way if its gear advertises; there is no "unmarked car" signal as such. Details: patrol-vehicle detection.

Q: Can it detect police radios?
A:

It flags radios that expose Bluetooth or WiFi: Motorola Solutions company ID 0x04EC and UUIDs 0xFD8E / 0xFE04, plus IEEE prefixes of P25 / TETRA radio makers. Those are weak on their own (Motorola radios are also used by security guards, schools and construction crews) and become meaningful as part of a patrol-vehicle group.

A phone alone has no receiver for the radio bands themselves (VHF, UHF, 700/800 MHz). With an RTL-SDR or HackRF plugged in, RF Sentinel also notices radios transmitting nearby and TETRA handsets by their bursts, follows a P25 control channel and can play clear (unencrypted) calls, experimental and off by default. Encrypted calls are never decoded.

Q: Is RF Sentinel a radar detector? Does it detect police radar guns?
A:

No. Police radar and lidar use X, K and Ka-band microwave or infrared laser, which a phone cannot receive. "Police radar" in RF Sentinel's list means the Bluetooth/WiFi signatures of radar makers' in-car units when they advertise. For fixed speed and red-light cameras, RF Sentinel uses the OpenStreetMap camera layer and warns about 30 seconds ahead.

Q: Can it detect e-ticket printers?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel can, with care. Zebra mobile printers advertise UUIDs 0xFE79 / 0xFD66. With a factory-serial name (^[A-Z0-9]{2}[A-Z]{3}\d{9}$), which fleets rarely rename, the score is 50; any other name stays at 30 because the same printers are everywhere in warehouses and retail. Next to a body camera or radio moving with it, it becomes part of a patrol-vehicle group.

Q: How will I be alerted?
A:

In RF Sentinel, matches above your alert threshold (default 50, probable) play a sound and vibrate: one pulse for weak, two for probable, three for strong. Optional spoken announcements use the phone's own text-to-speech engine, in full ("Axon body camera nearby") or short ("Body cam", "Police car", "Speed camera, 50"). Optional radar-detector beeps keep ticking after an alert, faster as the flagged device gets closer, like a radar detector. There is a discreet mode, a floating threat bubble over other apps (green / orange / red with a count, plus a pop-up card naming each new detection), a notification, a Quick Settings tile, a home-screen widget, and heads-up alerts in Android Auto.

Q: Why did it flag a device that is not police?
A:

An RF Sentinel match is a signature, not an identification. 00:25:DF means "registered to Axon Enterprise", not "a police officer". Some identifiers are shared with consumer products: Motorola Solutions radios are used by private security, Zebra printers by shops, Meta's company ID by Quest headsets. That is why every rule has a confidence, weak matches are amber and silent by default, and the detail screen shows the exact evidence and source. Long-press a device to whitelist it, or whitelist a WiFi network by its name (Menu > Whitelist > Network names) when it is on many vehicles, like a bus fleet's routers.

### Flock, ALPR, speed and hidden cameras

Q: How do I detect Flock Safety cameras?
A:

RF Sentinel uses two ways, combined in the app:

- Radio signatures. Flock units and their batteries broadcast identifiable signals: WiFi SSIDs starting with Flock- (88), BLE names FS Ext Battery (80), Penguin-<digits> or FS-<hex> (70, or 80 with company ID 0x09C8), and the XUNTONG company ID 0x09C8 alone (45, shared silicon).

- The known-camera map. Flock cameras mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap (via DeFlock) are downloaded and kept offline. You are warned when one is within about 20 seconds of travel and getting closer, even for cameras that only use cellular and emit nothing a phone can hear.

See the Flock / ALPR guide.

Q: How do I detect license plate readers (ALPR) on Android?
A:

Most non-Flock plate readers (Genetec AutoVu, Motorola / Vigilant, Perceptics, Quercus, Tattile) are wired or on cellular modems and don't broadcast anything a phone can match. RF Sentinel flags them by IEEE prefix when they do expose WiFi or Bluetooth, and covers the rest with the OpenStreetMap layer: every element tagged surveillance:type=ALPR, with manufacturer, operator and direction where mapped. The Download Flock option fetches every mapped plate reader in the US and Canada (~18 MB, about 143,000 cameras, refreshed weekly on WiFi); Download nearby cameras fetches a 10-200 km radius.

Q: Can it detect Flock Raven gunshot / audio sensors?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel does. Raven sensors advertise 128-bit service UUIDs whose short IDs fall in 0x3100-0x3500, matched at confidence 80 (field capture via all-cameras-are-beacons).

Q: Can it warn me about speed cameras and red-light cameras without Waze?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel does. Fixed speed and red-light cameras mapped in OpenStreetMap are downloaded automatically for the area you look at and kept offline, refreshed weekly. Speed cameras warn about 30 seconds ahead, with the speed limit when it's mapped. No account, no reporting, no location sent anywhere except the area request to the Overpass API. Coverage depends on how well your area is mapped in OpenStreetMap, and mobile speed traps aren't covered.

Q: Can I silence one specific camera I pass every day?
A:

Yes. In RF Sentinel, tap the camera on the map and choose Ignore alerts. It stays on the map, faded, and never alerts again. Alert again on the same camera, or Settings, turns it back on. Ignored cameras are kept permanently.

Q: Can I find hidden cameras with my phone?
A:

Only cameras that use WiFi or Bluetooth. RF Sentinel has an optional (off by default) network-camera category: SSIDs starting with ARLO_VMB_ / NTGR_VMB_ (88) and IEEE blocks of Arlo, Blink, Ezviz, Uniview, Amcrest, Wyze, Swann, Night Owl, SkyBell and WUUK (65, WiFi only). Turn on the Network / home security camera category in Settings.

RF Sentinel's optional Action & hidden cameras category also catches cheap WiFi spy cameras while they broadcast their setup hotspot (V380, LookCam Pro, TinyCam Pro, HDSmartIPC) and action cameras, and Watch this place reports devices that appear in a room after you arrive. See the hidden camera detector.

Limits you should know: a camera that joins an existing WiFi network as a client is invisible to an Android WiFi scan (only access points are listed), and wired, SD-card-only or cellular cameras emit nothing usable. A lens-reflection or IR check finds those, not a radio app.

Q: Can it identify hidden WiFi networks?
A:

Yes. Hidden networks still send beacons with information elements. RF Sentinel reads the WPS element (manufacturer, model name and number, device name, primary device type), the Cisco CCX AP name (IE 133), the BSSID's IEEE registrant and vendor IE owners, and links a hidden BSSID to the visible network on the same router (octets 2-5 equal, last octet within 16). Requires Android 11+ for the raw elements.

### AirTags and trackers

Q: How do I know if an AirTag is following me on Android?
A:

An AirTag away from its owner switches to a "separated" Find My frame: Apple company ID 0x004C, type 0x12, length 0x19. RF Sentinel matches that frame (confidence 70), keeps tracking the tag through its address rotations, and raises a may be following you alert when it has been with you for at least 10 minutes while you moved at least 800 m (both adjustable: 2-240 minutes). Tap the device and use Locate: it beeps faster as the signal gets stronger.

It reacts to the same frame Android's built-in unknown-tracker alerts use, but shows it live, with history and a signal graph, instead of after hours.

Q: Does it detect Tile, Samsung SmartTag and Google Find Hub trackers?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel detects all four. Google Find Hub tags via 0xFEAA service data frame 0x41 (separated; frame 0x40 means near the owner and is ignored), Samsung SmartTag via 0xFD5A and Tile via 0xFEED service data (55). All feed the same follow detection.

Q: Can it find a GPS tracker hidden on my car?
A:

RF Sentinel finds only Bluetooth trackers (AirTag, SmartTag, Tile, Find Hub tags). LTE / GSM GPS trackers report over the cellular network and don't broadcast anything a phone can identify. For those, a physical inspection or a dedicated RF sweep is needed.

Q: My own AirTag keeps showing up. How do I ignore it?
A:

In RF Sentinel, long-press it and ignore it. The ignore follows the tag when its address changes: it is carried over through the advert fingerprint link, so you don't have to ignore it again after each rotation. To leave every Apple Find My tag out of the Trackers category, turn on Settings → Exclude Apple AirTags (also in Android Auto → More); Google Find Hub, SmartTag and Tile trackers still alert.

### Drones and Remote ID

Q: How do I detect drones near me with my phone?
A:

Drones sold since FAA / EU Remote ID rules must broadcast an ASTM F3411 Remote ID signal over Bluetooth (service data 0xFFFA, app code 0x0D) or WiFi (vendor IE OUI FA:0B:BC, type 0x0D). RF Sentinel decodes it (confidence 95), places the drone on the map with heading, altitude and speed, and raises a "drone overhead" alert when it is within 200 m horizontally (once per drone per 5 minutes). Drone makers' own IEEE blocks (DJI, Parrot, Skydio, Autel, Yuneec...) are also matched at 60. See the drone guide.

Q: Can I see where the drone pilot is?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel shows it when the drone's Remote ID includes the System message: Remote ID carries the operator (or take-off) position. The detail screen shows it, and you can open both the drone and operator positions in your maps app. Remote ID also carries the serial number and, where used, an operator ID.

Q: Does it detect police drones?
A:

RF Sentinel detects any drone that broadcasts Remote ID, which includes most police drones (DJI, Skydio, Autel) under current rules. It can't tell who operates it unless the operator ID says so. Exempt or modified drones that don't broadcast Remote ID are not detected.

### Stingray / IMSI catchers

Q: How do I detect a Stingray or IMSI catcher on Android without root?
A:

Without root, Android exposes the cells your phone sees (network codes, cell IDs, area codes, radio technology, signal) but not ciphering or signalling messages. RF Sentinel reads them every 15 s and looks for the signs a cell-site simulator leaves in that data:

- serving cell on a test / reserved MCC (001, 002, 999): 85;

- sudden switch from 4G/5G to 2G while strong LTE is still visible (the visible side of the 2G downgrade EFF's Rayhunter watches for): 70;
