- a known cell number appearing in a different area (cloned identity), a reserved area code (0, 0xFFFE, 0xFFFF) or cell ID 0;

- a network country code that doesn't match the SIM while not roaming;

- the location area changing while GPS shows you standing still, a new cell with no neighbours.

A sign must persist across two checks; 2G drops during calls and area codes flipping at coverage borders are ignored. Several signs together score max + 15, capped at 90. See the IMSI catcher guide.

Q: How reliable is fake cell tower detection on a phone?
A:

It is heuristic. Each sign has innocent explanations (network maintenance, rural 2G, carrier misconfiguration), and a well-configured simulator copying a real cell's identity shows few of them. Treat it as a warning to look closer, not proof. The strongest protection is turning off Allow 2G in your SIM settings (Android 12+), and on Android 15+ enabling Cellular security → Network notifications, which warns when a network asks for your SIM identity or turns off encryption. RF Sentinel's Settings links there.

Q: How does this compare with EFF's Rayhunter?
A:

Rayhunter runs on a cheap mobile hotspot with root access to the modem's signalling (QMDL / diag), so it sees identity requests and ciphering changes directly. A normal Android app can't. RF Sentinel implements the parts of that analysis visible through Android's public cell APIs (2G downgrade, identity anomalies) and points to Android 15's own network notifications for the rest. For the strongest detection, use Rayhunter hardware alongside.

### Smart glasses

Q: How do I detect Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses nearby?
A:

Ray-Ban Meta glasses advertise over Bluetooth LE. RF Sentinel matches Luxottica's company ID 0x0D53 (70), company ID 0x058E together with the META_RB_GLASS token (72), and Meta's corporate company ID 0x01AB / UUIDs 0xFEB7 / 0xFEB8 (45, because Quest headsets share them). Snap Spectacles (0x03C2), Vuzix (0x060C) and HeyCyan-SDK glasses (full 128-bit UUID) are matched too. See the smart glasses guide.

Q: Can it tell if the glasses are recording?
A:

No. RF Sentinel tells you the glasses are near you and advertising. Recording state is not part of the advertisement.

### SØPHIA and other apps

Q: How can I get s0phia ops (SØPHIA) for free?
A:

SØPHIA is a paid product sold by its own developer, and this site doesn't distribute it or any copy of it. If what you want is the same kind of tool for free, RF Sentinel is a free, open-source (GPL-3.0) alternative: passive Bluetooth LE and WiFi scanning for police gear, plate-reader cameras, trackers and drones, installed as a signed APK, no account. Comparison: RF Sentinel vs SØPHIA.

Q: Is there a free alternative to SØPHIA / SophiaOps?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel covers passive BLE and WiFi recon with a radar view, risk scoring and a timeline, and adds sourced police, ALPR, tracker, Remote ID and smart-glasses signatures, patrol-vehicle grouping, fake cell tower signs, an offline camera map and Android Auto. It costs nothing and the full source is on GitHub. RF Sentinel is independent and not affiliated with SØPHIA or DetecX.

Q: Do I need Termux to scan for police on Android?
A:

Not with RF Sentinel. It is a regular Android app using the public BLE scan and WiFi scan APIs, so there's no Termux, Termux:API, Python or shell setup.

Q: How is it different from RF Party, BLE Radar (MetaRadar) or Flock You?
A:

RF Party (based on Alan Meekins' DEF CON 31 talk) and BLE Radar are general Bluetooth scanners: they list and track devices, with fewer police-specific rules. Flock You and OUI-Spy are ESP32 firmware focused on Flock and watchlist matching. RF Sentinel combines a sourced signature set (each rule cites the IEEE registry, Bluetooth SIG or published research), evidence fusion, patrol-vehicle grouping, WiFi and cell analysis, the OpenStreetMap camera layer and Android Auto in one Android app, and can ingest OUI-Spy and GhostESP boards. No code from those projects is included.

Q: Is there a Flock You app for Android? (Flock You alternative)
A:

Yes: RF Sentinel detects Flock Safety cameras on an Android phone with no extra hardware, and can also read a Flock You / OUI-Spy ESP32 board. Details

Flock You is open-source (MIT) ESP32 firmware focused on one target: Flock Safety cameras. It runs the radio in 2.4 GHz promiscuous mode, so it sees Flock cameras' WiFi probe requests and SoftAPs that a phone can't, plus Flock battery-pack BLE adverts, and beeps or feeds a dashboard.

RF Sentinel is a phone app that covers Flock as one category among many (body cams, patrol gear, trackers, drones, glasses, fake cell towers) and adds the OpenStreetMap / DeFlock camera map for cellular-only cameras. They combine well: plug an ESP32 running OUI-Spy's Flock-You mode into the phone and RF Sentinel shows its Flock detections next to its own. See ESP32 boards.

Q: Which Android app works with OUI-Spy? (OUI-Spy app for Android)
A:

RF Sentinel connects to OUI-Spy boards over USB OTG or Bluetooth and merges their detections with the phone's own. Setup

OUI-Spy is ESP32 firmware for the XIAO ESP32-S3 with several modes (Detector, Flock-You, Foxhunter, Sky Spy), a buzzer and LED, and a web flasher. OUI-APEX (lukeswitz's fork) runs those engines from one firmware and pairs with its own cross-platform app.

It isn't either/or: RF Sentinel reads OUI-Spy boards over USB, and OUI-SPY App-Controlled boards over Bluetooth, and merges their detections with the phone's own (blue ESP32 badge). The board gives range and radio modes a phone lacks; RF Sentinel adds its rule set, patrol-vehicle grouping, the camera map, alerts and Android Auto.

Q: Wardrive Go alternative: what's the difference with RF Sentinel?
A:

Wardrive Go (GPL-3.0, Android) is a wardriving app: it maps WiFi, Bluetooth and cellular networks, uploads to WiGLE and WDGWars, supports USB monitor-mode WiFi adapters and has channel / spectrum analyzers, Android Auto and a Wear OS companion. It also flags Flock cameras and Axon body cams.

RF Sentinel is built around detection and alerting rather than mapping for upload: sourced signatures with confidence tiers, evidence fusion, patrol-vehicle grouping, follower alerts, Remote ID decoding, fake-cell signs and warnings before mapped cameras. Use Wardrive Go to contribute to WiGLE; use RF Sentinel to be warned while you drive. Some of RF Sentinel's prefix data was cross-checked with Wardrive Go's lists.

Q: Fieldwatch alternative for detecting police and surveillance gear
A:

Fieldwatch (MIT, Android) is a receive-only WiFi and Bluetooth LE observer with customizable views, a filtering engine, an extensible signature library and reports, fully offline. It's a general field-survey tool.

RF Sentinel shares the receive-only, offline approach but is tuned for surveillance and police gear: alert tiers, patrol-vehicle grouping, tracker follow detection, drone and cell analysis, the camera map and Android Auto. Part of RF Sentinel's prefix data was cross-checked with Fieldwatch's list.

Q: SØPHIA vs RF Sentinel: what's the difference?
A:

SØPHIA is a closed-source passive BLE and WiFi recon app for Android sold by DetecX. RF Sentinel does the same kind of passive WiFi and Bluetooth recon for free and open source, with police, ALPR, tracker, drone and fake-cell detection, a camera map and Android Auto. Full comparison: RF Sentinel vs SØPHIA.

Q: Flock-You for Android alternative
A:

Flock-You (Android) is a separate counter-surveillance app with broad multi-protocol ambitions (BLE, WiFi, cellular, GNSS, ultrasonic) and Flipper Zero integration. RF Sentinel stays with what a phone's radios can verify, cites a source for every rule, and connects to ESP32 boards instead of a Flipper. Part of RF Sentinel's prefix data was cross-checked with its list.

Q: Best app to detect surveillance over both Bluetooth and WiFi (instead of AirGuard, BLE Radar, WiFi analyzers)
A:

Many good tools cover one radio or one job:

- Bluetooth only: AirGuard (AirTag / Find My tracker protection), BLE Radar (MetaRadar) (BLE environment monitoring and custom filters), nRF Connect (a developer's BLE scanner), RF Party (BLE from the DEF CON 31 talk).

- WiFi only: WiFi analyzer apps show access points and channels but don't identify police or surveillance gear.

- Cell only: EFF's Rayhunter (IMSI catcher detection on dedicated hardware).

- Mapping: WiGLE WiFi Wardriving and Wardrive Go map networks for upload.

RF Sentinel puts Bluetooth LE, WiFi and cell analysis in one app, so evidence from different radios can add up (e.g. a router, a radio and a printer moving together = possible police vehicle). A single-radio tool can't make that connection.

Q: Is there an iPhone version?
A:

No. iOS hides Bluetooth MAC addresses and most advertisement fields from apps, offers no WiFi scan API, and doesn't expose cell information, so most of RF Sentinel's detection can't run there. It is Android only.

### Install, update, devices

Q: Something isn't working. What should I send?
A:

In RF Sentinel, for hardware (USB adapters, RTL-SDR, ESP32, OUI-SPY, Meshtastic) and Sentinel Link: Settings → External hardware → Export all hardware logs makes one text file with every log that has something in it, or Export a hardware log sends just one. If the app closed by itself: Settings → Lists, tools & about → Export crash log. The logs hold no nearby device addresses or names, network names, positions or server names. Attach them to a GitHub issue. What each log records: Hardware logs.

Q: Why does the scan find 0 devices?
A:

Location is probably off. Android gives apps no Bluetooth or WiFi scan results while the phone's Location is off, even with every permission granted. Turn it on in the quick settings; RF Sentinel's main screen says so and opens the setting when you tap the warning. Also check that it has location and "Nearby devices".

Q: Is RF Sentinel free? Are there ads or in-app purchases?
A:

RF Sentinel is free, no ads, no in-app purchases, no subscription, no account. Licensed GPL-3.0.

Q: Is it on Google Play or F-Droid?
A:

RF Sentinel is not on Google Play. The signed APK is published on GitHub Releases for every version, and Obtainium can install it and keep it updated from there. An F-Droid listing has been submitted and is waiting for review. See the install guide.

Q: How do I install the APK?
A:

- On the phone, open the latest release.

- Under Assets, tap the file ending in -release.apk (not "Source code"). For a build with only free software, take the one ending in -foss.apk instead.

- Open the downloaded file from the notification or Files → Downloads.

- If Android blocks it, tap Settings, enable Allow from this source, go back and tap Install.

- Open RF Sentinel. The setup wizard covers theme, region, alerts, camera download radius and permissions.

Q: Is the APK safe?
A:

RF Sentinel's full source is public, every release is signed with the same release key (Android refuses an update signed with a different key), and you can build it yourself with ./gradlew assembleDebug. The app requests no contacts, storage or microphone permissions; the normal build asks for the camera only when you open Locate's camera view (which runs on Google Play Services for AR), and the -foss.apk has no camera permission at all. Play Protect may warn about any app installed outside Google Play; that warning is about the install source, not a scan result.

Q: How do I update?
A:

Install the newer RF Sentinel APK over the existing one. Settings, history and watchlist are kept.

Q: Which Android versions and phones are supported?
A:

RF Sentinel runs on Android 8.0 (API 26) and newer, on any ARM phone with Bluetooth LE, 64-bit or 32-bit: Pixel, Samsung, Motorola, OnePlus, Xiaomi and others. Hidden-network WiFi details need Android 11+. Bluetooth 5 extended advertising and LE Coded PHY (long range) are used automatically where the chip supports them.

Q: Does it need root?
A:

No. RF Sentinel uses only public Android APIs.

Q: Why does it ask for location?
A:

Android ties Bluetooth and WiFi scan results to the location permission (up to Android 11 always, and still for WiFi scans and cell info). RF Sentinel also uses GPS for traces, follow detection and camera warnings. Nearby devices (Bluetooth scan) is required; notifications, Display over other apps (bubble) and Nearby devices → connect (only to list your paired car) are optional.

Q: Scanning stops on Samsung / Xiaomi / OnePlus. What do I do?
A:

Some manufacturers kill background apps aggressively. Scanning runs as a foreground service with a notification, but you may still need to set RF Sentinel's battery usage to Unrestricted. Settings has a shortcut to Android's battery optimization screen.

Q: The map closes the app (or the app closes when I open the map). What do I do?
A:

This happened on some older phones (seen on Android 9) whose graphics chip has no Vulkan: earlier builds drew the map with Vulkan only, so opening the map closed the app, and it did it again at every launch until the app's data was cleared. Version 2.20 picks Vulkan only where the phone has it and OpenGL everywhere else. If the app closes while the map starts for any other reason, it now tries the map again with OpenGL at the next launch, and after a second failure it takes the map off the main screen and tells you, so the rest of the app opens (add it back with the Map view button). On an earlier build, clearing the app's data (Android Settings → Apps → RF Sentinel → Storage) opens the app again, but the map will close it again. If it still happens, Settings → Lists, tools & about → Export crash log and send it: it helps to know the phone model and Android version.

### How detection works

Q: How does passive Bluetooth LE detection work?
A:

BLE devices broadcast advertising packets on channels 37, 38 and 39 so other devices can find them. Each packet carries an address, flags and optional fields: device name, 16/128-bit service UUIDs, service data, manufacturer data with a Bluetooth SIG company ID, TX power. RF Sentinel receives these through Android's BluetoothLeScanner and matches every field against its rules. It never connects, so the device never knows it was seen.

Q: What is a MAC vendor prefix (OUI) and why does it matter?
A:

The first 3 bytes of a public MAC address (MA-L), or 3.5 / 4.5 bytes for MA-M / MA-S blocks, are assigned by the IEEE to a company. If a device uses its public address, the prefix reveals the maker, e.g. 00:25:DF is Axon Enterprise. RF Sentinel ships the IEEE registry offline and regional watchlist presets (Global, Canada, US) of law-enforcement and surveillance makers, each prefix re-checked against its registrant. Devices using random private addresses defeat prefix matching, which is why payload signatures and fingerprint linking matter more.

Q: What do weak, probable and strong mean?
A:

Every RF Sentinel match gets one of three tiers:

| Tier | Confidence | Meaning |

| Weak (verify) | < 50 | Identifier shared with many unrelated products. Amber, silent by default. |

| Probable | 50-79 | Vendor-specific identifier. Alerts at the default threshold. |

| Strong | 80+ | Payload tag, or a network name the vendor gives its own devices. |

Q: What is evidence fusion?
A:

In RF Sentinel, when different rules of the same category match one device, the scores combine by noisy-OR, with each supporting hit discounted by half because rules often share evidence: 1 - (1 - top) × Π(1 - 0.5 × support). Hits under 30 never corroborate, and fusion never exceeds 90. Example: watchlisted address 70 + Zebra serial name 50 → 78.

Q: Devices change their Bluetooth address. How does it keep track?
A:

RF Sentinel uses a structural advert fingerprint that survives address rotation: names, service UUIDs, service-data and company-ID payload sizes, TX power and connectable flag. When a new private address appears with the same fingerprint as exactly one device that went silent 1.5-30 s earlier, it inherits that device's matches (at −5), follow history and ignore state. Apple-Continuity-only adverts (phones) are never linked, and two identical candidates means no link.

Q: Can I add my own devices or signatures?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's watchlist takes exact addresses, vendor prefixes (MA-L / MA-M / MA-S) and name or vendor rules, each with a label and score, plus the regional presets. It exports as JSON. Long-press any device to add it.

Q: I found an unidentified device. How do I report it?
A:

In RF Sentinel, long-press it → Report unknown device. The report shows exactly what is shared before you send it: vendor prefix, name pattern with serial digits hidden, service and manufacturer IDs. No full address, serial, location or time. Paste it into a GitHub issue or share it on Discord. New signatures need a registry or published source; guesses aren't merged.

### Range, accuracy, battery, screen off

Q: How far away can it detect devices?
A:

RF Sentinel's range depends on the transmitter's power, walls, bodies and your phone's antenna. Bluetooth LE from a body camera is typically heard at tens of metres in the open and much less through a vehicle or building; WiFi access points carry further. Phones with LE Coded PHY hear Bluetooth 5 long-range adverts further. An external ESP32 board with a better antenna extends range. Phone radios are weaker than dedicated hardware, so expect fewer catches than purpose-built scanners.

Q: Can it tell the distance or direction of a device?
A:

RF Sentinel estimates distance from RSSI, often off by 2-3×. The radar view places stronger signals closer to the centre. A phone can't measure angle of arrival from one reading, so flagged devices get a direction from your turns: turn round slowly with the phone in front of you, and your body blocks the signal from behind. Two turns in different places cross into a position that stays put as you walk. To find a device, use Locate: its chest sweep locks a direction with an arrow (the normal build can also do it through the camera, which tracks the phone's own movement), and it beeps faster as the signal grows. Reflections can still point it the wrong way, so sweep again somewhere else to cross-check.

Q: Why does WiFi only update every 30 seconds?
A:

Android throttles apps like RF Sentinel to about four WiFi scans per two minutes. The default 30-second interval stays within that limit. Bluetooth LE is continuous.

Q: Why doesn't it see WiFi phones, laptops or cameras connected to a network?
A:

RF Sentinel uses Android's WiFi scan, which only lists access points (beacons and probe responses). Client devices, such as an in-car laptop connected to the car's router, need monitor mode, which Android doesn't offer without root and a supported chip. An ESP32 board can partly fill that gap.

Q: Does it work with the screen off?
A:

Partly, for RF Sentinel. Android pauses app Bluetooth scanning while the screen is off, and on some phones (a Pixel in our tests) no Bluetooth results arrive at all until the screen is back on. WiFi, the fake-cell checks, known-camera warnings and ESP32 / USB hardware keep working. Keep the screen on for Bluetooth: the car-mount default "keep screen on while charging" does that while driving. Android Auto warns you when a scan starts with the phone screen off and shows "Bluetooth limited" on its home screen.

Q: How much battery does it use?
A:

RF Sentinel's continuous scanning costs battery. Settings → BLE scan mode offers Low latency (default, catches the most), Balanced and Low power, and the WiFi interval is adjustable. Auto-start in the car scans only while you drive.

Q: What can't it detect at all?
A:

RF Sentinel can't detect anything that doesn't broadcast BLE or WiFi beacons: cellular-only devices (most non-Flock plate readers, LTE GPS trackers), wired cameras, radios' voice channels, radar and lidar, devices switched off or in a non-advertising state, and WiFi clients. Cameras in OpenStreetMap are covered by the map layer instead.

### Android Auto and driving

Q: Is there a police detector app for Android Auto?
A:

RF Sentinel runs in Android Auto: threat headline, the next known camera on your way, recent alerts, Start/Stop and mute on the home screen, device lists with the phone's filters, cell towers, hardware status, a live OpenStreetMap map with devices, cameras and drones, OSM navigation with spoken turns, and alerts as heads-up cards through the car speakers with Mute (snooze) and Ignore buttons. See Android Auto.

Q: RF Sentinel doesn't show up in Android Auto. How do I fix it?
A:

In a real car, Android Auto only shows apps built with Google's Car App Library, like RF Sentinel, when they were installed from a trusted store (Google Play or ONE store). Its Unknown sources developer setting covers media and messaging apps, not these (Google's testing guide), so the GitHub APK's car screens can't appear there; they run on Google's Desktop Head Unit emulator. It still works in the car through the app types that setting covers: in Android Auto settings tap Version ten times, open ⋮ → Developer settings, enable Unknown sources and reconnect. RF Sentinel then shows a media-style screen (threats, cameras, alerts, status, with Scan and Mute buttons), and each alert arrives as a message you can have read aloud; reply "mute" to snooze alerts (30 minutes unless you change it under Alerts). Tick it under Customize launcher if it's missing.

Q: Can I use it with Waze or Google Maps on screen?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel's floating threat bubble (needs Display over other apps) sits over any app: green when clear, orange for probable, red for strong or a follower, with the count. Each new alert shows a small card beside it for a few seconds saying what was detected, its type and distance. Tap to open, drag to move. Spoken alerts briefly lower other audio.

Q: Can it start by itself when I get in the car?
A:

Yes. In RF Sentinel, Settings → Start scanning automatically in the car: pick your car's Bluetooth. Scanning starts when the phone connects to it or to Android Auto, and stops when you leave if the car started it.

### ESP32, OUI-Spy, GhostESP, Marauder

Q: Can I use an ESP32 with RF Sentinel?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel supports them. Plug a board running OUI-Spy , GhostESP or ESP32 Marauder into the phone with a USB OTG cable while scanning, or pair an OUI-SPY board running the Bluetooth (App-Controlled) firmware wirelessly. Its detections merge into the list with a blue ESP32 badge. Native-USB boards (S2/S3/C3/C5/C6) and CP210x / CH340 bridges work. See ESP32 boards.

Q: How do I pair an OUI-SPY board over Bluetooth?
A:

With the board on, open RF Sentinel's Settings → Pair OUI-SPY board: the app looks for the board's Bluetooth service for a few seconds (scanning needn't be running) and lists OUI-SPY-xxxx. Pair only there, not in Android's Bluetooth settings: the board keeps no pairing keys, so a phone-side bond breaks the link (the app tells you to tap Forget if it finds one).

If no board is found: the board stops advertising while another app is connected to it, so force-stop the OUI-SPY app (Android App info → Force stop, not just swiping it away) and unplug the board for a few seconds. Use the App-Controlled (node) firmware, which shows up as OUI-SPY-xxxx, and check that Bluetooth is on and Nearby devices is allowed.

Q: Can I use a USB WiFi adapter like the ALFA AWUS036ACS, AWUS1900, AWUS036ACM, AWUS036AXML, AWUS036H or AWUS036NHA with Android?
A:

Yes, with RF Sentinel 2.11+. Plug an RTL8811AU / RTL8821AU adapter (e.g. AWUS036ACS) into the phone with an OTG cable while scanning and allow USB access. RF Sentinel drives it directly over Android's USB host API (no root), in receive-only monitor mode on the 2.4 GHz channels (5 GHz too since 2.17, experimental: Settings → External hardware): no 30-second scan limit, longer range, and it hears client devices (laptops, phones, cameras on a network) that a phone's WiFi scan can't. The driver is ported from Wardrive Go (GPL-3.0). Since 2.12, RTL8812BU / RTL8822BU adapters (TP-Link Archer T3U, ASUS USB-AC53/AC55/AC58, Edimax EW-7822U*, generic AC1200 dongles) work too, on 2.4 and 5 GHz, with a driver ported from OpenIPC devourer (GPL-2.0); single-antenna dongles are handled automatically. With an adapter plugged in, RF Sentinel can also list the WiFi names nearby devices ask for (Menu → Requested networks) and alert when a watched name is asked for. Since 2.13, RTL8814AU (AWUS1900) and MT7612U (AWUS036ACM) adapters work on 2.4 and 5 GHz, RTL8187 (AWUS036H) and RT3070 (AWUS036NH / NEH) on 2.4 GHz, and AR9271 (AWUS036NHA) experimentally; if one misbehaves, Settings → External hardware → Export a hardware log → USB WiFi adapter makes a text file to send. Since 2.19, the WiFi 6E MT7921AU (ALFA AWUS036AXML / AXM, Comfast CF-952AX, Netgear A8000, TP-Link TXE50UH) works on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz (tested on an ALFA), with a driver ported from mt76-usb-macos (BSD-3-Clause-Clear). RTL8812AU and RTL8811CU / 8821CU are recognised but not supported yet.

Supported chips and adapters: External hardware.

Q: How do I see the cell towers my Android phone is connected to?
A:

RF Sentinel's Tools button → Cell towers lists the serving cell and its neighbours live (2G-5G, operator, MCC-MNC, area code, cell ID, PCI, channel, signal) and every tower seen while scanning. They also appear in the live list (Cells filter) and optionally on the map at the spot where the signal was strongest. An optional alert says when the serving tower changes. No online lookup is made, so nothing reveals where you are.

Q: Is there a WiFi channel and spectrum analyzer in RF Sentinel?
A:

Yes: RF Sentinel's Tools → WiFi channels (networks and strongest signal per channel) and WiFi spectrum (each network as a curve across its channel width) for 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, from the phone's own scans.

Q: Does it work with Flipper Zero or a WiFi Pineapple?
A:

With RF Sentinel, a Flipper Zero with an ESP32 board running Marauder (for example the BFFB) works since 2.11.1: plug the Flipper into the phone and open GPIO → USB-UART Bridge. A WiFi Pineapple isn't supported. Other supported hardware: ESP32 boards running OUI-Spy, GhostESP or Marauder, and RTL8811AU / 8821AU or RTL8812BU / 8822BU USB WiFi adapters.

Q: Can I use ESP32 Marauder or an ESP32-C5 board for 5 GHz WiFi on Android?
A:

Yes, with RF Sentinel 2.11.1+. Plug a board running ESP32 Marauder into the phone with a USB OTG cable while scanning. RF Sentinel runs only its passive beacon and probe sniffers and adds the networks and client devices to the list. On ESP32-C5 boards (Marauder v8, BFFB v2, LilyGo T-Dongle C5, C5 DevKit) that includes 5 GHz. Keep Channel Hop on in Marauder's settings. See ESP32 boards.

### Sentinel Link and Meshtastic

Q: Can two phones running RF Sentinel share what they detect?
A:

Yes, with RF Sentinel's Sentinel Link. Linked phones show the same devices on their list, radar and map, whichever phone heard them first, including what any phone's ESP32 board, USB WiFi adapter or RTL-SDR picks up. A device another phone heard is marked VIA with that phone's name, its alerts say "via NAME", and the Sentinels filter chip shows only those.

- On both phones: Settings → Sentinel Link → Open Sentinel Link, and give each phone a name.

- Keep them close. Tap Link up a Sentinel on one and Join a Sentinel on the other; allow "Nearby devices" if asked.

- Both show a 6-digit code. Same code: tap Confirm on both. Different code: Cancel.

Linked phones then share while they scan, whenever they are in Bluetooth range, and find each other again by themselves. A third phone joins the same way, from any phone of the group. The link is encrypted with a key agreed through the 6-digit code; the phones' Bluetooth adverts only carry a changing tag that means nothing without the group's key; nothing goes through the internet.

Q: Can Sentinels far apart share through Meshtastic?
A:

Yes, through Meshtastic LoRa nodes, one paired with each phone over Bluetooth. This part is not yet tested on real hardware: it follows Meshtastic's phone API and passes its tests, but hasn't been tried with a real node. Reports are welcome on Discord or GitHub.

- Hardware: a LoRa board with the official Meshtastic firmware, e.g. Heltec V3, LilyGO T-Beam, or a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 with its Wio-SX1262 LoRa board (a plain ESP32 has no LoRa radio). Set its LoRa region once in the Meshtastic app.

- Set up: link the phones with Sentinel Link first, disconnect the Meshtastic app from the node, then in Sentinel Link → Meshtastic node turn on "Use a Meshtastic node" and pick it. If Android asks for a PIN, it's on the node's screen, or 123456. Start a scan: the status goes to "Meshtastic node · channel N, encrypted".

- Channel: RF Sentinel adds a private channel named RFSentinel to a free slot of the node, with a key made from the group's key, so only your group reads it. Packets are also encrypted and signed with the group's key.

- What goes out: LoRa is slow, so each packet carries the phone's position once and a few devices: watchlist matches first (within about 20 s, then every minute), then flagged devices, then everything else, one packet every minute by default (15 s to 5 min). Whitelisted devices are never sent.

- Step by step: Sentinel Link setup. Not working? See Sentinel Link & Meshtastic troubleshooting: every status line and what to do.

### Privacy, safety and legality

Q: Does RF Sentinel transmit or jam anything?
A:

No. RF Sentinel never transmits, jams, spoofs or connects to the devices it detects. (The phone's own WiFi scan sends standard probe requests like any phone looking for networks, and an OUI-SPY board in relay mode does the same; that can be turned off. Sentinel Link, when you set it up, sends encrypted messages to your own linked phones and Meshtastic node only.)

Q: Can police or anyone tell I'm running it?
A:

The app itself sends nothing to the devices it scans. Your phone, like every phone, may still advertise its own Bluetooth and probe for WiFi networks independently of RF Sentinel.

Q: What data does it collect?
A:

None leaves the phone: RF Sentinel has no accounts, no analytics, no crash reporting. Detections are stored in a local database excluded from cloud backup. Network requests go only to map services: the map (vector tiles, styles and fonts from OpenFreeMap, built on OpenStreetMap data, or from Mapbox if you choose it in Settings, with its usage statistics switched off), the roads of your area while the Waze option to alert only for reports on your road is on, Overpass camera data from overpass-api.de or its mirrors, DeFlock's region files and, navigation (on the phone or in Android Auto), Photon and Nominatim for place search and Valhalla for routes. They see your IP and the area or route, never your scans. Two optional sources are off by default: police aircraft (a position rounded to about 1 km is sent to the ADS-B feeds adsb.fi / adsb.lol, unless you turn the online feeds off and use only an RTL-SDR's own ADS-B receiver) and Waze reports, either through your own OpenWeb Ninja API key or straight from Waze (Waze direct: your IP address and a position rounded to a 1 km grid, never your exact position), third-party services used at your own risk.

Q: Is it legal to detect police equipment?
A:

RF Sentinel only receives signals that devices broadcast publicly by design, and it doesn't decode private communications. Passive reception of Bluetooth and WiFi advertisements is generally lawful, but rules differ by country and state, and some places restrict use in vehicles or of radar detectors. Check your local laws. This is not legal advice.

Q: What is it meant for?
A:

RF Sentinel is meant for awareness, research and personal privacy: knowing which surveillance devices are around you, finding trackers, documenting plate-reader deployments. A detection says a device with a given signature is nearby; it isn't proof of who is present or what they're doing.

### Themes, data, contributing

Q: Is there a Watch Dogs / DedSec or Mr. Robot theme?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel has both. DedSec (Watch Dogs 2-inspired: black, white and electric blue, poster banner, sliced wordmark, a marcus@ctOS-2.0:~$ terminal typing hacktivist lines) and fsociety (Mr. Robot-inspired: black and blood red, striped wordmark, a root@fsociety:~# terminal typing quotes from the show). Unofficial fan homages, not affiliated with Ubisoft or NBCUniversal. Eleven more themes include Night Drive (red-only HUD for night driving), Night Vision, Amber CRT, Synthwave, Tactical, Blueprint, Paper and Material You.

Q: Can I export detections?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel exports the current scan as CSV, JSON or KML; all devices ever seen as CSV or JSON; the match log as CSV, JSON, GPX or KML; GPS traces with their devices as GPX, KML, GeoJSON or CSV; the watchlist as JSON; or everything in one JSON file.

Q: Is it open source? Can I build it myself?
A:

Yes, RF Sentinel is GPL-3.0, 100% Kotlin. Requirements: Android Studio, or JDK 17+ with the Android SDK.
git clone https://github.com/CIS-C0/RFSentinel
cd RFSentinel
./gradlew assembleDebug

tools/gen_assets.py regenerates the offline IEEE and Bluetooth SIG databases and fails if any prefix used in code stops matching its registrant.

Q: How can I help?
A:

Help RF Sentinel: report unknown devices with the in-app report, submit sourced signatures, map cameras in OpenStreetMap / DeFlock, file bugs on GitHub, join the Discord, and star the repo so others find it.

---

# RTL-SDR on Android: Step-by-Step Guide | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/sdr-guide.html

Plug an RTL-SDR or HackRF into an Android phone and use it with RF Sentinel: radio sweep, waterfall, ADS-B without internet, P25 talkgroups and voice, pagers, every status line.

rf_sentinel / guides / sdr-guide

## RTL-SDR guide

An RTL-SDR dongle or a HackRF One on the phone's USB port lets RF Sentinel hear radios the phone can't: two-way radios transmitting nearby, aircraft on 1090 MHz, P25 trunked-radio signalling and pager messages. This page goes from plugging it in to reading each screen.

### What you need

- An SDR: an RTL-SDR with an R820T, R820T2, R860 or R828D tuner (RTL-SDR Blog V3 or V4, for example), or a HackRF One (receive only, its transmitter stays off). An RTL-SDR does everything here; a HackRF costs more and adds nothing.

- A USB-C OTG adapter or cable if the dongle has a USB-A plug. A short cable keeps the dongle's noise away from the phone.

- An antenna for what you want to hear. The stock telescopic antenna works for the radio sweep. For aircraft, a 1090 MHz antenna hears much farther (the stock one about 50 km).

- No dongle on the phone? An RTL-SDR plugged into a computer on your WiFi works too: run rtl_tcp -a 0.0.0.0 on it and enter its address under Settings → RTL-SDR radio → Network SDR (port 1234 if left out). It streams about 5 MB/s, and rtl_tcp has no password: only on a network you trust. A USB SDR plugged into the phone is used first.

### 1. Plug it in

- Start a scan in RF Sentinel, then plug the SDR in.

- Android asks to allow USB access: allow it. Tick "always" so it doesn't ask again.

- Check the status line under Settings → External hardware. It reads like "RTL-SDR · starting…", then names what it's doing. With more than one SDR plugged in, pick which one to use there.

- The USB port at the top suits a dongle: Settings → General → Screen rotation → Always upside down turns the app around.

### 2. Choose what it does

Settings → RTL-SDR radio → Scan with the SDR. Tick any mix:

| Scan | What it does | Also needs |

| Radio activity sweep | Sweeps the two-way radio bands and reports strong transmissions near you, by signal strength. With Play voice transmissions on, it also plays them. | What to detect → Two-way radio |

| ADS-B aircraft receiver | Hears aircraft on 1090 MHz and checks them against the police and government aircraft list, with no internet. | What to detect → Police / government aircraft |

| P25 control channel (experimental) | Finds a P25 trunked system's control channel (700 / 800 MHz, United States and Canada) and shows which talkgroups get a call, and when. | What to detect → Two-way radio |

| Pager messages (experimental) | Finds paging channels and decodes POCSAG and FLEX pages. | What to detect → Two-way radio |

One SDR hears one thing at a time. With more than one ticked, it takes turns (60 s each by default, 30 to 300 s, set per scan under each one's "Time for" slider), and each scan hears nothing while another has its turn. Tick only one to give it all the time. "idle: no scan ticked" in the status means nothing is ticked.

Receiving radio signalling, pages or calls is legal in many places but not all, and some places forbid it in a vehicle or forbid passing on what you hear. Check the law where you are.

### 3. Radio activity sweep

Alerts say "Radio transmitting nearby". The settings under Radio sweep tune it:

- Sensitivity (default 30 dB above the noise): lower hears farther, with more false alarms. Below about 10 dB the noise itself sets off alerts: only for testing how far a known radio carries.

- Bands to sweep: untick the bands you don't care about to sweep faster. Your own bands adds ranges in MHz ("380-400 TETRA").

- Never report these ranges: a busy business band or your own radio that keeps alerting.

- Watch these frequencies: always reported when active, whatever the sensitivity ("154.4300 County fire dispatch").

- Frequency names: import a CSV (a RadioReference export, CHIRP or any file with a frequency and a name column) so hits are named. In the US, RadioReference can also name nearby FCC licences with your own Premium login and developer key.

- Detect TETRA radios (on by default in Europe), DMR radios and cellular transmitters (experimental) look for each one's burst rhythm or uplink energy. Each is a weak sign on its own.

- Say the frequency: alerts say the frequency (and its name) instead of "Radio transmitting nearby".

- TETRA hunting: a second (and third) RTL-SDR plugged in watches 380-385 MHz nonstop while the first keeps sweeping; with two extra dongles each takes half of the band. TETRA only puts every dongle on that band and pauses the other scans. City mode needs a stronger signal, for towns full of radios. TETRA beeps speed up as a radio gets closer, and the main screen shows a TETRA bar (Far / Closer / Very close) while one is heard. The status line shows which part of the band each dongle watches ("TETRA watch · RX2 380.0-382.4 MHz").

- Play voice transmissions (experimental, off by default): when the sweep hears a new transmission, the SDR tunes to it and plays the voice through the speaker, headphones or car, then sweeps on once it goes quiet (1 minute at most). Analog radios (walkie-talkies, businesses) and digital radios that aren't encrypted: P25, DMR (MOTOTRBO, Hytera) and NXDN48 (Kenwood NEXEDGE, Icom IDAS); encrypted and other digital radios stay silent. Walkie-talkies (FRS / GMRS / MURS) are played on their own channel, not the ghosts a strong one makes next to it, and a reply on that channel plays at once. Spoken alerts wait for a pause in the voice (10 s at most). Not while the radio waterfall is open.

- Tire sensors: the 315 and 433.92 MHz tire-pressure sensors of cars around you. The same car's wheels heard with you at place after place is a vehicle following you; your own car's sensors are learned first and never alert. A tire sensor heard with a flagged Bluetooth device again after a gap, or across 3 places 2 km apart, ties them to one vehicle.

#### Radio waterfall

Tools → Radio waterfall shows each sweep as a row; zoom into a few channels for a live view. The sweep and ADS-B pause while it's open. Tune offers:

- Listen: plays the frequency you zoomed into, at the phone's media volume.

- Find a remote's frequency: like a Flipper Zero's frequency analyzer. Wait for "Ready", then press and hold a button on a key fob, garage opener or sensor a few times. It shows the frequency heard and how strong; Tune to it zooms there. It first learns what's already on the air, so that isn't shown.

- Presets: FM radio, aircraft voice, weather radio, marine, walkie-talkies (FRS / GMRS), ham 2 m, sensors and European car keys (433.92 MHz), North American car keys and garage openers (315 MHz), and aircraft transponders. Or type a frequency.

### 4. ADS-B aircraft

- Turn on What to detect → Police / government aircraft overhead, then tick ADS-B aircraft receiver.

- The status reads "ADS-B · listening on 1090 MHz…", then "N aircraft heard, N with a position".

- Open Tools → Aircraft. The sources line shows how many came from your SDR and how many from the online feeds. With the SDR working you can turn the online feeds off and send nothing to anyone.

"the tuner didn't lock on 1090 MHz": unplug and plug the dongle back in. Few aircraft heard: put the antenna higher and clear of the car's roof, or use a 1090 MHz antenna.

### 5. P25 talkgroups

- Tick P25 control channel (on by default when your region is the United States or Canada).

- The status reads "P25 · looking for a control channel…". It sweeps 769-775 and 851-869 MHz and keeps the first channel whose messages check out. No calibration needed.

- Once found: "P25 · control channel … · N messages". Open Tools → P25 talkgroups to see which talkgroups get calls, live, and History for the past days.

"no control channel heard here · looking again shortly": there is no 700 / 800 MHz P25 system in range, or the antenna can't hear it. Systems on VHF or UHF aren't searched.

#### P25 settings

- Watch these talkgroups: one per line, number and optional name ("1234 Sheriff dispatch"). 23* watches every talkgroup starting with 23, * all of them. A watched talkgroup alerts when a call starts.

- Talkgroup alerts: untick Voice or Sound so alerts don't talk over P25 voice.

- Keep the P25 call log: days of calls kept on the phone (about 1 MB per busy day) for History and Export. 0 keeps nothing.

- Alert on unusual talkgroup activity: a talkgroup three times busier than usual for that hour. Needs a few days of call log first.

- Listen for radios keying up nearby: a strong signal where a call's radio transmits means that radio is close to you, not just on the system.

#### Listening to P25 voice (experimental)

Listen to P25 voice: Off, Watched talkgroups, or All clear calls. Clear (not encrypted) calls play through the speaker, headphones or car, one call at a time, up to 2 minutes each. Encrypted calls can't be played. On the P25 talkgroups screen, Mute pauses it, and Hold (or tapping a talkgroup) plays only that talkgroup until Release. While a call plays, the SDR is off the control channel and misses its messages.

Save played calls (on by default) keeps the sound of every call played, and of every transmission Play voice transmissions plays, on the phone only. Listen again on the P25 talkgroups screen → menu → Played calls: tap one to hear it, Share sends them as WAV files. The last 200 are kept, about 1 MB per minute of P25 voice (walkie-talkies take about 4 MB per minute).

Transcribe P25 calls (experimental, Android 13+, off by default): each saved call is turned into text by Android's own on-device speech recognition and shown under the call in Played calls. Nothing leaves the phone. Android allows its speech recognition only with the microphone permission, so it is asked when you turn this on; the microphone is never opened. For other languages, download them for offline speech in Android's settings.

A call that sounds wrong? Tick Record P25 voice calls: the next clear calls are saved as raw radio files (about 1 MB each, the last ones kept), and Share P25 recordings sends them to the developer to fix the decoder.

### 6. Pager messages

- Tick Pager messages. The status reads "pagers · looking for a paging channel…".

- If you know your paging frequency, enter it under Pager frequencies ("466.075 Fire dispatch"): the SDR stays there instead of searching, so a quiet channel isn't missed. With two or more, the Pager messages screen gets a button for each.

- Read pages in Tools → Pager messages. They stay in the phone's memory only: never saved, exported or sent, and gone when the app closes.

- Watch these pagers: a capcode (a line starting with a number) or words in the page text. One alert a minute at most per line.

- Ignore these pagers: capcodes dropped with no list entry and no alert.

- Show page text in alerts: off by default; pages can hold private or medical details.

### What the status line means

| Status | What to do |

| … found - allow USB access on the prompt | Allow it on Android's prompt. No prompt? Unplug and plug it back in. |

| couldn't open it | Another app may hold the dongle: close it, then replug. |

| idle: no scan ticked | Tick a scan in Settings → RTL-SDR radio. |

| unplugged or not answering | Check the OTG cable and replug. The status clears after 15 s once it's gone. |

| can't reach it (Network SDR) | Check rtl_tcp runs with -a 0.0.0.0 and that the phone is on the same WiFi. It retries every 10 s. |

| waterfall … radio watch paused | Normal while Tools → Radio waterfall is open. |

| no samples from the SDR · restarting it | The dongle stalled; the app restarts it. Often it's weak USB power: try a powered hub or a shorter cable. |

### Something not working? Send the log

Settings → External hardware → Export a hardware log → RTL-SDR / HackRF saves what the SDR did: start-up, turns, errors and restarts. Each piece of hardware (USB WiFi, USB Bluetooth, ESP32, mesh radio, OUI-SPY) and each Sentinel Link path has its own log; Export all hardware logs puts them in one file. It holds no nearby device's address or network name. Attach it to a GitHub issue with your dongle's model and what you expected.

### Q&A

Q: Does the radio sweep listen to calls?
A:

Not by default in RF Sentinel. It measures how much energy each channel carries. Two experimental options play audio: Play voice transmissions (the sweep's new transmissions: analog radios and unencrypted P25, DMR and NXDN) and Listen to P25 voice (unencrypted calls on a P25 trunked system). Encrypted calls can't be played.

Q: Can I use ADS-B and the sweep at the same time?
A:

With one SDR, RF Sentinel has them take turns. Two SDRs don't split the work yet: one is used, picked under External hardware.

Q: How much battery does it use?
A:

With RF Sentinel, the dongle is powered by the phone, so the battery drains faster than with the phone alone. In a car, keep the phone charging.

---

# Share Detections Between Phones: Sentinel Link | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/sentinel-link-setup.html

Set up RF Sentinel's Sentinel Link: link phones over Bluetooth, reach phones kilometres away with Meshtastic LoRa nodes, or anywhere through your own MQTT broker.

rf_sentinel / guides / sentinel-link-setup

## Sentinel Link setup

Sentinel Link lets RF Sentinel phones share what they detect: each phone of a group shows the devices the others hear on its list, radar and map, marked VIA with the phone's name. Phones reach each other three ways, and you can use any mix of them.

| Path | Reach | Needs | Speed |

| Bluetooth | About 10 to 30 m | Nothing extra | Everything, right away |

| Meshtastic | Kilometres, more through other nodes | One Meshtastic LoRa node per phone | A few devices per packet, one packet a minute by default |

| Internet relay | Anywhere with mobile data | An MQTT broker, ideally your own | Up to 8 packets every 5 s |

Every path needs the phones to be linked into a group first (step 1). All of them only share while a scan runs, and everything is encrypted with the group's key.

### 1. Link the phones (once)

- Install the same RF Sentinel version on every phone.

- On each phone: Settings → Sentinel Link → Open Sentinel Link, and fill in This phone's name. It's the name the others see next to VIA and in "via NAME" alerts.

- Put the two phones side by side. Tap Link up a Sentinel on one and Join a Sentinel on the other. Allow "Nearby devices" if Android asks.

- Both screens show a 6-digit code. Same code on both: tap Confirm on both. Different code: Cancel on both and start again.

- A third phone joins the same way, from any phone already in the group.

The phones agree on the group's key through that code; a phone that wasn't there can't read the group. To leave, tap Leave the group: that phone forgets the key and stops sharing.

### 2. Bluetooth (phones nearby)

On by default once linked (Share over Bluetooth). Start a scan on both phones: the status reads "Sentinel Link · 1 Sentinel linked" when they're in range, and they find each other again by themselves after going out of range. Their devices show under the Sentinels chip.

For phones that are always far apart, turn Share over Bluetooth off and use one of the paths below, so the status doesn't sit on "waiting for Sentinels".

### 3. Meshtastic (phones kilometres apart)

#### What you need

- One node per phone: a LoRa board running the official Meshtastic firmware, for example a Heltec V3, a LilyGO T-Beam, or a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 with its Wio-SX1262 LoRa board. A plain ESP32 has no LoRa radio.

- Its antenna, always screwed on before the node is powered.

#### Prepare each node in the Meshtastic app

- Flash the official firmware if the board doesn't have it (Meshtastic's web flasher).

- Connect to it with the Meshtastic app and set Settings → LoRa → Region to your country's region. A node without a region doesn't transmit.

- Give both nodes the same modem preset (the default, Long Range - Fast, is fine), the same frequency slot and the same primary channel (channel 0). Leaving every node on the defaults does all of that.

- Check they hear each other: each node should list the other in its node list, and a text sent from one reaches the other.

- Disconnect the Meshtastic app from the node: a node serves one app at a time.

#### Connect the node to RF Sentinel

- Sentinel Link screen → Meshtastic node → turn on Use a Meshtastic node.

- Tap Choose a node and pick yours from the list. If Android asks for a PIN, it's on the node's screen, or 123456.

- Start a scan. The status goes through "reading its settings…" and "adding the RFSentinel channel…" to "Meshtastic node · channel N, encrypted".

- Do the same on the other phone with its own node.

RF Sentinel adds a private channel named RFSentinel to an empty slot (1 to 7) of the node, with a key made from the group's key. It never sends on the primary channel 0 or a channel you set up, and never to Meshtastic's MQTT. Strangers' nodes may relay your packets but only see encrypted bytes. Within a minute of both phones scanning, the node line reads "heard X ago".

#### Settings on the Sentinel Link screen

| Setting | What it does |

| Alert for what they hear | Alerts for devices that arrive this way. Each path has its own switch, so the mesh can stay quiet while nearby phones still alert, or the reverse. |

| Send a packet every | 15 s to 5 min, 60 s by default. Watchlist matches go out sooner anyway. Shorter sends more devices but uses more air time on a mesh others share. |

| Hops | 1 by default: only nodes in range of yours pass it on. Raise it when your nodes reach each other only through other nodes (at most your node's own hop limit). |

| Channel slot on the node | Automatic takes the first empty slot. Pick a slot only if you want the channel in a particular place; a slot holding another channel is never changed. |

| Silence the node's buzzer | Turns off the node's buzzer, vibration and LED alerts; switched back on when you turn this off. The node may restart once. |

#### What gets through

A LoRa packet holds about 6 to 19 devices. Watchlist matches go first (within about 20 s, then every minute while heard), flagged devices every 3 minutes, everything else once and again every 15 minutes. Only devices heard in the last 2 minutes are sent, and whitelisted devices never. The receiving phone keeps them listed for 16 minutes. For the most complete picture, keep the sending phone's screen on: with the screen off Android allows only a few WiFi scans an hour.

### 4. Internet relay (phones anywhere)

Every phone of the group connects to the same MQTT broker. Packets are encrypted with the group's key before they leave the phone and go on a topic made from that key, so the broker only sees encrypted bytes, your IP address and when you send. It uses a few small packets a minute of mobile data and carries far more than LoRa: up to 8 packets every 5 seconds.

- Sentinel Link screen → Internet relay → turn on Use an MQTT broker.

- Broker: mqtts://broker.example.com (encrypted, port 8883 unless you add one) or mqtt://host:port (unencrypted: the username and password travel in clear, so only on a network you trust).

- Username and Password if the broker asks for them.

- Check the certificate: leave on. Turn it off only for your own broker with a self-signed certificate.

- Same broker on every phone, then start a scan: the status reads "Connected to HOST". Devices from the relay show under the Mesh chip.

#### Running your own broker

Any MQTT 3.1.1 broker works. With Mosquitto on a server you control, a minimal setup with a password and a TLS certificate (for example from Let's Encrypt) looks like this:
# /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/rfsentinel.conf
listener 8883
certfile /etc/letsencrypt/live/broker.example.com/fullchain.pem
keyfile /etc/letsencrypt/live/broker.example.com/privkey.pem
allow_anonymous false
password_file /etc/mosquitto/passwd

Create the user with mosquitto_passwd -c /etc/mosquitto/passwd sentinel, open port 8883 in the firewall, restart Mosquitto, and enter mqtts://broker.example.com with that username and password on every phone.

### 5. A phone that only watches

A phone left in the car or at home can show only what the others send: on its Sentinel Link screen, turn on Show only the other Sentinels. While it's in a group it stops its own Bluetooth, WiFi, cell tower, GPS spoofing and drone checks and the online aircraft and Waze feeds; your Settings stay as they are, and hardware plugged into it keeps working. Leave it off on the phones that do the detecting.

### 6. Check it works

- Members list on the Sentinel Link screen: each Sentinel shows how it's reached, "Linked now", "Over the mesh · last heard X ago" or "Over the internet relay · last heard X ago".

- Main list: rows from other phones carry a VIA badge with their name; the Sentinels chip filters Bluetooth ones, the Mesh chip mesh and relay ones.

- Something stuck? Every status line and its fix is in Sentinel Link troubleshooting.

### Q&A

Q: Does Sentinel Link need the internet?
A:

No. RF Sentinel's Bluetooth and Meshtastic links work without any network. Only the internet relay uses mobile data, and only if you turn it on.

Q: How many phones can be in a group?
A:

RF Sentinel links any number: each new phone joins from any phone already in the group, with the 6-digit code. Over Meshtastic, every extra phone adds packets to the same slow channel, so keep the interval at the default or longer with many phones.

Q: Can two phones share one Meshtastic node?
A:

No. A node talks to one RF Sentinel phone at a time over Bluetooth. Each phone that sends or receives over the mesh needs its own node.

Q: Is it safe to use Sentinel Link on a public Meshtastic mesh?
A:

Other nodes can relay RF Sentinel's packets, but they're encrypted twice, by the RFSentinel channel's key and by the group's key, both made from a key only your phones have. They do see that a node is sending, and when. Your packets also use shared air time, so don't set the interval shorter than you need.

Q: Can I use a public MQTT broker?
A:

It works, since RF Sentinel encrypts everything before it leaves the phone, but the broker's owner sees your IP address and when you send, and a public broker can go down or drop clients. Your own broker is better.

---

# Sentinel Link & Meshtastic Troubleshooting | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/sentinel-link-troubleshooting.html

Fix RF Sentinel's Sentinel Link: Bluetooth link, Meshtastic LoRa nodes and the MQTT relay. What every status line means and how to check two Meshtastic nodes hear each other.

rf_sentinel / guides / sentinel-link-troubleshooting

## Sentinel Link & Meshtastic troubleshooting

RF Sentinel's Sentinel Link shares what one phone detects with the others in its group, over Bluetooth nearby, Meshtastic LoRa nodes far away, or an MQTT broker over the internet. When devices don't show up on the other phone, the status lines on the Sentinel Link screen say where it stops. This page goes through each one.

### Start here

- Same version on every phone. Update all of them to the latest release. Mesh packets from a different packet version are counted as "from another group or version" and dropped. Mesh devices staying listed until the next resend needs 2.40.1 or later on the phone that receives them.

- A scan must run on every phone. Sentinel Link only shares while scanning ("Links while scanning - start a scan to share", "Starts while scanning").

- Open the Sentinel Link screen on both phones (Settings → Sentinel Link → Open Sentinel Link) and read the status under each section: the top line for Bluetooth, the line under Meshtastic node, the line under Internet relay. Compare the two phones: the tables below say what each line means.

- Know where each row on the list comes from (below): not everything on the watching phone comes from the other phone.

- Still stuck? Settings → External hardware → Export all hardware logs on both phones makes one text file each, with the Bluetooth link, Meshtastic node and internet relay logs (no server name or IP address). Attach them to a GitHub issue.

### What the list shows, and from where

| On the list | Comes from |

| VIA badge with a phone's name | Another phone of the group heard it. |

| Sentinels chip | Devices from phones linked over Bluetooth. |

| Mesh chip | Devices from phones reached over Meshtastic or the internet relay. |

| External chip, ESP32 / USB badges | This phone's own hardware. A Meshtastic node also reports the other Meshtastic nodes it hears over the air, including strangers' nodes miles away. Those are not from your other phone. |

| Cells, Aircraft | This phone's own cell modem and the online aircraft feeds. Never shared over Sentinel Link. |

To see only what the other phones send, turn on Show only the other Sentinels on the watching phone's Sentinel Link screen. While it's in a group, that phone stops its own Bluetooth, WiFi, cell tower, GPS spoofing and drone checks and the online aircraft and Waze feeds; your Settings stay as they are. Hardware plugged into it keeps working. Leave this switch off on the phone that does the detecting, or it has nothing to share.

The distance shown for a device heard by a Meshtastic node is a Bluetooth estimate and means nothing for LoRa.

### Bluetooth link (phones nearby)

| Status | What it means / what to do |

| Not linked yet | This phone isn't in a group. Tap Link up a Sentinel on one phone and Join a Sentinel on the other, close together, and confirm the same 6-digit code on both. |

| Different codes on the two phones | Tap Cancel on both and start again. A different code means the two phones didn't talk to each other directly. |

| Bluetooth sharing off | "Share over Bluetooth" is off. The Meshtastic and internet relay paths still work without it. |

| Sentinel Link · waiting for Sentinels | Sharing, but no linked phone is in Bluetooth range (about 10 to 30 m, less through walls). Normal when the other phone is far away and you use Meshtastic or the relay instead; turn "Share over Bluetooth" off to hide it. |

| Sentinel Link · N Sentinels linked | Working. Their devices show with VIA and under the Sentinels chip. |

| Sentinel Link: allow "Nearby devices" to link Sentinels | Android → Apps → RF Sentinel → Permissions → Nearby devices → Allow. |

| Sentinel Link: Bluetooth is off | Turn the phone's Bluetooth on. It is also how the phone talks to its Meshtastic node, so turning Bluetooth off cuts the mesh too. |

| Sentinel Link: Bluetooth link failed to start | Turn Bluetooth off and on, then stop and start the scan. |

### Meshtastic node: connecting

Each phone needs its own Meshtastic node (a LoRa board with the official firmware), paired over Bluetooth. A node serves one app at a time: while RF Sentinel uses it, the Meshtastic app on that phone can't, and the other way round.

| Status under Meshtastic node | What it means / what to do |

| Off / Choose a node | Turn on Use a Meshtastic node and tap Choose a node. |

| Starts while scanning | Start a scan. |

| not paired - tap here to pair | Tap the line. Android asks for a PIN: it's on the node's screen, or 123456. |

| pairing - enter the PIN Android asks for | Finish the PIN prompt in Android's notification or dialog. |

| allow "Nearby devices" / Bluetooth is off | As for the Bluetooth link above. |

| choose the node again | The saved node is gone (unpaired or reset). Tap Choose a node. |

| connecting… / can't connect / no answer - retrying / stopped answering - retrying | Close the Meshtastic app (it may hold the node), keep the node powered and within a few metres, and make sure it isn't connected to another phone. It retries by itself. |

| not a Meshtastic node | The board chosen doesn't run Meshtastic's firmware. Choose the right one. |

| restarted - retrying | The node rebooted (it can happen once after changing its settings). Wait. |

| set its LoRa region in the Meshtastic app first | A new node has no region and won't transmit. Stop the scan, set the region in the Meshtastic app (Settings → LoRa → Region), then start the scan again. |

| its LoRa transmit is off | Turn "Transmit enabled" back on in the Meshtastic app (Settings → LoRa). |

| no free channel - free one in the Meshtastic app | Channel slots 1 to 7 are all in use. RF Sentinel only takes an empty slot or its own RFSentinel channel; delete a channel you don't need. |

| channel N is in use - pick another slot | The slot chosen under Channel slot holds a channel you set up. Pick another slot or "automatic". |

| couldn't add the RFSentinel channel | The node refused the change. Restart the node, then the scan. |

| channel N, encrypted | Connected and ready. Now see whether packets get through. |

### Meshtastic: nothing arrives on the other phone

Once connected, the node line adds "sent X ago" when this phone hands a packet to its node, and what the node has received. Read it on both phones:

| The line says | Where it stops |

| · nothing heard yet | This node hasn't received any packet from any other node since it connected. Its radio isn't reaching the mesh: see the radio checks. |

| · nothing from the group yet (the node hears other traffic) | The node's radio works (it hears other nodes) but nothing from your other phone's node arrives. Check the other node's line, then the radio checks on both nodes. |

| · heard X ago | Packets from the group arrive. If devices are still missing, see only some devices arrive. |

| · N from another group or version | Packets on the RFSentinel channel that this phone can't open: the phones aren't in the same group, or they run different versions. Update both; if it keeps counting, leave the group on one phone and join again from the other (Bluetooth, close together). |

| · N too old (check the phones' clocks) | Packets more than 15 minutes off this phone's clock are refused (so they can't be replayed). Set both phones to automatic date and time. |

"Sent" means the phone handed the packet to its node over Bluetooth. Whether the node transmits it, and whether the other node hears it, is up to the radios.

### Meshtastic: radio checks

Stop the scan in RF Sentinel on both phones (or turn off "Use a Meshtastic node"), open the Meshtastic app, and compare the two nodes:

- Antenna screwed on firmly. A node without its antenna barely hears anything, and transmitting without one can damage the radio.

- Settings → LoRa: same Region, same Modem preset (for example Long Range - Fast), same Frequency slot, and transmit enabled. Nodes with a different preset or slot are on another frequency or speed and never hear each other.

- Primary channel (channel 0): same name and key on both. With the frequency slot at 0, Meshtastic picks the frequency from the primary channel's name, so a renamed primary channel moves the node to another frequency. RF Sentinel never touches channel 0.

- Do they see each other? Each node should list the other in the node list with a recent "heard" time and a signal reading. Send a text from one to the other on the primary channel. If that fails, RF Sentinel can't get through either: it's the radios, the settings or the distance.

- Not too close, not too far. Two nodes side by side (under a metre) can overload each other's receivers: keep them a few metres apart. Far apart, LoRa range depends on height and terrain; a node indoors or in a pocket reaches much less.

- Hops (Sentinel Link screen): 1 means only nodes in range of yours pass it on. If your nodes only reach each other through other nodes, raise it to the number of hops between them.

When the text gets through, start RF Sentinel again on both phones. Within a minute the line should change to "heard X ago".

### Meshtastic: only some devices arrive

LoRa is slow. Each packet is at most 233 bytes and carries the phone's position and as many devices as fit: about 6 to 19, fewer with long names or matches. One packet goes out per interval (60 s by default, 15 s at the fastest on the Send a packet every slider). Devices take turns:

- Watchlist matches first, within about 20 s, then every minute while heard.

- Flagged devices next, every 3 minutes.

- Everything else once, then every 15 minutes, newest first. 40 ordinary devices take a few packets, so a few minutes at the default interval.

- Only devices the sending phone heard in the last 2 minutes go out. Whitelisted (trusted) devices are never sent.

- The receiving phone keeps a device heard over the mesh for 16 minutes, until the sender's next repeat (2.40.1 and later). Older versions dropped it after about a minute, so only the last packet or two showed.

If devices still go missing:

- Keep the sending phone's screen on, RF Sentinel open. With the screen off, Android allows an app only a few WiFi scans an hour, so the sender hears few networks and has little to send. Bluetooth is limited too.

- Lower the interval on the sending phone (15 s sends 4 times more than the default). More packets use more air time, which a busy public mesh shares with everyone.

- Check the sending phone has the devices: its own list should show them, and "Show only the other Sentinels" must be off there.

### Internet relay (MQTT)

| Status under Internet relay | What it means / what to do |

| Off | Turn on Use an MQTT broker on every phone of the group. |

| Set the broker | Enter the broker's address, the same on every phone. |

| Not a broker address | Write it as mqtts://host (encrypted, port 8883) or mqtt://host:port. |

| Starts while scanning | Start a scan. |

| Connecting to HOST… | Wait; if it stays there, the phone has no internet or the broker is down. |

| Can't reach HOST - …, retrying | Wrong host or port, the broker is down, or the network blocks the port. With mqtts:// and Check the certificate on, a self-signed certificate is refused: use a real certificate, or turn the check off only on a broker you run yourself. |

| The broker refused the username or password | Fix the username and password on that phone. |

| The broker refused the connection (code N) | The broker turned the client away for another reason (see its log). |

| Connected to HOST | Working. Devices from the relay show with VIA and under the Mesh chip. Packets are encrypted with the group's key: the broker only sees encrypted data. |

### Q&A

Q: RF Sentinel says "sent" over Meshtastic but the other phone shows nothing. Why?
A:

"Sent" only means RF Sentinel handed the packet to the phone's own node. Read the node line on the receiving phone: "nothing heard yet" means its node hears no LoRa traffic at all, "nothing from the group yet" means it hears other nodes but not yours. In both cases the two nodes aren't reaching each other: check the antennas, that both use the same region, modem preset, frequency slot and primary channel, and send a text between them in the Meshtastic app (radio checks).

Q: Why do only a few of the other phone's devices come through Meshtastic?
A:

LoRa carries one small RF Sentinel packet per interval (60 s by default), so devices take turns: watchlist matches, then flagged devices, then everything else, once and again every 15 minutes. Only devices heard in the last 2 minutes are sent, and a sending phone with its screen off scans WiFi only a few times an hour. Update both phones to 2.40.1 or later (devices then stay listed until the next resend), keep the sender's screen on, and lower the interval to 15 s (details).

Q: Why does RF Sentinel list Meshtastic nodes I don't own?
A:

Your Meshtastic node reports the other nodes it hears over the air, and RF Sentinel lists them as external hardware (ESP32 badge, External chip), like any other radio around you. They can be miles away. They don't come from your other phone; those show with a VIA badge under the Mesh chip.

Q: How do I see only what the other phone detects?
A:

On the watching phone, open RF Sentinel's Settings → Sentinel Link → Open Sentinel Link and turn on Show only the other Sentinels. It turns off that phone's own scans and online feeds while it's in a group, without changing your Settings. Hardware plugged into it keeps working. Leave the switch off on the phone that does the detecting.

Q: Sentinel Link says "waiting for Sentinels". Is something wrong?
A:

No. In RF Sentinel it means Bluetooth sharing is on but no linked phone is in Bluetooth range. If the other phone is far away and you use Meshtastic or the internet relay, turn "Share over Bluetooth" off; the other paths keep working.

Q: What does "too old (check the phones' clocks)" mean?
A:

RF Sentinel's mesh packets carry the time they were sent. A packet more than 15 minutes off the receiving phone's clock is refused, so an old packet can't be replayed. Set both phones to automatic date and time.

---

# Smart Glasses Detector: Ray-Ban Meta & More | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/smart-glasses-detector.html

RF Sentinel detects Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, Snap Spectacles, Vuzix and HeyCyan camera glasses nearby from their Bluetooth signals on Android. Free, open source, no root.

rf_sentinel / guides / smart-glasses-detector

## Smart glasses detector

Camera glasses keep a Bluetooth LE link to their phone app and advertise while worn. Their company IDs and service UUIDs give them away, and RF Sentinel matches them.

### How camera glasses give themselves away

Smart glasses with a camera stay paired to a phone app (Meta AI for Ray-Ban and Oakley Meta, Snapchat for Spectacles, Vuzix's own app) so photos and videos can sync. To keep that link, they advertise over Bluetooth Low Energy while worn: a short radio packet several times a second that any phone nearby can receive.

RF Sentinel listens to those packets passively. It never connects to the glasses and never sends anything to them. Each packet carries identifiers registered with the Bluetooth SIG: a company ID in the manufacturer data and sometimes a service UUID. Those identifiers belong to the glasses' maker, so they name the product even when the device's name and address are hidden or change.

### Detection rules

| Glasses | Identifier | Score |

| Ray-Ban Meta (Luxottica) | Company ID 0x0D53 | 70 |

| Ray-Ban / Oakley Meta | Company ID 0x058E with the META_RB_GLASS token only | 72 |

| Snap Spectacles | Company ID 0x03C2 or service UUID 0xFE45 | 70 |

| Vuzix | Company ID 0x060C | 70 |

| HeyCyan SDK glasses | UUID 7905FFF0-B5CE-4E99-A40F-4B1E122D00D0, full 16-byte match | 68 |

| Meta (corporate) | Company ID 0x01AB, UUID 0xFEB7 / 0xFEB8 | 45, Quest headsets share it |

0x058E alone is deliberately not matched: Quest headsets use it too. The HeyCyan rule needs all 16 bytes because Apple's notification service UUID differs from it by only two.

### What the score means

Scores of 50 and above are probable matches and alert with the default settings; the product-specific rules above (68 to 72) all land there. The generic Meta rule scores 45, a weak match: it shows in the list with a "verify" label but doesn't alert unless you lower the alert threshold in Settings, because a Quest headset in the next car would trigger it too.

### Finding the glasses

- Signal and distance: each match shows its signal strength and a rough distance. Bluetooth from glasses usually reaches a few metres to a few tens of metres, depending on walls and bodies in between.

- Locate mode: open the device and turn on Locate; it beeps faster as you walk closer.

- Look for the LED: Ray-Ban Meta and Spectacles light a capture LED while recording. RF Sentinel can tell you glasses are near, not whether they are recording.

### Limits

- Glasses that are off, folded and asleep, or charging in their case usually stop advertising, so they can't be heard.

- Glasses connected to their phone may advertise less often; keep scanning for a minute in a room before concluding none are there.

- Camera glasses without Bluetooth, or models not in the table, aren't detected. New identifiers can be added to your watchlist or reported on GitHub.

- A match means the hardware is nearby, not who is wearing it.

### Questions

Q: Does a match mean I'm being recorded?
A:

No. RF Sentinel's alert means camera glasses are nearby and advertising. Recording state isn't broadcast; look for the capture LED.

Q: Will it see glasses that are folded or in their case?
A:

Usually not, for RF Sentinel or any scanner: glasses stop advertising when off or charging in the case.

Q: Does it need root or a special phone?
A:

No. RF Sentinel uses Android's normal Bluetooth LE scanning on any phone with Android 8.0 or later. It also merges detections from an ESP32 board running OUI-Spy if you connect one.

Q: Why did a Meta Quest headset show up?
A:

Quest headsets use the same Meta company ID as the glasses. RF Sentinel keeps that rule as a weak match for that reason; the stronger Ray-Ban and Oakley rules only match the glasses.

Q: Is there an app that detects Meta Ray-Ban glasses nearby?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel recognises Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles, Vuzix and HeyCyan from their Bluetooth signals on Android. It shows that glasses are nearby, not whether they are recording.

---

## SØPHIA alternative

### Questions

Q: Is there a free version of s0phia ops / SØPHIA?
A:

SØPHIA is sold by its developer and isn't distributed here. If you're looking for a free app that does the same kind of passive Bluetooth and WiFi recon, RF Sentinel is free and open source: no payment, no account, and every line of code is public.

Q: What's the best open-source app like SØPHIA for Android?
A:

RF Sentinel: a GPL-3.0 Android app with a radar view, passive BLE and WiFi scanning, tracker follow alerts and hidden-camera checks like SØPHIA, plus sourced police body cam, Flock ALPR, patrol-vehicle, Remote ID drone and fake cell tower detection, an offline camera map, Android Auto and ESP32 support.

Q: Can I run RF Sentinel and SØPHIA together?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel and SØPHIA both only listen, so they don't interfere, though Android shares one WiFi scan budget between apps (about four scans per two minutes).
