# Speed Camera & Red-Light Camera Alerts for Android, Offline
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/speed-camera-alerts.html

Free speed camera, red-light camera and plate-reader alerts for Android, offline from OpenStreetMap and DeFlock: which way each camera faces, routes that avoid them, Android Auto.

rf_sentinel / guides / speed-camera-alerts

## Speed camera & red-light camera alerts

RF Sentinel keeps a map of known speed, red-light and plate-reader cameras on the phone and warns before each one, offline, with no account and no reporting. Its built-in navigation can also plan a route around them.

### Where the cameras come from

- Speed and red-light cameras: fixed cameras mapped in OpenStreetMap, with the speed limit when it's mapped.

- Plate readers (ALPR, Flock): DeFlock's hourly snapshot of OpenStreetMap, plus cameras it leaves out, straight from OpenStreetMap.

- Download cameras around me (Settings → Known cameras) fetches them within your radius (10-200 km, 100 by default); US & Canada plate cameras fetches every plate reader mapped in both countries (~18 MB, refreshed weekly on WiFi).

- Everything is kept on the phone: the warnings work with no signal.

### How the warnings work

- A speed or red-light camera warns about 30 seconds ahead at your speed, a plate reader about 20 seconds ahead.

- Where the direction is mapped, a cone shows which way the camera faces, and a camera watching a cross street doesn't warn.

- Known cameras raise the threat headline as you get closer (strong within 50 m, fading out by 500 m).

- Spoken alerts can be short: "Speed camera, 50". Alerts play through the car speakers in Android Auto, and over Waze or Google Maps through the floating bubble.

- Tap a camera → Ignore alerts to never hear about it again, or Set direction when its direction isn't mapped (kept on your phone only).

### Routes that avoid cameras

Turn-by-turn navigation is built in. Avoid speed cameras and Avoid plate readers plan the route around the known cameras: the route is asked for, the cameras on it are found, the road each one is on is left out and the route is asked for again, until none is left or there is no way round. Each route says what is left on it ("no plate readers", "2 speed cameras"), and the fastest one stays on offer to compare. A camera at the start or end, or on the only bridge, can't be avoided and is counted. It also works when you are re-routed and in Android Auto. Routes come from Valhalla on OpenStreetMap data; there is no live traffic.

### CCTV map layer

Optional (Settings → Known cameras → Show CCTV cameras, off by default): street, shop and building cameras mapped in OpenStreetMap, with a shaded view cone where the direction is mapped. Map only, no alerts: most are wired, so no scanner can detect them.

### Cameras it hears, not just maps

Flock plate readers also broadcast WiFi and Bluetooth, so RF Sentinel can detect one that isn't on any map. See the Flock camera detector. Speed cameras don't broadcast anything a phone can identify, so for them the map is the only source. Mobile speed traps reported by other drivers can come from Waze reports (optional).

### Questions

Q: Does the speed camera warning work offline?
A:

Yes. Once RF Sentinel has downloaded the cameras of your area, they are kept on the phone and every warning is computed there. Only the download (Overpass API, DeFlock) needs internet, and it sends the area, never what you scan.

Q: Does it detect mobile speed traps and police radar?
A:

Not by radio: RF Sentinel can't hear them, as police radar guns work on microwave bands a phone can't receive. Mobile traps reported by drivers can come in through the optional Waze reports, and police cars carrying Bluetooth and WiFi gear are picked up by the police detector.

Q: Are speed camera alerts legal?
A:

It depends on the country. Some countries (France and Germany, for example) restrict apps that warn about traffic enforcement while driving. In RF Sentinel you can turn each camera kind off in Settings. Check the law where you drive.

Q: What's a free speed camera app for Android with no ads?
A:

RF Sentinel is free and open source: offline speed camera, red-light camera and plate-reader alerts from OpenStreetMap and DeFlock, aware of which way each camera faces, with routes that avoid them and Android Auto support. No account, no ads, no analytics.

---

# Free Tetra Hunter Alternative: TETRA Detector | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/tetra-hunter-alternative.html

RF Sentinel is a free, open-source Tetra Hunter alternative for Android: detect TETRA radios on 380-385 MHz with one, two or three RTL-SDRs, plus police and camera detection.

rf_sentinel / guides / tetra-hunter-alternative

## Tetra Hunter alternative

Tetra Hunter is a paid Android app that uses two RTL-SDR dongles to detect TETRA radios, the encrypted digital radios emergency services carry in much of Europe. RF Sentinel detects TETRA radios the same way for free, with its full source on GitHub: one dongle to start, a second or third to watch the band nonstop, and police, camera and tracker detection on top.

### Side by side

| | RF Sentinel | Tetra Hunter |

| Price | Free, no ads, no account | Subscription: about €30 for 6 months, €50 a year or €90 lifetime |

| License | GPL-3.0, full source on GitHub | Closed source |

| Dongles | Works with one RTL-SDR; a second (and third) watches the TETRA band nonstop | Two RTL-SDRs |

| TETRA burst detection | Yes, by the time-slot rhythm, 380-385 MHz | Yes |

| Signal meter | TETRA bar on the main screen: Far / Closer / Very close, with a getting-closer arrow | Yes |

| Beeps that speed up when closer | Yes | Yes |

| City / highway mode | City mode (a stronger signal needed) | Yes |

| TETRA only mode | Yes: every dongle on 380-385 MHz | Dedicated app |

| Other police bands (P25, DMR, NXDN, 700 / 800 MHz) | Yes, with an SDR | See vendor |

| Police body cams, Flock ALPR, patrol vehicles over Bluetooth / WiFi | Yes, no SDR needed | See vendor |

| Speed and ALPR camera map | Yes, offline | Speed cameras (from V1.9) |

| Android Auto | Yes | See vendor |

| Decodes TETRA / breaks encryption | No: energy and timing only | No |

Tetra Hunter details come from its public pages at the time of writing; "see vendor" means we couldn't verify it. RF Sentinel is independent and not affiliated with Tetra Hunter or its developer.

### Hunting TETRA radios with RF Sentinel

- Plug an RTL-SDR (RTL-SDR Blog V3 or V4) into the phone with a USB OTG adapter and turn on Detect TETRA radios in Settings → RTL-SDR radio.

- For nonstop watching, add a second RTL-SDR through a powered USB hub. It watches 380-385 MHz while the first keeps sweeping; a third splits the band with it (380-382.4 and 382.6-385 MHz). The status line shows what each one watches.

- Antenna: a vertical whip about 19.5 cm long (a quarter wave), on the roof if you can. Two dongles share one antenna through a 2-way splitter.

- Turn on TETRA only to put every dongle on the TETRA band, and City mode in towns full of radios.

- While a radio is heard, the TETRA bar on the main screen shows how strong it is (Far / Closer / Very close) and the beeps speed up as you get closer.

Every setting is explained in the RTL-SDR guide.

### Questions

Q: Is there a free alternative to Tetra Hunter?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel is free and open source (GPL-3.0): no subscription, no account. With an RTL-SDR dongle it watches the TETRA handset band (380-385 MHz) for the time-slot bursts TETRA radios send, and with a second or third dongle it watches that band nonstop.

Q: How does a TETRA detector work?
A:

TETRA handsets and car radios transmit on 380-385 MHz in short time slots: a burst of about 14 ms every 57 ms. RF Sentinel measures the energy on each 12.5 kHz channel and reports only bursts with that rhythm, so plain carriers and other radios don't count. It doesn't decode anything, and TETRA's encryption isn't touched.

Q: What hardware do I need?
A:

For RF Sentinel, an Android phone with USB OTG and one RTL-SDR dongle (an RTL-SDR Blog V3 or V4, for example) is enough to start. For hunting, add a second dongle on a powered USB hub: it watches the band nonstop while the first keeps sweeping the other bands. Use a vertical antenna about 19.5 cm long, on the roof if you can; two dongles can share it through a 2-way splitter.

Q: Does it work in France or Switzerland?
A:

No, RF Sentinel doesn't, and neither does Tetra Hunter: those countries use TETRAPOL, a different system. TETRA detection works where emergency services use TETRA on 380-385 MHz, which covers most of Europe and many other countries.

---

# AirTag, Tracker & Car-Following Detector for Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/tracker-detector.html

Is an AirTag or a car following you? RF Sentinel finds AirTags, SmartTags, Tile, Chipolo and Find Hub tags on Android, locates them, and spots cars by their tire sensors.

rf_sentinel / guides / tracker-detector

## AirTag & tracker detection

Bluetooth trackers away from their owner change what they broadcast. RF Sentinel catches that frame, follows the tag through its address rotations, and tells you when it has been travelling with you.

### What a separated tracker looks like

| Tracker | Separated frame | Score |

| Apple AirTag / Find My accessories | Manufacturer data, company 0x004C, type 0x12, length 0x19 | 70 |

| Google Find Hub tags | Service data 0xFEAA, frame 0x41 (0x40 = near owner, ignored) | 70 |

| Samsung SmartTag | Service data 0xFD5A | 55 |

| Tile | Service data 0xFEED | 55 |

| Chipolo | Service UUID 0xFE33 (even when the tag broadcasts no name) | 55 |

### Follow detection

Trackers rotate their Bluetooth address to stay anonymous. RF Sentinel links the new address to the old one by an advert fingerprint (payload sizes, UUIDs, TX power, connectable flag; new address within 1.5-30 s of the old one going silent, exactly one candidate) and carries the time-with-you and GPS path across. A FOLLOWING alert fires once a tracker or flagged device has stayed with you for at least 10 minutes while you moved at least 800 m. Both are adjustable (2-240 minutes).

### Finding the tag

- Tap the device → Locate. The beep rate rises with signal strength, and it keeps following the tag when the tag changes its address. Open the map and a live read card shows the signal, rough distance and whether you're getting closer.

- Walk around the car or bag; RSSI changes fast within the last metre.

- Check the signal graph and history on the detail screen to see when it first appeared.

### A car following you: tire-pressure sensors

With an RTL-SDR on the phone (Settings → RTL-SDR radio), RF Sentinel decodes the 315 and 433.92 MHz tire-pressure sensors (TPMS) in car wheels, which each send an ID. The same car's sensors heard with you at place after place means a vehicle following you. Your own car's sensors are learned first and never alert. A tire sensor heard together with a flagged Bluetooth device again after a gap, or across 3 places 2 km apart, ties them to one vehicle (kept 30 days, never backed up). Decoders follow rtl_433. See the RTL-SDR guide.

Without an SDR, a flagged device or tracker that keeps turning up at 3 or more places along your way within 2 hours also raises may be following you, even with gaps between.

### Your own tags

Long-press your own AirTag or SmartTag and ignore it. The ignore follows it through address changes, so it stays quiet.

### Questions

Q: Android already has unknown tracker alerts. Why use this?
A:

Android's alerts are good but run on Google's schedule and thresholds and show little detail. RF Sentinel shows trackers live, with raw evidence, signal history, the path they followed and adjustable thresholds, alongside everything else around you.

Q: Why don't I see AirTags that are with their owners?
A:

Near its owner an AirTag broadcasts a different, shorter frame and isn't a threat to you. RF Sentinel only flags the separated frame, so people's own keys in a café don't alert.

Q: What about LTE GPS trackers?
A:

RF Sentinel can't see them: they report over the cellular network and broadcast no Bluetooth a phone can identify. Inspect the vehicle physically.

Q: How do I detect an AirTag on Android?
A:

Install RF Sentinel and start scanning. It lists AirTags away from their owners as soon as it hears them, alerts when one stays with you, and its Locate beeps faster as you get closer to the tag.

Q: Is Apple's Tracker Detect app enough on Android?
A:

Apple's Tracker Detect scans only when you ask it to, and only for Find My items. RF Sentinel scans in the background and covers AirTags, Samsung SmartTags, Tile, Chipolo and Find Hub tags, with follower alerts and a Locate screen.

Q: Can I find lost Bluetooth earbuds or a lost tag with my phone?
A:

Often, if it still has battery and is advertising. Open it from RF Sentinel's nearby devices list and tap Locate: the beeps speed up as the signal gets stronger, and it keeps following the device when it changes its address.

# Fewer False Alerts: Tuning RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/tuning-guide.html

Cut false alerts in RF Sentinel: alert threshold, whitelist rules, Ignore all like this, ignoring your own tracker, marking false alerts, and how long devices stay listed.

rf_sentinel / guides / tuning-guide

## Fewer false alerts

RF Sentinel errs on the side of warning you. A few minutes of tuning keeps the alerts that matter and silences your own devices, your neighbour's printer and the bus stop's screens. Everything here can be undone.

### Where to start

- Turn off what you don't need: Settings → What to detect. Each kind of equipment has its own switch. Network / home cameras are off by default because they alert everywhere.

- Raise the threshold: Settings → Alerts → "Alert for matches that are at least": Weak alerts on every match, Probable on most, Strong only on near-certain ones. Matches below it still show on the list, flagged, without the alert.

- Silence one device or one kind from the list: long-press the row (below).

- Space out repeats: Settings → Alerts → "Re-alert the same device after".

### Long-press a device

Long-press any row on the list for these. Each one shows an Undo right away.

| Choice | Use it for |

| Whitelist (trust & ignore) | Your own devices and fixed things you know. Trusted devices are never logged, flashed or alerted on. The dialog asks how wide: only this device, every device by the same maker, every address starting the same way, every name starting with or containing a text (handy for a whole network's access points), the same Bluetooth advert pattern, or the same probe fingerprint. |

| Ignore all like this | Every device matched as the same thing (for example every "Zebra printer"), even ones you haven't met yet. It warns you when the match is police or emergency equipment. |

| Ignore this tracker… | Your own AirTag or tag. Its address changes about once a day, so it can't be whitelisted: choose "It's mine" (the app follows it across address changes, best effort), "today only", or pause all tracker follow warnings for 24 h. Only ignore a tag you know: a hidden tracker would stay silent too. |

| False alert… | A match that's wrong. Its alerts are muted, and it's saved under History → False alerts with an optional note on what it really is, so you can export it and help fix the signature. |

| Add to favorites ★ | Devices you want to keep an eye on: they stay on the list longer. |

A whitelisted device still shows on the list by default. To leave them off the list and radar too: Settings → Scanning → Hide trusted devices (they stay in the history).

### Changing your mind

- Whitelist and rules: Settings → Lists, tools & about → Whitelist. "Ignore all like this" rules are under Rules.

- Network names you whitelisted: Settings → Lists, tools & about → Ignored network names.

- Ignored trackers: Settings → Trackers & followers → Clear ignored trackers, or long-press the tracker → Stop ignoring this tracker.

- False alerts: long-press the device → Remove from false alerts, or open History → False alerts.

### Follow warnings

Settings → Trackers & followers → "Warn when a device moves with me", for at least a time and over a distance you set. In a car, a short time warns about every device stuck in the same traffic; a longer one (and a longer distance) keeps only what really follows you.

### How long devices stay on the list

Settings → Scanning has one slider per source: how long a device stays on the list and radar after it was last heard.

| Slider | Default | Notes |

| Bluetooth | 30 s | Down to 5 s. |

| WiFi | 60 s | Below 30 s only with "Wi-Fi scan throttling" off in Android's Developer options. |

| External hardware | 60 s | Devices heard only by an ESP32 board or a USB WiFi adapter. |

| Other Sentinels | 16 min | Devices another phone sent over Meshtastic or the internet relay. The sender repeats each one about every 15 minutes, so a shorter time empties the list between repeats. A device this phone hears itself follows its own slider. |

Favourite and following devices stay 3 minutes. A flagged device stays as long as it's in range and alerting.

### Quieter alerts, same detection

- Settings → Alerts: alert sound, volume and which audio stream it plays on, vibration (1 pulse weak, 2 probable, 3 strong), and the optional radar-detector beeps.

- Settings → Voice: what gets spoken, and how short.

- P25 and pager alerts each have their own Sound / Voice chips in Settings → RTL-SDR radio (RTL-SDR guide).

- Waze reports: Settings → What to detect → the alert distance, and "Only alert for reports ahead" while you drive.

### Q&A

Q: Can I whitelist a police device that's always parked near my home?
A:

Yes, in RF Sentinel, with "Only this device". Avoid "Ignore all like this" for police or emergency equipment: it would also silence every other one, everywhere. The app warns you before saving such a rule.

Q: I whitelisted a phone and it came back. Why?
A:

Most phones change their Bluetooth and WiFi address every few minutes or hours. To RF Sentinel, a new address is a new device. Use a wider rule if one fits (same name, same advert pattern), or leave ordinary phones alone: they don't alert unless they match something.

---

# Waze Police Alerts with Sound & Voice on Android | RF Sentinel
URL: https://cis-c0.github.io/RFSentinel/waze-police-alerts.html

Get Waze police reports as loud alerts on Android: alert range you choose, only reports on your road ahead, spoken call-outs at 1 km, 500 m and 200 m, Android Auto. Optional, free.

rf_sentinel / guides / waze-police-alerts

## Waze police alerts, louder and sooner

RF Sentinel can pull the police reports Waze users post near you and turn them into real alerts: sound, voice and the car speakers, only for reports on your road ahead, next to what the app hears itself. Optional and off by default.

### Two ways to get the reports

| Source | What it needs | What it sends |

| Waze direct | Nothing: no key, free. Opt-in. | An anonymous Waze account made on the phone sends Waze (Google) your IP address and a position rounded to a 1 km grid. |

| OpenWeb Ninja | Your own API key (billed per check by OpenWeb Ninja) | Waze never sees you; OpenWeb Ninja gets the area. |

Both are third-party services RF Sentinel isn't affiliated with; use them at your own risk.

### What you get

- Police reports, and any other kind you tick: accidents, hazards, road closures, traffic jams. Each kind has its own level: sound and voice, notification only, or silent.

- What Waze says it is: hiding, mobile speed camera and so on.

- Alert range from 100 m to 10 km, and a separate map range.

- Only alert for reports ahead: checked against the map's roads, so a parallel road, a cross street, an overpass or a report behind you stays quiet. While you are guided to a destination, only reports on the part of the route still ahead count.

- Spoken call-outs at 1 km, 500 m and 200 m as a report gets closer.

- Reports are scored by distance, age and driver confirmations and re-scored every second as you move, so the alert fires the moment a report comes into range, not at the next check.

- How often Waze is asked: 15 s to 5 min (direct) or 2 to 10 min (OpenWeb Ninja), slower when parked and faster on fast roads.

- In the car: alerts through the car speakers with Android Auto, a Waze chip on the live list, and the floating bubble over the Waze app itself.

### Why combine both

Waze only knows what other drivers reported. RF Sentinel's police detector hears the equipment itself (body cams, in-car routers, radios), even where nobody reported anything. With both on, one list and one alert voice cover both.

### Questions

Q: Can I get louder Waze police alerts on Android?
A:

Yes. With Waze reports on, each police report becomes an RF Sentinel alert: a sound, an optional spoken call-out, a voice boost up to +15 dB, and an option to pause music while it's spoken. It plays through the car speakers too.

Q: Do I need a Waze account?
A:

No. RF Sentinel's Waze direct makes an anonymous account on the phone by itself (stored encrypted). With OpenWeb Ninja, Waze isn't contacted at all.

Q: Can I keep using the Waze app at the same time?
A:

Yes. RF Sentinel runs in the background, and its floating bubble and mini map sit over Waze with a pop-up card saying what was just detected.
